ASRS:1840206.n: I was holding short of Runway XX at Taxiway XX at ZZZ preparing to take off, a PA18 made one radio call that they were entering a right base for Runway XX when left traffic is standard. I continued to hold short of the runway. Aircraft landed prior to the displaced threshold and runway, taxied to the runway entryway [Taxiway] XX and stopped nose to nose with my aircraft. Pilot made a motion with his hands that he wanted me to move out of his way so he could taxi past.
ASRS:1840206.s: A PA18 pilot entered a right base for Runway XX at ZZZ, contrary to standard left traffic, and landed prior to the displaced threshold. The pilot then taxied nose-to-nose with the reporter's aircraft and gestured for them to move to allow passage.

ASRS:1840211.n: While taxing to Runway XL, we encountered some COM issues. I did transmit over the ground frequency but they could not hear us. Upon reaching the hold Short Line for Runway XL, I was unable to stop the plane. The brake pedals lost complete pressure and I had no control over the plane. I immediately applied the parking brakes, however, the plane went past the hold short line and turned left into the grass. There was no damage to the plane, or any airport environment. Airport Personnel arrived and assisted me. They took down all my information and then towed me to the FBO. A local ground staff did check out the plane and confirmed that the brakes have failed and lost all pressure. I did inform the flight school and squawked the airplane for all the issues. There were no people harmed nor any damages reported.
ASRS:1840211.s: The pilot experienced communication issues and total brake pressure loss while taxiing to Runway XL, causing the aircraft to overrun the hold short line and enter the grass. Ground staff confirmed the brake failure, towed the undamaged aircraft to the FBO, and no injuries or environmental damage occurred.

ASRS:1840229.n: Cruising north from ZZZ1 at 4500 ft. MSL, I had just completed two take off and landings at ZZZ1. As we flew north (at approximately 340 degrees), 3-5 miles south of ZZZ2, I noticed that the dash lighting had begun to dim. Checked the amp/volt meter on the panel and noticed that voltage was at 12V and amps were reading -6.8 (from previous experience amperage runs at or close to 0 and volts run at about 28 volts). Noticed that the discharge light on the amp/voltage indicator was on. At this point, I cycled the alternator in the hope that doing that would solve the problem. I also verified that the breaker was still in. When the alternator was cycled and turned back on, the condition remained the same. At that point the GPS system shut off. Transponder was still functioning. At that point ZZZ Tower was called on the radio and the situation was described. ZZZ was told that we were unaware how much power remained to run the radio. At that point ZZZ Tower told me that our radio was cutting in and out. ZZZ was accommodating, they requested that we IDENT, they told me that they would contact ZZZ2 for us and clear all traffic for us enroute to ZZZ due to our NORDO condition. At that point we were also cleared to land on Runway XXL at ZZZ. During this time, the transponder showed an error message that it was not receiving power (or something to that effect), and I am not clear if the tower received the IDENT. Once permission to land was received (flying over ZZZ2) all unnecessary electrical systems (avionics, lights) were shut down to preserve any battery power needed for the radio once we neared ZZZ. Using major streets on the ground as checkpoints, we made our way to ZZZ. We flew left pattern to ZZZ and extended our downwind leg as we did not have adequate battery power to lower the flaps. On final approach attempted to turn the landing light on, however it did not come on. My flight companion had a flashlight throughout this so that we could monitor flight conditions on the panel (altitude, heading, etc.). As we came in for the flare we could not see the Runway centerline or the Runway number until just above the Runway (as it was dark and we had no lights). Touched down on the Runway XXL without incident and rolled down the Runway.At that point we turned on the radio and were able to communicate with ZZZ ground, their instructions were to take any Taxiway from the Runway. Exited at Taxiway XX However due to the closeness and the dim Taxiway/Runway lighting, inadvertently exited short and onto the grass separating Taxiway from Runway. Realized the error and my flying companion opened the window of the aircraft and used a flashlight to light up the Taxiway. Using the flashlight, we were able to make our way down the Taxiway until our parking area came into view. At that point we parked the aircraft and went to the gas shack at the FBO. Reported what had occurred to the fuel personnel and told them that the aircraft should not be put into service until maintenance had examined it. Next morning, first thing, I called the FBO and reported what had happened. They said that they had received the report from the fuel personnel and were in the process of canceling the morning's flights on the aircraft. I later received a call telling me that maintenance had discovered a wiring issue in the aircraft and that they were reconciling it.Just like to take the opportunity to mention that everything was executed well, the Tower was very helpful, we flew the plane without significant incident even though we had no functional electrical system. The only issue was that upon landing it was very difficult to negotiate the Runway/Taxiway due to dim lighting and faint Runway paint. The fact that the Runway and Taxiway lights are spaced the same also led to confusion as we were trying to negotiate them in the dark. After a difficult flight and a complicated landing, to think that negotiating the ground would be the most difficult part was stressful.
ASRS:1840229.s: The pilot experienced a total electrical failure due to a wiring issue while en route to ZZZ, resulting in NORDO conditions and a dark landing on Runway XXL. After a safe touchdown, the crew inadvertently exited onto the grass due to poor lighting but successfully taxied to parking using a flashlight.

ASRS:1840257.n: Training flight flying southbound along the beach at 3,500 straight and level. Started descending and right when we started descending a Piper aircraft climbed above us and missed us by 100-200 ft. Turned on my [software] after to get the traffic ADS-B on my iPad afterwards and found the tail number of the other aircraft involved to be Aircraft Y.
ASRS:1840257.s: During a southbound training flight at 3,500 feet, a Piper aircraft climbed above the reporting aircraft during descent, resulting in a 100–200 foot vertical separation. The reporter later identified the Piper as Aircraft Y using ADS-B software on an iPad.

ASRS:1840261.n: Name and I are both CFII's (Certified Flight Instructor Instrument). I was pilot flying, he was pilot monitoring. In the descent into ZZZ my flight instruments started reading erroneously- attitude indicator showed climbing left turn, altimeter and VSI showed descent, rate of turn showed wings level, heading indicator and mag compass showed present heading. Name and I decided to [advise ATC] and divert to an airport that reported VMC, asked for vectors to get out of IMC as quickly as possible. While diverting we decided the attitude indicator was reading incorrect, suction was within proper tolerances and heading indicator read correctly. We were able to land safely at an airport (ZZZ1) we are both very familiar with in VMC conditions. Left the plane overnight to take next steps in VFR day conditions. Two people on board. Two CFII's, I was monitoring the approach and not the pilot flying. In a descent into ZZZ, we had conflicting information on our instruments, eventually, we settled it was the attitude indicator that was not working properly. We were in hard IMC and we decided to request priority with ATC and ask for vectors out of IMC into VMC weather nearby. We then diverted to ZZZ1 which is a very familiar field for both of us. We landed safely in VMC conditions and left the plane there until a VFR flight can be conducted to check the airplane's instruments in VMC.
ASRS:1840261.s: Two CFII pilots experienced conflicting instrument readings during a descent into ZZZ, identifying a faulty attitude indicator while in IMC. They diverted to ZZZ1, landed safely in VMC, and left the aircraft for later inspection.

ASRS:1840278.n: I was returning from a pleasure flight from ZZZ to my home airport ZZZ1 and had joined Runway XX right downwind via the right 45. I had made all my radio calls: joining the right 45 Runway XX, established on the right 45 Runway XX, Right downwind XX, Right downwind abeam XX numbers. There were at least 2 other aircraft in the pattern and my pattern entry was quite seamless - I was careful to maintain the headings and altitudes - and monitor every other plane's position both on ADS-B and visually. Frankly, I think I did a very good job. As I was turning base, I made my radio call ('turning right base Runway XX') then I saw ***RIGHT IN FRONT ON ME***, at 11 o'clock, a Cessna 172 converging to me, same altitude, apparently on a dogleg to Runway XX. I took evasive action immediately by leveling off and stopping my turn. I think he missed me by less than 20 feet. It was incredibly close. Then I rejoined final, and went around. As I went around I saw the offending 172 landing in front of me. I vehemently asked for an explanation, as I was very shaken by what had happened. The 172 pilot finally replied and stated: 'This is an uncontrolled airport, I don't have to make radio calls'. I told him that he did something incredibly dangerous and we could have collided. He said again 'This is an uncontrolled airport, I don't have to make radio calls'. I rejoined the pattern and landed without incident.There is a lot to unpack here and I am still processing what happened. I can't see anything I could have done different. This individual had no ADS-B transponder and wasn't making any radio calls while landing at an airport with multiple aircraft in the traffic pattern.I find this absolutely unacceptable. The FAA needs to do something about this.
ASRS:1840278.s: The pilot reported a near-midair collision with a Cessna 172 while turning base at an uncontrolled airport. The other pilot, who lacked ADS-B and made no radio calls, converged at the same altitude, forcing evasive action and a go-around before the Cessna landed.

ASRS:1840281.n: Was in the in the flare to landing. Aircraft bounced once, increased angle of attack to arrest oscillation. On second touchdown, tail came down first and a loud snap was heard. Taxied off the runway and saw the damaged tail spring. It broke just at the top of the tail wheel head. Total time in service is 600 hours approximately.
ASRS:1840281.s: During the flare to landing, the aircraft bounced and touched down tail-first, causing a loud snap. The pilot taxied off the runway and found the tail spring broken at the top of the tail wheel head.

ASRS:1840291.n: Cleared for the ILS XXR into ZZZ. ZZZ was running simultaneous approaches to XXL as well at the time. We were established on the middle of the localizer for XXR inbound when an OAL I assume was supposed to be on XXL came over onto our course, and caused us to get an RA. We had to descend roughly 300-700 feet per the RA guidance to avoid the conflict.
ASRS:1840291.s: The crew, cleared for the ILS XXR approach into ZZZ, received a Resolution Advisory when an OAL aircraft on the simultaneous XXL approach crossed onto their localizer course. They descended 300–700 feet per RA guidance to avoid the conflict.

ASRS:1840299.n: What led to the event happening: I had just gotten back from leave. I worked the mid the night before after returning from that leave, and then had an OT shift to work an early morning. Traffic was fairly light, but complexity was fairly high due to multiple things happening all over the sector. The sector is fairly complex in that it requires changing transmitters and receivers constantly to talk to and hear aircraft in the sector. This sector often has a D side. My D side had just gone on break and the sector seemed to be fine, but then I was overcome with some additional challenges, and my D side returned from break right about as this situation was happening. Terrain in this sector is the highest in the center and it requires a lot of monitoring of aircraft to make sure they are meeting MIA's. We have been on 6 day work weeks for a long time due to the staffing issues FAA wide, but it definitely has impacted the moral and has exhausted myself. I was slightly blind-sided by the call from the aircraft due to no weather reports south of ZZZ1.As the complexity was rising in the sector due to multiple different situations, I had a departure aircraft of type I am not familiar, depart one of the busiest departure airports in our center. The aircraft was a slow climber and requested to deviate below the terrain. The call caught me off guard and I approved his request to deviate noticing the terrain close to him but not the MIA he was currently in. I approved a slight deviation to avoid the higher terrain to his right, and shortly after noticing my mistake, I corrected myself and asked the pilot to tell me the conditions (IFR/VFR) to see if that could save me, but then ultimately told him that I cannot approve his request to deviate below the terrain until he was above unless he was declaring an emergency. He said that he was not declaring an emergency and was correcting back on course. I then issued a proper clearance to deviate out of the MIA. The pilot had already turned off of the SID a few degrees before I caught the mistake and corrected it.-Hiring needs to improve in the FAA so that we are not working 6 day works weeks constantly and getting exhausted-Staffing needs to improve from hiring more people so that we can not be overcome with sick leave requests and the constant COVID happenstances that we are finding ourselves in today. There is a constant out flux of people due to sickness or the FAA medical office taking peoples medical clearances away even when they are not sick and are testing negative for COVID. -People are abusing the system most likely due to the two reasons above and are finding every way they can to get out of work because of the poor mental health and low staffing numbers that we are in every day. My recommendation is that the FAA fixes their hiring issues immediately so that more problems don't continue to arise from the extreme apparent staffing issues we are currently seeing.
ASRS:1840299.s: An exhausted air traffic controller, working a six-day week due to staffing shortages, initially approved a slow-climbing departure aircraft's request to deviate below terrain in a complex sector. The controller realized the error, revoked the clearance, and issued a proper deviation instruction after the pilot had already turned off the SID.

ASRS:1840314.n: Aircraft X in left closed traffic to runway XX. I gave Aircraft X traffic to follow, an E145, on final. When he reported the traffic in sight, I told him to follow that traffic and additional traffic was Aircraft Y on a 7 mile final. I was watching helicopter traffic on runway XY. I looked at Aircraft X and realized the sequence was not going to work. I cancelled Aircraft X approach clearance and gave him a 050 heading to clear him of the traffic on final. Aircraft Y called local control stating they are having a near miss with Aircraft X off their nose. I informed Aircraft Y it was Aircraft X, that was on a 050 heading and will continue on it. I should have extended Aircraft X on the downwind to follow Aircraft Y.
ASRS:1840314.s: An air traffic controller issued a 050 heading to Aircraft X to resolve a sequencing conflict with an E145 and Aircraft Y on final approach. Aircraft Y reported a near miss with Aircraft X, which the controller attributed to failing to extend Aircraft X on downwind.

ASRS:1840323.n: Approaching ZZZ on the ZZZZZ3 RNAV Arrival Runway XXR transition and while joining an approximate 20 mile final, ATC advised us of traffic joining the [Runway] XXL approach course. Traffic was in sight and within a few moments we received an RA command of 'Descend'. The First Officer, who was the Pilot Flying, disengaged the automation and complied with the RA. I advised ATC of the conflict and we continued our approach for XXR with autopilot/autothrottle disengaged. While continuing the approach, we heard an aircraft executing a 'Go-Around' on XXL due to windshear. The F/O (First Officer) and I communicated with one another to 'Be ready' in case windshear was encountered. During the approach I observed unremarkable wind speeds 7-15 knots, however, winds varied from direction as descent continued. The aircraft was fully configured and on airspeed well before 1,000 ft., landing clearance was received and the Before Landing Checklist complete. At the 500 ft. call, the traffic that we were following to XXR, had landed and was just clearing the runway. Light unremarkable turbulence was encountered during the approach with little fluctuations in airspeed until approximately 200 ft. AGL. At that point I felt the aircraft sink and observed what seemed to be an instantaneous decrease in airspeed. 'Pull Up' appeared on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and then I called 'Pull Up'.The F/O appeared to have observed the same warning and was initiating the escape maneuver. I called 'Windshear' and as pitch and power was applied, the aircraft performed as commanded. No change to configuration occurred until both the F/O and I agreed that the aircraft was no longer in jeopardy. A normal go-around procedure was then completed. ATC advised several aircraft (after our go-around) of 'Microburst Alert! Loss of 40 knots on short final'. ATC gave a frequency change to Departure Control, that neither the F/O nor I heard. After several minutes of distraction, ie. ACARS Dispatch for alternate, excessive radio traffic, communication with passengers, I contacted Tower and communication with Departure Control was attained. A divert plan was received from Dispatch, however, ATC advised that approaches and landings had resumed in ZZZ. Due to the lengthy delayed vectors, we determined that conditions had improved and enough fuel was on board, to attempt another approach and landing. A normal approach and landing was performed to Runway XXL in ZZZ.As a note, the F/O informed me of the two-tone aural alert and windshear warning. It's quite possible that when I said windshear it was due to what I saw on the PFD and or me repeating what was already said by the aircraft. The event happened so quickly I can't recall. We began our descent on the ZZZZZ 3 Arrival [Runway] XXR transition. As we approached the ZZZ terminal area ATC vectored us off the arrival with an intercept heading and cleared us for the visual approach to XXR. A descending RA ensued during LOC interception to XXR with the autopilot on. The conflict aircraft was in sight and I disconnected the automation and complied with the RA command. This lasted a few seconds and only descended a few 100 feet, whilst maintaining localizer centerline. Once the RA was clear we opted to continue the approach. As we were configuring on the visual approach to XXR we heard an aircraft transmitting to ATC that they were going around on XXL due to windshear. At that time we received no predictive windshear/or reactive windshear warnings and all indications in the flight deck seemed normal. In fact the aircraft we were following to XXR had not transmitted any adverse conditions as well. We continued fully configured by 1,000 ft. AGL to XXR.At approximately 150 ft. the aircraft felt as if it started to drop/fall and the Captain called 'Windshear' and a 'WINDSHEAR' warning followed. I performed the windshear escape maneuver. The threat only lasted what seemed like a few seconds and we were through the microburst. ATC then issued microburst warnings after our encounter. Once we were in the clear, we were vectored back to ZZZ for an approach to XXL. At that time the microburst was no longer a threat and three or four aircraft already landed XXL. We agreed that returning was the most viable option instead of diverting to ZZZ1. We landed with no further incident. It wasn't until we were getting vectored back to ZZZ that the Captain informed me that a PULL-UP was also received. During the event I did not hear or see a PULL-UP warning. I was so focused on not hitting the ground and executing a WINDSHEAR escape maneuver. Before the event we discussed the possibility of a windshear encounter due to the other aircraft go-around. So when the Captain and aircraft called windshear, windshear was on the forefront of my mind and a WINDSHEAR escape maneuver was executed.
ASRS:1840323.s: Pilots on a ZZZZZ3 arrival to Runway XXR encountered a microburst at 150 ft AGL, triggering windshear and pull-up warnings that necessitated a go-around. After ATC issued microburst alerts, the crew returned to land safely on Runway XXL once conditions improved.

ASRS:1840438.n: There was a possible revision made on the flight's Departure Staging Guide (DSTG) in which I was not made aware of. So the flight was finalized with the assumption that the load was unchanged.
ASRS:1840438.s: The pilot reported that a possible revision to the Departure Staging Guide (DSTG) was made without their knowledge. Consequently, the flight was finalized under the incorrect assumption that the load remained unchanged.

ASRS:1840440.n: I have been dealing with this issue with ZZZ for some weeks now they continue to stage cabin supplies using the AOG (Aircraft on Ground) code instead of the cabin code. I've sent several emails and have spoken with the ZZZ Cargo Supervisor and told them the correct way to stage their cabin supplies I've even emailed them DSTG's (Departure Staging Guide) from ZZZ1 and ZZZZ showing the correct way to stage the items but she refuses to use the correct code, so now I'm filing a report because this needs to stop. Not only is it wrong the ramp in ZZZ is looking for an AOG and they are calling to advise the item isn't AOG it is cabin supplies. I don't know if this is report worthy or not but we need to correct this and make sure ZZZ is using the appropriate code for cabin supplies and that code isn't AOG.
ASRS:1840440.s: A cabin crew member reported that ZZZ cargo staff repeatedly staged cabin supplies using the incorrect AOG code despite receiving guidance. This error caused ramp personnel to search for non-existent AOG items, creating operational confusion that the reporter seeks to resolve.

ASRS:1840442.n: UN3373 Biological Hazmat accepted through the corporate process is bypassing the load planning communication.
ASRS:1840442.s: The reporter states that UN3373 Biological Hazmat accepted via the corporate process is bypassing load planning communication. No specific aircraft, phase of flight, or outcome is described in the narrative.

ASRS:1840447.n: Local cargo leadership was notified by freight handler in regards to AWB [Airways Bill] X shipment. Original booking shows 5 pieces of radioactive for single leg. When shipment was tendered at facility a total of 11 pieces were tendered under AWB with a total TI [Transportation Index] of 12.7. This is over the maximum amount acceptable to travel on the 737 fleet type which is set at 6 TI total. The AWB will now have to be adjusted for transport across 3 separate trips to comply with the maximum TI allowable per fleet type.
ASRS:1840447.s: A freight handler notified cargo leadership that 11 pieces of radioactive material with a total TI of 12.7 were tendered for a 737, exceeding the 6 TI limit. The shipment must now be split across three separate trips to comply with fleet restrictions.

ASRS:1840452.n: We were ready to push so I grabbed the wands and raised them up and was walking to the [Vehicle Service Road] VSR. A small Air Carrier X vehicle was speeding fast on the VSR. My arms were raised showing we were pushing. They never showed any intention of stopping, so we had to stop the push back. Training taught my class we were supposed to stop push back and not give vehicles on the VSR the X unless it was an air-start.
ASRS:1840452.s: A ground handler stopped a pushback when a speeding Air Carrier X vehicle on the Vehicle Service Road showed no intention of stopping despite raised wands. The handler followed training to halt the operation rather than yield right-of-way to the vehicle.

ASRS:1840454.n: Aircraft X arrived Gate XX at XA57. RSE (Ramp Service Employee) marshaling Aircraft was not on ramp 5-10 minutes prior to arrival failed to do a Safety and FOD walk. Another RSE placing tires away went running to the gate with cross arms to stop the marshaling of the aircraft, to the point he had to run in front of the aircraft to get her attention to stop, she noticed him and stop the aircraft abruptly. the RSE who came running over move a belt loader that was parked in the OSZ (Operating Safety Zone) and inches away from making contact with the aircraft engine. The marshalling agent and wing walker did not have on headsets. The flight deck unaware that they were stopped short, turned off engines, and by headset was told they would need to tow them up a few feet. Once tow bar was connected. the marshalling RSE proceed to tow and went to fast and pop the shear pin on the tow bar. When asked if she reported the incident so maintenance for the Airline can come and inspected the nose of the aircraft to make sure no damages she said no, it was fine. She then tried to cancel everyone else was at fault, when mention that she needed to be at the gate 5 minutes prior to do Safety and FOD walk she said the crew before should have check the gate.
ASRS:1840454.s: A ramp service employee failed to perform a pre-arrival safety walk, forcing another employee to stop Aircraft X abruptly to avoid a belt loader in the Operating Safety Zone. Subsequent towing caused a tow bar shear pin failure, and the employee refused to report the incident or allow maintenance inspection.

ASRS:1840478.n: Bird Strike On takeoff out of ZZZZ at XA:21Z on date. We noted a flock of about 50 to 75 birds that were a little more than halfway down the runway. The aircraft was about 10 knots below V1. The flock took off around the aircraft. The only bird the crew physically saw hit the aircraft was one that impacted over the captains windshield. We continued the takeoff roll and the takeoff and subsequent climb were normal. We notified departure control that we had a bird strike. They asked if we wanted to return. We told then to standby while it was discussed. At approximately 8,000 feet, an abnormal high vibration was noted in the N1 section of he right engine. The vibration was noted to be 5.0. The Captain consulted the Flight Mechanic. The Mechanic stated that he thought he felt a vibration and heard unusual sounds in the back. We opted at that point to return to ZZZZ. The Captain assigned duties to each of the 3 flight crew members. He had the FO fly the airplane. The Captain worked the checklist to begin a needed fuel dump to prevent an overweight landing. The observer FO was designated to contact the company and talk to the flight attendants about the issue. As the observer, I contacted the company via sat phone. Told them we would be returning to ZZZZ, and that we would be dumping fuel. After that I contacted the purser to advise her we were a return. I asked if she had any questions. She indicated she did not. I then, under the direction of the Captain, made a brief announcement about the fuel jettison so passengers would not be alarmed When I was done with my duties, I asked the Captain what I could help with. He had just finished up the dump. Finished the checklist and said that he was caught up. He had also retrieved numbers for both a normal and a single engine landing to runway XX. At this point we had descended, descent and approach checks were complete, and we were set up for a left base entry visual runway XX. The approach and landing were uneventful. On the landing roll we encountered another flock of birds and hear a couple strikes forward. Upon exiting the aircraft, severe damage to the right engine fan and shroud were noted. At 10 knots prior to V1 we encountered several bird strikes at ZZZZ Airport on takeoff. At least 50 plus birds flew from the right to the left side of the aircraft and one bird hit the airplane just above the Captains head and some on the right side of the aircraft near the right engine. It was my takeoff (FO) and we continued. The Captain reported it to ATC. ATC asked if we needed to return to the airport and the Captain initially said that we do not need to return. We weren't sure of the damage at that moment and shortly there after around 8,000 feet the relief pilot said the right engine FAN vibrations are at a max of 5.0 with all other engine indications normal. The Captain then called ATC to request a level off at FL150 and I maintained a reduced airspeed of 280 knots to avoid any unnecessary stress on the airplane. At that time the relief pilot was communicating with dispatch per the Captains request and the flight attendants as to the status of our aircraft, plus a PA to our passengers to keep them all informed of our situation. The Captain was in constant communication with ATC.The Captain then consulted with maintenance and he told us it was really loud in the aircraft, so we all were in agreement and made the decision to return to the airport.The Captain then told ATC that we wanted to return to ZZZZ, but we need to jettison fuel to be able to land below landing weight. The Captain then requested to jettison fuel with ATC. The Captain was running the QRH to jettison fuel as I followed along and the Captain also was getting our performance numbers for landing.We received authorization to fly in the vicinity of the airport and jettison fuel for 14 minutes. Then the Captain requested runway XX for landing and I (FO) shot the visual approach and landed. As I was rolling out around 130 knots we encountered numerous bird strikes again and reported that to the tower and ground frequency. At 60 knots the Captain took control of the aircraft from me and taxied to our assigned parking. On my post flight walk around I noticed severe damage to the inside cowling and all the fan blades on the right engine. Plus a marking above the Captains L1 window.I would suggest that ZZZZ finds a method of bird control at their airport to avoid this situation from happening again to another aircraft.
ASRS:1840478.s: The flight crew encountered a bird strike during takeoff at ZZZZ, resulting in severe right engine fan damage and high vibration at 8,000 feet. They returned to ZZZZ after jettisoning fuel, landing safely despite additional strikes on the rollout.

ASRS:1840527.n: During the final climb phase of Aircraft X (ZZZ-ZZZ1), the aircraft experienced a high-altitude decompression event, the result of a L BLEED DUCT Master Warning and subsequent automatic left and right bleed valve closures. The crew requested priority with ZZZ2 [Center], initiated a descent and diverted to ZZZ3 for a precautionary landing. The process and procedure of preparing and securing the aircraft for the abnormality, as directed by the appropriate priority and QRH Checklists, was complicated and slowed somewhat by a temporary vision impairment of the Pilot Monitoring (myself) due to an unknown dust or contaminate in the smoke goggle portion of the mask during donning. While climbing through FL316 to a filed cruise altitude of FL360, we were alerted to a potential bleed duct leak by a triple chime, aural 'Bleed Air Duct' and red EICAS message of 'L Bleed Duct'.I would STRONGLY suggest that maintenance inspect, clean and blow out the crew o2 masks / smoke goggles on a regular basis. These masks are checked for air pressure and operation by the flight crew every morning, but the condition and cleanliness of the actual mask is widely unknown until it is needed. The white powdery dust that blew all over my face and lap during the initial use of this very important safety gear could have been a lot worse than it was, possibly creating a crew incapacitation during critical emergency operations.
ASRS:1840527.s: During the climb of Aircraft X, a left bleed duct leak triggered an automatic decompression and diversion to ZZZ3. The Pilot Monitoring's emergency response was temporarily hindered by dust inside the oxygen mask smoke goggles, prompting a recommendation for regular maintenance cleaning.

ASRS:1840531.n: Near Miss on the COKTL 1 RNAV Arrival just prior to MEZKL at 12,000 ft. Near Miss on the COKTL 1 RNAV Arrival just prior to MEZKL at 12,000 ft. The other Aircraft was not talking to anyone. That was way to close. Lesson learned, Stay Alert, Alert, Alert.
ASRS:1840531.s: A pilot reported a near miss on the COKTL 1 RNAV arrival just prior to MEZKL at 12,000 ft involving another aircraft that was not communicating with anyone. The reporter described the encounter as too close and emphasized the need to stay alert.

ASRS:1840551.n: Encountered significant wake turbulence immediately after rotation behind A321. Wake turbulence was constant so we informed Tower we would require offset from departure course (34R.Bangor9). Reported A321 in sight and offset appx. 0.2mi left of course. We were cleared for takeoff while the A321 was rotating and my first thought was to delay a bit. I wish I had as I have never encountered wake turbulence so close to the ground nor do I wish to try it again.It is worth noting this is the second time recently I have encountered wake turbulence behind an Airbus 321 in Seattle and my First Officer was recently cleared for takeoff behind a Boeing 757 without standard separation in Seattle. In the future, I will not accept a clearance to takeoff so close to another aircraft and I believe it would be wise to follow up with Seattle Tower to ensure standard departure separation is being used and they are not getting rushed with the high amount of departures they work these days.The Seattle Controllers do a remarkable job handling the heavy traffic load we have seen this summer but perhaps there is a trend here and they are getting a bit rushed. As a pilot, I will ask for a bit of time before taking off behind another aircraft next time.
ASRS:1840551.s: The pilot encountered significant wake turbulence immediately after rotation behind an A321 on runway 34R at Seattle, prompting an offset departure. The reporter attributed the event to insufficient separation clearance while the preceding aircraft was rotating and noted a pattern of similar incidents in high-traffic conditions.

ASRS:1840591.n: Obviously the instructors and check airmen doing this have no idea of the possible repercussions of this act. To quickly review, like inputs are summed, opposed inputs are cancelled. To actually have your hand on the side stick while the other pilot is flying can have catastrophic consequences. A subtle, unconscious input by the pilot monitoring say during the flare or strong crosswind landing to 'help' the pilot flying may generate a dual input warning but by then recovery may be unattainable. The reason given during training is to be quick to push the take over button. I can have my hand in my lap and in 1/2 second can reach to the button, depress it, and have control of the aircraft. When flying a conventional airplane, one with a control wheel, does the pilot monitoring actually have their hands on the controls while the other person is flying. No! The PM can have their hand on the side console, rubber grommet around the base, or arm rest, but should not be actually on the side stick while the other person is flying. Stop this training practice.This is the X time this year I have flown with a new pilot where they have actually had their hand on the side stick while I was flying the airplane. This is expressly forbidden in the pilots operating manual, 'Only one person will fly the aircraft at a time'. They all tell me that is the policy during training that the instructors and check airmen have been telling them to do this not only during training but on their initial operating ride as well!
ASRS:1840591.s: The pilot reported that new pilots, instructed by check airmen, placed their hands on the side stick while the pilot flying operated the aircraft. This training practice violates the operating manual's rule that only one person flies at a time and risks catastrophic dual input warnings during critical phases like landing.

ASRS:1840593.n: In the vicinity of ZZZZZ intersection power was reduced to idle as aircraft intercepted descent path on the ZZZZZ 5 arrival. Master Caution, Fuel, and Filter Bypass light on #1 Engine illuminated. Flying duties were transferred to First Officer and QRH procedure was accomplished. Only the #1 Engine Filter Bypass was illuminated and the engine was operating normally. Decision was made to continue to ZZZ and request priority handing as a precaution and to avoid any unnecessary delays. ATC controllers were very helpful with one exception. When we checked in with Approach Control (I believe the frequency was X) the controller immediately issued us a 40 knot reduction in airspeed to sequence another aircraft in front of us. This would have created an unstable approach and was the exact situation we were trying to avoid by asking for priority handling. We reminded him that we were a priority aircraft and were beginning to slow as we configured. Normal landing was uneventful with Tower and Ground controllers again very helpful. Dispatch, FODO [Flight Officer Duty Officer] and line maintenance in ZZZ were contacted and briefed. Flight Attendants were debriefed.Brief Approach controller on importance of assisting Emergency Aircraft.
ASRS:1840593.s: The crew experienced a #1 engine filter bypass light during the ZZZZZ 5 arrival, transferred flying duties, and requested priority handling. An Approach controller issued an inappropriate 40-knot speed reduction that risked an unstable approach, but the crew maintained priority and completed an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1840602.n: Early morning departure from ZZZ Runway XXR. Cleared for takeoff direct ZZZZZ. On the takeoff roll all engine indications were normal. As I pitched up to takeoff and receiving positive rate from my First Officer I asked for gear up. As the gear was in transit we heard and felt a bang. At first we thought it was gear related then the gear was in and another bang is heard. At that point tower tells us that we have 'sparks' coming from our engine. The bangs were intermittent about every 3-5 seconds. As we analyzed the situation we knew the right side engine was the issue sign ITT (Inter-stage Turbine Temperature) was hotter then normal. Once I seen the ITT start to shoot up into the red I put the engine from TOGA to Climb and ITT some what reduced. By this time we were also reaching 3,000 ft. so I was in the process of leveling off and reducing power. At no point did we get any alerts or indications that anything was wrong other then the weird ITT indications. The bangs only happened when throttle was in TOGA position. Once level all indications were green and we quickly decided to return to ZZZ. We requested priority handling and received vectors back to ZZZ. I contacted the Flight Attendants and told them we had issues with the right engine they quickly responded with 'Yeah, we know it was really loud back here'. Asked if any smoke is present they said no. Told them were going back to ZZZ and that everything is good and normal as of now and if that changes I will let them know. Continued to land Runway XXR with no other engine indications. We told the Tower to have fuel trucks waiting just in case of a fire. Upon landing we stopped on the runway, and Tower tells us no fire is visible and I make a PA letting everyone know of the situation and that we will be returning to the gate. Fire Trucks verified no fire and followed us back to the gate. Engines were working as normal on landing and taxi as if nothing happened.
ASRS:1840602.s: During takeoff from ZZZ Runway XXR, the crew heard intermittent bangs and observed high right engine ITT while in TOGA thrust, with tower reporting sparks. The pilot reduced power, returned to ZZZ, and landed safely with no fire or further engine indications.

ASRS:1840603.n: While departing [Runway] 9L from PHL, I observed a drone pass down the right side of the aircraft. We were passing through approximately 1,500 feet. The drone appeared to be a couple hundred yards to our right and below the aircraft. I informed PHL departure when I checked in with them.
ASRS:1840603.s: During departure from PHL Runway 9L, the pilot observed a drone approximately 200 yards to the right and below the aircraft while passing through 1,500 feet. The pilot reported the sighting to PHL departure upon checking in.

ASRS:1840634.n: Upon entering aircraft for preflight FA (Flight Attendant) 2&1 smelled strange burning smell in cabin. Specially strong near aircraft right window exit. Notified Captain, he smelled same odor. Captain turned off APU, smell persisted. Captain called maintenance and saw brown oily looking substance above window exit. FA's were onboard for approx 15-20 min and began to all notice mild symptoms, funny taste in mouth, mild headache, dizziness. FA's deplaned and sat at gate. Captain refused aircraft, FA's were removed from trip by manager.
ASRS:1840634.s: Flight Attendants and the Captain detected a burning smell and oily substance near the right window exit during preflight, causing mild symptoms. The Captain refused the aircraft after turning off the APU, resulting in the crew being removed from the trip.

ASRS:1840696.n: Student pilot departed ZZZ to the North and during initial climb, initiated a descent due to numerous birds in the aircraft flight path. Aircraft leveled off at 1,200 feet toward rising terrain. Aircraft may have descended below 500 feet before instructor intervention and clear of conflict and climb initiated.
ASRS:1840696.s: A student pilot departing ZZZ descended during initial climb due to birds, leveling at 1,200 feet near rising terrain. The aircraft may have dropped below 500 feet before the instructor intervened to clear the conflict and resume the climb.

ASRS:1840705.n: Student did have a runway excursion, student was taxing at a safe speed and the plane kept veering right. I tried to help and apply left rudder and brake and the plane would not stop as if the right brake was stuck. The plane rolled off the taxiway. No damage to airport property, personnel, or aircraft. Plane was inspected by maintenance and we then continued our flight without further incident. The location was at ZZZ on a taxiway heading east to Runway XX.
ASRS:1840705.s: A student pilot and instructor experienced a runway excursion at ZZZ while taxiing east to Runway XX due to suspected stuck right brakes causing the aircraft to veer right. Maintenance inspected the plane, found no damage, and the flight continued without further incident.

ASRS:1840707.n: At approximately XB:45 PM Mountain daylight time I departed ZZZ on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1. I had an estimated 14 gallons of fuel upon arrival earlier in the day and I instructed the FBO at ZZZ2 to add 50 gallons total, 25 per side to the tanks giving me an estimated fuel load of 64 gallons. I set up the avionics in my airplane showing that I had 60 gallons of fuel, which is what my flight plans said I needed including legal minimums leaving the four extra gallons as my 'Just in case' which was as I was taught.I had previously created a flight plan (2 weeks prior to the actual date of the flight) in ForeFlight that I updated almost daily including the day prior to the flight and again at approximately XA:00 PM that afternoon (on the day of the flight, approximately 30 minutes prior to departure)using the winds as of XA:00 Zulu and the TAF as of XA:25 Zulu. I have saved all of these documents for the record and have copies of the original filings and the original NAV logs and terminal air forecast data. Winds were estimated to be average 23 knot headwind at 260 and the NAV log showed that the block fuel required was 60 gallons including a 14 gallon legal reserve for the flight. Since I landed with 14-15 gallons in the tanks and added 50 gallons total, 25 per side I felt confident that I had a sufficient amount of fuel for the flight based on the current and forecast winds, the aircraft performance and my ForeFlight briefing and NAV log and should land at ZZZ1 with 14 to 18 gallons of fuel.Upon departure from ZZZ2, ZZZ3 Approach vectored me to a 250 heading and left us on that heading for vectors around a military operating area. ZZZ3 Approach handed us off to ZZZ4 Center which kept us on the 250 heading for quite some time. In checking my direct to function on ForeFlight (which I had operational on my knee board)I could have went direct to ZZZ5 VOR and kept well south of the military operating area. Wanting to get back on course, I made a radio call to ZZZ4 Center asking if we could go direct at this point to the ZZZ5 VOR. ZZZ4 Center did not clear us direct ZZZ5. They then cleared us to ZZZ6 VOR. Then direct ZZZ5 then ZZZ2 AT 14,000. The flight proceeded normally except that winds were showing to be 35 to 45 knots direct headwind. The fuel totalizer showed 17 to 18 gallons fuel over destination so I continued the flight keeping an eye on the fuel over destination. Conditions were VMC The entire flight.At approximately ZZZ7 VOR, the winds began to pick up dramatically and instruments start showing 45 to 50 knot direct headwind. At this point the fuel totalizer began to show 8 to 10 gallons fuel over destination. I activated the nearest function on my avionics to find an airport where I could deviate to, in order to take on more fuel and then finish the flight. The nearest function showed that ZZZ8 had 24 hour self-service fuel and was approximately 30 miles to my south. At this point I had over 20 gallons of fuel good for over an hours worth of flight time and ZZZ8 was a 10 to 15 minute diversion and decided to divert to ZZZ8 for fuel.I decided that if the winds did not die down and the fuel totalizer returned to a minimum of 14 gallons fuel over destination within the next 10 minutes that I would divert to ZZZ8 and take on fuel. The winds persisted and I advised ZZZ4 Center that I would need to divert to ZZZ8 for fuel due to the wind being much stronger than anticipated or forecasted and that I did not want to be minimum or emergency fuel arriving into the ZZZ1 area. The center controller asked me if I wished to declare an emergency. I said no that I had sufficient fuel to reach ZZZ8 which was approximately 30 miles away and not into a direct headwind and that I plan to land at ZZZ8 take on fuel and resume the flight.The controller cleared me to ZZZ8, l and I had a bearing up on my nearest screen and it showed a bearing of 218 to ZZZ8 so I switched from NAV on the auto pilot to heading and dialed in 220 and started toward ZZZ8. The controller asked me what approach I wanted at ZZZ8 and I looked on ForeFlight and noticed the ZZZ8 had a GPS approach to runway XX.Add this point I put what I thought was the identifier for ZZZ8 in my avionics as 'ZZZ9' which is an airport in [completely different state]. I selected NAV on the auto pilot and the airplane made a turn to the left from a hearing of 220 approximately 090 turning the aircraft back toward a mountain range. I immediately saw that I was turning away from the airport but at this point did not understand why as at this moment. I didn't realize that I had put the airport identifier in the avionics incorrectly as ZZZ9 instead of ZZZ8. I attempted to re-enter the airport identifier as ZZ8 again and the avionics again tried to guide me toward the wrong airport. At this point I did not realize that I was entering the wrong airport identifier but I could see ZZZ8 on my moving map and knew that I was navigating away from ZZZ8. Although I was in VMC conditions it took me approximately one to two minutes to realize my error and to reprogram the avionics to the correct airport identifier and locate the approach charts for ZZZ8 for the GPS runway XX. During this time the controller told me that it appeared I was navigating away from ZZZ8 and the airport off to my right was not the ZZZ8 airport and gave me a heading to ZZZ8 and the controller issued me a low altitude alert. I started a right turn toward ZZZ8 and attempted to load the approach to ZZZ8 but my avionics had ZZZ1 as my final destination and wanted to load approaches to ZZZ1 and not ZZZ8. I deleted the remainder of my flight plan out of my avionics except for ZZZ8 located the approach and flew the GPS to ZZZ8 and landed normally without incident. I found the frequency on the approach plate for the lights at ZZZ8 and using the pilot controlled lighting at ZZZ8, l turned the lights on positively identified the runway and landed safely without incident at ZZZ8.I told the controller at ZZZ4 Center that I had the airport in sight (identified the airport by turning on the runway lights) and was established on the approach and would land normally and take on fuel. The controller issued me a possible pilot deviation notice and asked me to call when I landed. I landed the airplane and took on 40 gallons of fuel and called ZZZ4 Center on the number provided.The person who answered the phone was polite asked me my name and then asked me 'Hey what happened here?' I related the basic details of the events above (although not in the detail provided here). They thanked me for calling and asked me for my name address and pilot certificate number all of which I gave to them. They told me thank you and if anyone else had any questions they would be in contact with me.I continued the flight to ZZZ1 by getting an IFR clearance from Center out of ZZZ8 to ZZZ5 direct ZZZ1 was cleared for an ILS approach to Runway XY Via a 15 DME arc and landed normally at ZZZ1 at approximately XG:50 PM MDT.I've had a lot of time to think about this at length. As the avionics attempted to turn the airplane toward ZZZ9 I immediately realized that I was going in the wrong direction but for a period of about 1 to 2 minutes I didn't understand why the airplane was attempting to take me an airport in [different state]. I knew it was taking me in the wrong direction but I didn't understand why, initially. As I was turning the airplane back toward ZZZ8 as I could see it on my map I was trying to figure out why the avionics wasn't taking me there. Then I realized that I had put in the wrong airport identifier, by one digit. When I fixed that I tried to load the approach for ZZZ8 edit brought up the ZZZ1 approach charts. That took me a few seconds to realize that the avionics was thinking I wanted at my destination was ZZZ1 and I'm now landing at ZZZ8. I deleted the rest of my flight plan leaving ZZZ8 as my destination located the approach chart activated the approach to ZZZ8, l and landed there. I did all of this during a right turn and flying back toward ZZZ8 and lining up to the runway.In retrospect I realize that the controller at ZZZ4 Center had no idea why I was turning in the wrong direction except that I was turning toward high elevation terrain. The controller was doing his job in notifying me that I was headed the wrong direction and giving me Low altitude alert. However I was also doing my job in Aviating first, navigating second and communicating third. At this point the controller was trying to correct my direction of flight and I was flying the airplane in VMC conditions while trying to correct my avionics to direct me to ZZZ8. In my estimation of what happened, both the controller and I were doing our jobs to the best of our abilities. I made the unfortunate mistake of entering the fix for ZZZ8 airport in my avionics incorrectly which took me in the wrong direction however I realized the error immediately and corrected the error promptly and remained in VMC conditions throughout.I believe that my decision making was sound, correct and timely to divert to ZZZ8 to take on additional fuel and I also believe that my flight planning utilizing ForeFlight the terminal air forecast and predicted winds were all carefully studied and factored into the decision on how much fuel to take on for the flight to ZZZ1 considering weight and balance.If I had this all to do over again I would probably have continued my flight toward ZZZ1 for an additional 5 minutes or so and reprogrammed ForeFlight on my IPad, reviewed the route and approach options, and then once I had it where I wanted it, requested it from center and then once approved, send it from my tablet to the panel and activated the new route from the panel. The day following this event I flew from ZZZ1 to ZZZ10 and then from ZZZ10 TO ZZZ11. On departure from ZZZ1 I was assigned the ZZZZZ4 departure ZZZ12 transition from runway XY @ZZZ1. As I was preparing for taxing out ZZZ1 switched runways from XY to YX. I was still on the ramp and although it is the same SID procedure it has different routing and I had to take out the runway XY routing and replace it with the YX routing. The controller acted a little aggravated as he asked me if I was ready for taxi but I told him I needed a minute to update my SID routing. What I didn't want to do is being taxing out 'heads down' reprogramming my route. Why not do it while stopped and in the ramp? About a minute later I advised ground that I had the route reprogrammed and was ready for taxi. They taxied me to Runway YX and I did it with heads up and eyes out. Minutes later they cleared me for takeoff, and canceled the SID routing while issuing me the takeoff clearance and put me on a departure heading. No problem. ZZZ13 Approach directed me off heading to an interim fix on the SID which I navigated to and executed without problem. But ATC is busy and used to giving immediate instructions to be complied with immediately, and moving on to the next guy. But now that I am on the other side of the mike, I now understand what it takes to fly the airplane, take into consideration the concerns of non-pilot passengers and reprogram avionics on the fly due to changing conditions. The day following this incident I flew 1,365 NM in two legs and practiced during the 3 hour en-route phase, practiced my reaction to this incident by selecting a nearest to airport and then entering the fix into the avionics and walking through the steps to delete the rest of the flight plan and load a deviation airport approach. I also use ForeFlight as my back up NAV source and practiced programming a divert flight plan an exporting it to the panel.During the leg from KZZZ10 to ZZZ11 I got to put it to the test due to weather. My route taking me from SZZZ14 TO ZZZ11 was through a line of severe thunderstorms. I was able to see this developing at my destination an hour ahead
ASRS:1840707.s: The pilot diverted to ZZZ8 due to stronger-than-forecast headwinds but inadvertently entered the wrong airport identifier (ZZZ9) in the avionics, causing a deviation toward a mountain range. After ATC issued a low altitude alert and provided a heading, the pilot corrected the navigation error, landed safely at ZZZ8, and received a pilot deviation notice.

ASRS:1840712.n: I was performing the duties of the Supervisor for the afternoon shift (XA:00-XF:00). I reviewed and endorsed a student pilots flight planning to do a solo cross country from ZZZ-ZZZ1-ZZZ. I found the flight planning accurate and correct and so went forward endorsing the student to make the flight. The weather for the day was VFR and well within his PQ card limitations with the only major concern being a crosswind of approximately 6 knots (his max x-wind was 8 kts). Also, prior to letting him make the flight I just expressed to him if the clouds were by chance going to drop to immediately come back to the field because clouds in the local practice areas had been reported at various heights around 4,000 feet MSL. Other than that I saw no issue with the student pilot making the flight to ZZZ1. However, after maybe 45 mins after the students departure I received a call on the cell phone from the student saying that in the process of landing he had gone off the side of the runway and was in the grass. I immediately informed someone up the chain of command who then helped getting the correct people to help and develop a plan of action and try to learn what exactly happened. With the help of the Flight Ops, Chief Pilot, and maintenance personnel, we learned that the student had possibly porpoised upon landing which resulted in the aircraft going off the runway and experiencing damage. A rescue crew including one maintenance pilot and the student pilot's instructor flew down to ZZZ1 to assess the situation and bring the student pilot back to ZZZ.
ASRS:1840712.s: A flight supervisor endorsed a student pilot for a solo cross-country flight in VFR conditions with a 6-knot crosswind. The student subsequently veered off the runway into grass during landing at the destination, likely due to porpoising, resulting in aircraft damage and requiring a rescue crew to recover the pilot.

ASRS:1840713.n: Landing ZZZ Runway XX, on roll out aircraft pulled left, counter controls had little affect. Aircraft struck runway lights. Amphibious aircraft departed ZZZ1 after being stuck in mud. Aircraft taxied in water with gear down to wash mud from wheels. After one hour flight at above freezing conditions, landed ZZZ.Suspect debris in wheels made left wheel resist rolling and right brake less effective. After aircraft stopped, was able to taxi to parking with differential braking.
ASRS:1840713.s: An amphibious aircraft pilot reported a left pull and runway light strike during landing at ZZZ, suspecting wheel debris caused uneven braking. The aircraft later departed after being stuck in mud and taxied in water to clean the wheels.

ASRS:1840718.n: Two pilots were flying a second bridge [mission] in ZZZ construction site under a BVLOS waiver from [a] Government Agency when they experienced a lost link message while the drone was under the bridge. Drone had eventually regained connection, issue was due most likely to the bridge obstructing the radio signal. Two pilots were operating in ZZZ construction site inspecting bridges under a BVLOS waiver from [a] Government Agency, when connection was lost. Drone issued return to home function, and signal was regained. Most probable cause was the bridge obstruction causing the interference.
ASRS:1840718.s: Two pilots operating a drone under a BVLOS waiver at a ZZZ construction site lost radio link while inspecting a bridge, likely due to signal obstruction. The drone executed a return-to-home function and regained connection.

ASRS:1840720.n: 2 Pilots were inspecting their third bridge under a BVLOS waiver from [Goverment agency] when the drone had lost its signal/connection. Eventually during the return to home phase connection was regained. Most likely due to bridge obstruction interference.
ASRS:1840720.s: Two pilots operating a drone under a BVLOS waiver lost signal while inspecting a third bridge, likely due to bridge obstruction interference. Connection was eventually regained during the return-to-home phase.

ASRS:1840721.n: 2 Pilots were inspecting their third bridge on a construction site while operating under the BVLOS waiver from [government agency]. The drone lost link/connection and initiated the return to home function from which connection was regained. Most likely due to bridge obstruction interference.
ASRS:1840721.s: Two pilots operating a drone under a BVLOS waiver lost link while inspecting a bridge, triggering a return-to-home function. Connection was regained, and the loss was likely caused by bridge obstruction interference.

ASRS:1840722.n: While shooting drone footage of the street construction, I accidentally hit a cable line while piloting the small UAS. I was flying the drone along with a required [Visual Observer], in a closed off portion of the street that remains blocked from vehicular traffic due to past construction activity. This area was not an active construction zone at the time of the incident. From both of our perspectives, it looked as though I was clear to safely rise the drone, however as the drone went up, the back end of the drone hit a low hanging cable line. The drone immediately fell to the street directly below and two propellers were damaged as well as some of the plastic protective shell of the drone's legs, and wiring within. There was no damage to any vehicles, persons, or equipment other than the UAS.
ASRS:1840722.s: A pilot and Visual Observer operating a small UAS in a closed street construction area struck a low-hanging cable line while ascending. The drone crashed, sustaining damage to two propellers, the protective shell, and internal wiring, with no injury or damage to other persons or equipment.

ASRS:1840738.n: I accepted a handoff on Aircraft X, a M20 level at 030, on a vector westbound from ZZZ1 that was requesting an RNAV approach to [Runway] XX at ZZZ. I was working several other aircraft and allowed Aircraft X to continue on that heading while I worked other aircraft. I became distracted as an aircraft called to request Class B clearance to an airport that would be a conflict to Arrival sectors and then again when they stated their intention to climb above the Class B, which would also be a conflict for Arrival sectors. I tagged and identified the aircraft and coordinated with the overlying arrival sector of the aircraft's intentions. During this time I was distracted, Aircraft X was continuing westbound level at 030 and approaching the 034 Minimum Vectoring Area north of ZZZ2. When I realized that Aircraft X was entering a higher Minimum Vectoring Area at a lower altitude, I turned Aircraft X southbound to exit the Minimum Vectoring Area and issued them a climb up to the Minimum Vectoring Area (034).It was an honest mistake, I need to be more vigilant in my scan so as not to get overly focused on one thing to the detriment of another. Another thing I could have done would be to issue a vector earlier that would delay any potential Minimum Vectoring Area conflicts so that if I did prioritize other aircraft then it wouldn't become an issue.
ASRS:1840738.s: An air traffic controller allowed a M20 at flight level 030 to enter a higher Minimum Vectoring Area (034) while distracted by another aircraft's Class B clearance request. The controller subsequently vectored the M20 south and issued a climb to the required altitude, attributing the error to a lack of vigilance in their scan.

ASRS:1840778.n: I was very concerned to read a pilot bulletin a short time back about the intercom issue on the Max 8's where if certain switches are left in the wrong position the passengers in the back can hear the pilot's conversation up front. I know the easy answer is to make sure the switches are in the correct position. However we all forget things, and it is just a matter of time until someone forgets and a career or two are potentially ended as well as the airline put into a difficult PR position based upon a thought to be private conversation being overheard by a passenger. Is there any plan to have this system permanently disabled? If so, when might that occur? Any information you can pass on regarding this would be greatly appreciated. This is a topic of common concern in conversation on the flight deck amongst pilots.
ASRS:1840778.s: Pilots expressed concern that incorrect switch positions on the Boeing 737 MAX 8 intercom system allow passengers to overhear flight deck conversations. They requested information on plans to permanently disable this feature to prevent potential career and public relations issues.

ASRS:1840813.n: On Date on the flight departing ZZZ at XA:57z and landing ZZZ1 at XC54z the transponder started to send out incorrect altitude information. We were departing on the ZZZZZ 6 and just past ZZZZZ1, ATC asked us our altitude. We were level at 1,500 feet and ATC was reading 1,900 feet. At this time our radar altimeter was reading 1,500 feet also. During our climb we checked as we were passing 10,000 feet. ATC was reading 10,600. We were assigned to level off at 16,000 feet and ATC was reading 16,700 feet. We tried the second transponder and ATC said all they were receiving was XXX go back to number one. We did and continued to climb to 28,000 feet. We elected to stay at 28,000 feet out of RVSM airspace because of the unreliable transponders. Level at 28,000 feet we checked with ATC and the transponder was reading correctly. We contacted Company maintenance, discussed the problem and we told to continue the flight to ZZZ1. Upon decent into ZZZ1 we were instructed to level at 3,600 feet which we did. At this time ATC said we were at 3,000 feet and issued an alert and said climb immediately to 5,000 feet. We did and were vectored for another approach. We finished the flight with an ILS XX approach. Departed ZZZ on ZZZZZ6 climbed to 1,500 feet MSL no problems. ATC reported check our altitude they were showing 1,900 feet. I quickly took a picture because this was incorrect. They asked we change transponders. We did and they reported they were only getting 'XXXX'. We changed back. We checked in multiple times to verify altitudes. Level at 10,000 feet, they said we were 10,600 feet. Level at 16,000 feet, they reported 16,700 feet. After reaching our adjusted cruise altitude of 28,000 feet (respecting RVSM) and cycling transponders off then on, ATC reported they showed level 28,000. No further issues until the ILS approach into ZZZ1. Weather was marginal VFR. When cleared for the approach starting at 3,600, ATC issued an altitude warning, we asked to go around and try again. On the 2nd approach we had no issues, but did check in to verify each altitude.
ASRS:1840813.s: The flight crew experienced transponder altitude discrepancies during climb and approach, causing ATC to issue an alert and a go-around at 3,600 feet. The crew avoided RVSM airspace, cycled the transponder to restore correct readings at 28,000 feet, and completed the flight after a second approach.

ASRS:1840820.n: Upon loading of the aircraft in ZZZ the DG (Dangerous Goods) paperwork was presented to me (Pilot In Command) for inspection. On the paperwork was a IDG (Inaccessible Dangerous Goods) package of Toxic (less than 1KG) that was to be loaded into an aft zone. While observing the loading of the aircraft this package was not seen or identified while loading. Since I did not inspect or see the package I had it removed from the DG paperwork. Upon reaching our destination I inspected the unload and found the package.The package was improperly labeled or inadequately labeled. There were no identifiable TOXIC labels on the package. The only way I was able to identify that this was the package in question was a DG inspection sticker and the shipping label had the toxic chemical printed on it.Better separation of DG and normal cargo prior to loading the aircraft would allow for a more proper inspection by all Pilots In Command.
ASRS:1840820.s: The Pilot in Command discovered an improperly labeled toxic IDG package in the aft zone upon unloading, despite it being listed on the DG paperwork and removed from the manifest before departure. The reporter attributed the oversight to inadequate labeling and poor separation of dangerous goods from normal cargo during loading.

ASRS:1840827.n: At XA:10 we arrived at the aircraft in ZZZ for Flight X parked at gate X. In the logbook of Aircraft X was an open write up for Air Pack 2 REG fault. I spoke with the gate agent about it and then called dispatch. Dispatch conferenced me in with maintenance. It was known about the open write up since the night before. Maintenance advised me maintenance was on the way. We completed all the preflight duties and walk around items at about XA:35. Maintenance had come out to ascertain the problem at about XA:50, 10 minutes prior to our scheduled push time. Maintenance informed me that we would be delayed about one hour at the gate for a solution. Eventually maintenance informed me the pack would be selected off and the valve had to be visually scanned closed. To do that he would have to open a panel. Upon completion of the procedure by maintenance, I walked outside to see all the panels were closed on the right side of the aircraft. They were. Once back on the flight deck I received the signed off logbook with the deferred MEL item and proceeded with our checklists. As we were being pushed back, the maintenance member drove up to the guide man. We were asked to look on the flight deck and 1st class galley for an iPad. We found none and relayed the message back. We continued our start of both engines normally with no issues. We taxied out via Taxiway 1 to Taxiway 2 and took off from ZZZ on runway XX at about XC:48 local. After takeoff rotation there was just a slight rumble that sounded like an out of round tire usually does as the gear is raised. It abated quickly and no engine anomalies noted. Upon cruise to ZZZ1 we received an ACARS message from dispatch at XI:03, regarding FOD on the runway after our takeoff. Dispatch noted the possibility it was the maintenance member's iPad he was looking for. I told dispatch all engine parameters are normal and we proceeded to ZZZ1 with a normal landing on runway XXR. After the shutdown, I met the ZZZ1 Maintenance manager outside by the number 2 engine. It had signs of ingesting FOD. It is apparent that contract maintenance at ZZZ left the iPad inside the nacelle after our initial preflight and caused damage to the engine.Maintenance having laid an item in an engine nacelle and leaving it there after our preflight was complete.Not laying any tool or item in the nacelle of an engine. At XA:10 we arrived at the aircraft in ZZZ for Aircraft X parked at gate XX. In the logbook of Aircraft X was an open write up for Air Pack 2 REG fault. I spoke with the gate agent about it and then called dispatch. Dispatch conferenced me in with maintenance. It was known about the open write up since the night before. Maintenance advised me maintenance was on the way. We completed all the preflight duties and walk around items at about XA:35 maintenance had come out to ascertain the problem at about XA:50, 10 minutes prior to our scheduled push time. Maintenance informed me that we would be delayed about one hour at the gate for a solution. Eventually maintenance informed me the pack would be selected off and the valve had to be visually scanned closed. To do that he would have to open a panel. Upon completion of the procedure by maintenance, I walked outside to see all the panels were closed on the right side of the aircraft. They were. Once back on the flight deck I received the signed off logbook with the deferred MEL item and proceeded with our checklists. As we were being pushed back, the maintenance member drove up to the guide man. We were asked to look on the flight deck and 1st class galley for an iPad. We found none and relayed the message back. We continued our start of both engines normally with no issues. We taxied out via Taxiway 1 to Taxiway 2 and took off from ZZZ on runway XX at about XC:48 local. After takeoff rotation there was just a slight rumble that sounded like an out of round tire usually does as the gear is raised. It abated quickly and no engine anomalies noted. Upon cruise to ZZZ1 we received an ACARS message from dispatch at XI:03, regarding FOD on the runway after our takeoff. Dispatch noted the possibility it was the maintenance member's iPad he was looking for. I told dispatch all engine parameters are normal and we proceeded to ZZZ1 with a normal landing on runway XXR. After the shutdown, I met the ZZZ1 Maintenance manager outside by the number 2 engine. It had signs of ingesting FOD. It is apparent that contract maintenance at ZZZ left the iPad inside the nacelle AFTER our initial preflight and caused damage to the engine.Maintenance having laid an item in an engine nacelle and leaving it there after our preflight was complete.Not laying any tool or item in the nacelle of an engine.
ASRS:1840827.s: Contract maintenance at ZZZ left an iPad inside the number 2 engine nacelle of Aircraft X after preflight, causing FOD ingestion during takeoff. The flight crew completed a normal flight to ZZZ1, where post-landing inspection confirmed engine damage from the foreign object.

ASRS:1840839.n: Several minutes after selecting APU bleed on the aircraft starting emitting an odor consistent with an oil fume event. Turned off the APU bleed and contacted Maintenance. There were no passengers onboard. Flight crew and cabin crew vacated the aircraft. FO (First Officer) and FA's (Flight Attendants) initially did not want medical attention. After an Inflight Supervisor spoke with them the FO and all FA's chose to go to the hospital. When I called Dispatch to relay what was going on with the aircraft I used the term 'Fume Event' He had no idea what I was talking about. He had received information regarding a smelly sock issue. He said he never heard it called a 'Fume Event'. Maybe this was an isolated incident regarding the terminology or possibly a need to disseminate what a fume event is across the Dispatch department.Airbus needs to fix this reoccurring problem. During preflight setup of the aircraft, APU Bleed Air Pushbutton was selected on. All 6 crew members noticed an unusual 'musty' smell in both the cabin and flight deck. After a few minutes of discussion, the CA (Captain) and I both agreed that the APU Bleed Air should be selected off and Maintenance should be called. After Maintenance was called, the entire crew exited the aircraft to the jetway to allow the aircraft to ventilate. All 6 crew members experienced eye and throat irritation.
ASRS:1840839.s: Six crew members on an Airbus experienced eye and throat irritation from a musty odor after selecting the APU bleed air pushbutton on during preflight. The crew turned off the APU, vacated the aircraft, and sought medical attention, while the reporter noted a terminology gap with Dispatch regarding the "fume event."

ASRS:1840890.n: Flying RNAV Runway 27 SAN appeared to be a drone approximately 1,000 ft. below and offset to the north of our position as we turned past SAYAE. The drone was moving east. No evasive action was required. Reported to Tower and no approved drone activity was sanctioned at that time. Same as above. All drones should be equipped with transponders.
ASRS:1840890.s: A pilot flying an RNAV approach to Runway 27 at SAN observed a drone 1,000 feet below and north of the aircraft while turning past SAYAE. No evasive action was required, but the pilot reported the unauthorized drone to the Tower.

ASRS:1840931.n: FO turned on the packs, a terrible smell filled the cabin-dirty socks and cow manure. The #3 and I (#4) immediately found it difficult to breathe and my eyes started to burn mildly. I went to the flight deck to notify the FO (the Captain was not on board) of the smell, I told her it smelled like the last fume event I was in but she did not turn off the packs and wanted to see if the smell would dissipate. I returned to the flight deck again and told her that the #3 was having chest tightness and having a hard time breathing. I reiterated that my eyes were burning and that it was difficult to breathe. She finally turned off the packs.I should not have had to visit the flight deck twice to convey something that was pretty clear...this was not a normal smell and, coupled with the fact that two flight attendants were having adverse reactions-which was conveyed in the first visit- action should have been taken immediately. A wait and see approach was unacceptable. Right before boarding the #3 and #1 were standing at 2L/R when she noticed a horrible smell. We both took our masks off to confirm the issue. It smelled like a dirty diaper that then smelled like dirty socks. It was most noticeable in my area then it spread to other areas of the cabin. The 3 went to the flight deck and alerted the First Officer since the Captain had not boarded the aircraft yet. It became so strong I went to the front galley and got another mask for the #3 and I to layer on top of our masks. Once the Captain boarded he removed the aircraft from service. My chest was very tight and was hard to breath, I was nauseous, and a bit dizzy.
ASRS:1840931.s: Cabin crew reported a strong odor and respiratory symptoms after the First Officer turned on the packs, but the FO delayed shutting them off despite repeated warnings. The Captain eventually removed the aircraft from service after boarding, citing the unacceptable wait-and-see approach to the fume event.

ASRS:1840951.n: At ZZZ1 I departed Runway XX in VFR conditions, with a 4-ft. fiberglass ladder used at the fueling station, accidentally hanging from my right main landing gear. The takeoff was notable [at a] less-than-ideal climb performance of 95 kt. but more than adequate. Then, while cruising at approximately 3,500 ft., I noticed cruise speed to be below ideal, approximately 109 kt. where 135 kt. was expected and the autopilot trim more forward than usual. I figured the right wheel pant might have come loose and was hanging at an angle making it less aerodynamic, resulting in the diminished cruise performance. I was able to directly visualize the elevator, both Left and Right sides, and did not notice any abnormalities. To get a better view from the pilot's seat without removing my seat belt, I used my cell phone to take a picture out of the right copilot's window of the right main landing gear and noted the dented wheel pant and a small ladder hanging from the right main landing gear. I did not attempt to slow nor speed up nor any maneuvers to attempt to shake the ladder free. The plane was in stable flight and [in] no imminent danger. I was concerned the ladder might come loose and fall, causing injury on the ground. I was in radio contact with ZZZ2 Approach, notified them of the situation, squawked 7700, and headed directly to ZZZ, my home airport which was approximately 14 minutes away. The descent and approach pattern and landing to ZZZ Runway XY were uneventful. I taxied directly to the ramp to park and tie down. Aside from cosmetic damage to the right wheel pant and the landing strut cover, no other damage was noted. The ladder in question was easily removed using only my hands, as it had only hooked onto the landing gear strut.Recalling filling up with fuel at ZZZ1, I took note of the short green ladder used to fuel my aircraft. It was awkward to stand on top of the ladder and fuel. I had taxied to the fuel pump on the left side. Filled left tank first, then right tank. After retrieving the fuel hose and grounding wire back to the pump area, I was walking back to the plane to retrieve the ladder in front of the right wing, but was distracted by a small piece of paper - a fuel receipt from a prior pilot - which I picked up [and] walked over to the trash can which was behind and to the left of the aircraft [at an] approximately 8 o'clock position. As I walked back to the plane, my view of the ladder was blocked by the fuselage and I forgot about the ladder.
