Though I was conscientious enough to remove a small piece of litter from the taxiway, that piece of paper had disrupted my usual flow and preflight walk-around.Startup was normal and as I started to taxi, I may have noted a very brief soft clang of plastic or light metal, which I believed sounded like a loose wheel pant bracket on the right side, which has happened many times before for both right and left wheel pants and usually required only a small adjustment or a replacement bracket. The noise was louder with throttle up vibration but extinguished with low idle and rolling smoothly, there was no vibration from the right landing gear. But with the loud engine noises of taxi and noise-canceling headphones, the audible signals were very faint and overall unremarkable to me. The plane rolled and taxied normally so I did not shut down the plane to get out and inspect the gear as I had just done so at the fueling station a few minutes earlier.The short 4-ft. green fiberglass ladder made it easier to miss as viewing it was blocked by the plane's fuselage when approaching from the left/pilot's side, and was not visible from the pilot's seat. It was green in color and not a bright red or yellow color - which are also popular colors - which made it less visually notable against a green grassy background of the taxiways. Perhaps a recommendation of a bright colored ladder could help avoid this in the future. Pre-flight walk-around distraction of a small piece of litter disrupted my usual preflight walk-around routine and the essential item of removing the ladder was overlooked. I appreciate how preflight distractions should be consciously minimized so a normal routine and flow are maintained and essential checklist items not overlooked. I've dedicated myself to avoid distractions during procedures like preflight walk-around in the future. I did not attempt any abrupt maneuvers nor unusual attitudes to shake the ladder free as it might fall back, damaging the right elevator, or fall from the sky, causing injury on the ground. I did not attempt anything outside my usual scope of piloting, which might have made a situation worse. Though questionably an in-flight emergency, I maximized the utilization of all resources available to me, including immediately advising ATC of my concerns and diverting immediately to an airport where fire and rescue services would be readily available. I had considered the right landing gear might have been damaged or the tire [was] flat, and had planned to land softly on the right gear first and perform an immediate go-around if I felt an abnormality during touchdown, which I did not. So, I performed a normal landing without incident.Discussion with Operation's Manager - he recommended and I agree, it may have been prudent to have circled the airport or go to a hold, pending fire/rescue to get into position for the landing, as they did not arrive at the airport until after I had already landed and taxied to the ramp. Though the time from advising ATC to touchdown was approximately 20 minutes, ZZZ Operations claimed they had only about 10 minutes notice before I landed. Perhaps earlier notification of rescue resources could be facilitated to allow ample time for these resources to be in place at landing, rather than having an aircraft pilot have to circle or hold pending their getting into their positions. After landing, I was taxied immediately from Runway XY and back to the ramp. It may have been prudent to have parked and shut down there on the taxiway to avoid dragging the ladder or damaging landing gear along the long taxiways, which then required Operations to have to inspect the runway and taxiways for FOD on a more expansive runway environment, adding to the risk of FOD hazarding subsequent flights on those taxiways.
ASRS:1840951.s: The pilot departed ZZZ1 with a 4-ft. fiberglass ladder hooked to the right main gear due to a preflight distraction, causing reduced climb and cruise performance. After squawking 7700 and notifying ZZZ2 Approach, the pilot landed safely at ZZZ with only cosmetic damage to the wheel pant and strut cover.

ASRS:1840953.n: I was the pilot flying on this empty leg, Part 135 repositioning flight to ZZZ. I was flying with a XX-year Part 121 pilot who was a recent upgrade and very new to Part 135 flying. We were on our second week-long rotation together and had been working exceptionally well together on all our previous flights. Because I had been to ZZZ before, i was pointing out all the important details of the area and what I knew of the airport and local ops prior to descending for the approach. On this morning, we arrived over the ZZZ area to find a thick morning fog/haze layer over the entire area. We were in hopes of visually acquiring the airport and making a visual approach, but were unable to see the airport until just before passing overhead, so we elected to shoot the RNAV (GPS) XX. We had been cleared down to 10,000 feet or 11,000 feet before requesting the RNAV approach, but were instructed to climb and maintain 12,000 feet for the approach. We were kept at 12,000 feet until crossing ZZZZZ intersection (the IAF). Twelve thousand feet was significantly higher than the 10,600 feet the procedure calls for prior to ZZZZZ (from that direction) and the 7,500 foot minimum on the leg immediately to follow. The MSA in the area is 12,400 feet, however. We initiated a 2,000 FPM descent from 12,000 feet to get established. I believe we crossed ZZZZZ1 at (or near) the published 7,500 feet. Because we picked up the field visually when crossing overhead and I knew the area (once established inbound) was flat and free of obstructions, coupled with the relatively good visibility near ZZZZZ2 intersection (GS intercept at 6,800 feet), I suppose I transitioned (erroneously) into a 'visual approach, backed up with the RNAV' mentality and, as a result, continued the steeper descent beyond ZZZZZ2 and wound up at least 500 feet low. I believe the early morning hour, featureless terrain, relatively good (though reduced) visibility and knowledge that the mountainous areas were now behind us lulled me into a more relaxed, visual approach mindset. The PM was heads-down and neither of us recognized how low we really were until we got an altitude alert from the aircraft. At that point, I leveled off, recognized the fact we were just under 1,000 feet AGL at approximately 4 NM from the field climbed to correct the deficiency and elected to continue the approach, as we were now re-established with the field clearly in sight. We immediately called the field and continued visually. We waited until we were parked at the FBO before debriefing the flight.
ASRS:1840953.s: The pilot flying and a new Part 135 pilot on a Part 135 repositioning flight descended 500 feet below the RNAV (GPS) approach minimums due to a mistaken visual approach mindset. An altitude alert prompted a level-off and climb to correct the deviation before continuing visually to the airport.

ASRS:1840965.n: Upon departure from airport 47N, I noticed my GPS position shifted to a position north of the field even though I was tracking south followed by a fault indication... I suspected possible interference or spoofing or an issue with GPS unit itself as I have experienced this in the past and had to troubleshoot the issue with my avionics shop and manufacturer on numerous occasions so I immediately restarted my GPS unit in the aircraft. As I continued to track south and my unit was resetting I noticed WRI airport just south of us and immediately turned right and initiated climb to try to avoid their airspace. I then immediately contacted WRI for flight following and was advised I did indeed fly into the norther portion of their airspace.. This was completely unintentional and was the result of an equipment failure...
ASRS:1840965.s: The pilot departed airport 47N when a GPS fault caused a position shift, leading to an unintentional entry into WRI airspace while tracking south. The pilot attributed the airspace incursion to equipment failure and immediately restarted the GPS unit to correct the issue.

ASRS:1840997.n: While flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1 a 7 mile flight at 700 feet. I attempted to change Fuel tanks from Left to Right while passing the off position the valve stuck in the off position, it would not budge. The engine quit and I made an uneventful landing in a pasture. The pasture was smooth so the aircraft was fine. I found a #8 PK sheet metal screw was lodged under the handle while trying to change tanks. I dislodged the screw and flew the aircraft out of the pasture.The fuel selector in this model of Mooney is located on the floor under the pilot's legs it is difficult to reach. Also, the valve handle is in a recessed plastic fixture that allows things like this screw to collect.
ASRS:1840997.s: A pilot flying a Mooney at 700 feet experienced an engine quit when the fuel selector valve stuck in the off position due to a lodged #8 sheet metal screw. The pilot made an uneventful landing in a pasture, removed the screw, and flew the aircraft out.

ASRS:1841020.n: I was PF (Pilot Flying) on this leg, we were cleared to descend via KIDDZ 3 RNAV Arrival into HOU. Winds aloft were light and we were about eight miles behind a Company aircraft also following the same clearance and flight path, which led to some intermittent moderate turbulence. We were at 12,000 ft from the crossing restriction at SNIFY [when we] encountered the wake turbulence. I elected to descend early to 11,000 ft to avoid the conditions.The first attempt to do this I selected the ALT INT option to start the descent early to the next 11,000 ft restriction at RVEEE. That did not work for some reason, and the turbulence was not letting up, so I set the altitude to 11,000 ft from 6,000 ft (from the descend via clearance) and descended in Vertical Speed mode to get the aircraft down. I selected VNAV again once established at 11,000 ft to continue the arrival. Shortly after reaching 11,000 ft and selecting VNAV, we crossed RVEEE and I was expecting the aircraft to descend to make AAHZZ at 10,000 ft. The aircraft did not descend and I couldn't figure out why, and immediately was in the Yellow if not Red per the RRM (Risk and Resource Management) model. I quickly figured out the altitude selection in the MCP (Mode Control Panel) was not reselected to 6,000 ft. I quickly set the lower altitude and initiated a descend as quickly and safely as I could, but the delay in descent put us 700 ft high over AAHZZ. ATC didn't say anything, nor did we as there weren't any other aircraft conflicts.It is vital to maintain situational awareness and vigilance especially when changing descent modes during an RNAV arrival. The turbulence distraction should have been a trigger to do so to avoid errors such as not resetting the clearance altitude after reselecting the original MCP vertical mode VNAV. Another option was to request vectors from ATC or a delay vector to laterally escape and avoid the wake and alleviate the VNAV demand until we were well clear of the rough air.
ASRS:1841020.s: The Pilot Flying encountered wake turbulence while descending via the KIDDZ 3 RNAV arrival into HOU. After manually descending to 11,000 ft, the crew failed to reset the Mode Control Panel altitude, causing the aircraft to cross the AAHZZ waypoint 700 ft high before correcting the error.

ASRS:1841038.n: I filed due to almost aborting takeoff on an ORD departure because we thought there was a barricade up partway down the runway. In reality, it was the LAHSO (Land and Hold Short Lights) for Runway 9C. Company contacted the Tower and talked about the dangers of having these lights on when the runway is being used for takeoff. They can be easily confused for a barrier on the runway if you are not expecting them. This can cause an early rotation or a rejected takeoff. In our case we did and aggressive rotation. It a perfect set up for an accident.My last flight I again took off from Runway 9C and as I was partway down the runway, I noticed the LAHSO lights were if fact on again during takeoff. Knowing that this was the LAHSO lights, I knew this was not a problem but my First Officers were a bit concerned as they had not seen these lights before. We don't need someone making an unnecessary high-speed abort. This is going to cause an accident and maybe get someone killed. These lights should never be on when we are taking off. It is very disconcerting to say the least. We notified tower that they had the lights on when they told us to go to departure frequency.
ASRS:1841038.s: A pilot reported an aggressive rotation on an ORD departure from Runway 9C after mistaking active LAHSO lights for a runway barricade. The crew later notified the Tower that these lights were illuminated again during a subsequent takeoff, creating a risk of unnecessary high-speed aborts.

ASRS:1841044.n: I went off of comm one briefly to call ramp. We were approaching taxiway 1 for the ramp and parking. I got cleared in from ramp. I turned my head up and left and saw Aircraft Y that seemed to fill the entire windshield. The Captain was already starting to brake and I added additional braking from my side because he was so close. I told ground we almost hit Aircraft Y. Ground said sorry. Aircraft Y said ground told him we would give way. I never heard that clearance or acknowledged it. Aircraft Y was taxiing fast down taxiway 1. Was not stopping for anything obviously. Landed at ZZZ, taxi instructions taxiway 3, 2, 1 to enter ramp for gate.Making the left turn from 2 onto 1, had to slam on the breaks to avoid a collision with Aircraft Y traveling at a high rate of speed southbound on taxiway 1. Asked ground what happened and they said 'sorry' while Aircraft Y stated that we were supposed to give way to them.We did not hear or acknowledge any such instructions. Continued the taxi to gate.
ASRS:1841044.s: The flight crew landed at ZZZ and nearly collided with Aircraft Y while taxiing from taxiway 2 to 1. The incident occurred because Aircraft Y was taxiing at high speed under a clearance to proceed that the crew did not hear or acknowledge.

ASRS:1841046.n: During taxi in we entered the ramp from the south north bound for gate XX. While abeam XX1 the Captain had spotted our gate and I was looking out the right side clearing out wing tip. I looked over to the Captain's side and saw headlights going under our airplane from the left side. I immediately tip the Captain 'Stop, Stop, Stop!'He slammed on the brakes and we stopped the airplane. The truck off our left continued and almost ran into the left side of our nose wheel. I personally believe the driver was on his phone or was distracted and almost collided with us.I immediately reported this truck to ramp control. The truck reversed and drove away under the terminal the opposite direction he was traveling (in an attempt to hide).I checked with the FAs that all were sitting down and that everyone was okay. No damage to the aircraft resulted nor any passenger or crew member was injured.
ASRS:1841046.s: During taxi, the First Officer spotted a truck passing under the aircraft's left side and alerted the Captain, who applied brakes to stop. The distracted truck driver nearly struck the nose wheel but reversed away; no damage or injuries occurred.

ASRS:1841073.n: Tires and brake were on DSTG but I did not put them on [aircraft], did not show at the gate. I did pit [brakes] by mistake, thinking that the tires were going to show up on time, but never did and I forgot to take them off on the scanner before closing the flight, causing a weight discrepancy.
ASRS:1841073.s: A mechanic mistakenly included tires and brakes in the flight weight calculation while they were still at the DSTG and never loaded onto the aircraft. This error occurred because the mechanic forgot to remove the items from the scanner before closing the flight, resulting in a weight discrepancy.

ASRS:1841171.n: I was informed by my supervisor that an aircraft I worked on as an inspector had a #1 Engine [Vibration] Amber during climb. Pilot ran QRH and after 5 min. amber went away. Message came up again in cruise. Pilot ran QRH again after power reduction. We sent a crew of 2 for a road trip to address the issue along with what looks like had a bird strike event on said engine. The corrective action was that they found engine fan blades 21 and 23 on left engine to have bumpers missing and found later at the units hub.On my first day of the week on ZZZ Company hangar, I was informed by the supervisor that we had an aircraft with a dual engine blade and blade pin replacement due to flight crew reporting L/H (left hand) engine amber LP (Low Pressure) vibration of 4.0 on climb. I was the inspector on duty. When I got to work, all engine blades and pins had been removed. They had one mechanic per each engine and I was the inspector for both. We performed all maintenance IAW (in accordance with) ST Cards and maintenance manuals as required. I was there for the installation of all blades from start to finish, including bumper gap inspection.I am submitting this report in case of an assumption that we might have deviated from any maintenance procedure. We did not. This is a way for me to tell my side of the situation. Like I said I was there for all the installation process and I believe that if somehow the bumpers where incorrectly installed it would have reflected on the blade gap checks and at the time they were all within engine specs. It is also important to notice that said aircraft had a bird strike ingestion event resulting in some blade damage on said engine location. I hope this information helps. Thank you.
ASRS:1841171.s: An inspector reported that a ZZZ Company aircraft experienced left engine vibration and a bird strike, leading to the replacement of fan blades 21 and 23. The inspector confirmed all maintenance followed procedures and bumper gaps were within specs, refuting assumptions of procedural deviation.

ASRS:1841178.n: I was approaching FNL from the southeast with the intention to land. When 10 miles out and at pattern altitude, I called the temporary Tower to report my position and intentions. I was instructed to report 4 miles out. When 4 miles out, I reported and was instructed to enter the midfield left downwind for Runway 15. I was also informed to look for departing traffic headed to the northwest. Suddenly, my ADS-B traffic alerted me to traffic at same altitude, same position. I saw a low wing aircraft at the top left of my windscreen headed for me. The other pilot dived and passed approximately 300 feet under me and continued seemingly barely missing two water towers seemingly flying between them. It should be noted that the tower at FNL is temporary and has no current access to radar but relies on visual observation from the ground level. Though, radar has been installed, it has not been certified for almost a year now due to FAA imposed Covid restrictions. Seems to me that having radar access would have avoided this situation and not having radar is likely to lead to similar such close calls.
ASRS:1841178.s: A pilot approaching FNL for Runway 15 received a downwind clearance from a temporary tower lacking certified radar. Another aircraft passed 300 feet below the pilot after a sudden dive, an incident the reporter attributes to the tower's inability to provide radar traffic information.

ASRS:1841179.n: Approach to ZZZ flying with my wife from our home base at ZZZ1 via ZZZ2. conditions were good and VFR throughout. On approach to ZZZ Wind was 10 kts. gusting to 20 kts. from 320 degrees. I was confirmed to enter the left downwind for Runway XX. Runway XY was also available and another airplane was confirmed to land on [Runway] XY at the same time. Even thought [Runway] XY was shorter at 2;XXX ft. instead of over 4000 ft., I chose [Runway] XY for the wind. I was given clearance to land on [Runway] XY and flew a 180 to join the right base for Runway XY.I failed to treat Runway XY as a short field landing (slowing to 80 kts. and striking within the first 200 ft. of runway). Instead I was thinking of the gusty conditions and approached at normal landing speed plus. We touched down and then had a gust give us added lift extending our runway roll when we didn't have any margin. I thought to go around but it did not appear to be the safest maneuver. So I used the elevator and hard wheel brakes but we rolled beyond the runway and impacted a fence before we came to a stop.No injuries.On post [event] review, contributing factors could include the fact that I made a sudden runway decision change after 6 hours of flying time, a small portion (20 minutes) of which was above 12000 ft. I should have landed on [Runway] XX as assigned and dealt with the added 20 degrees of crosswind. It would have been within my capabilities and experience and would have given me a margin for the unexpected that I simply did not have on [Runway] XY.
ASRS:1841179.s: The pilot, flying a VFR approach to ZZZ after six hours of flight, elected to land on the shorter Runway XY instead of the assigned Runway XX due to wind conditions. Failure to execute a short-field landing technique in gusty winds resulted in an overrun and fence impact, though no injuries occurred.

ASRS:1841181.n: Aircraft X VFR Flight Operations Sight Seeing Hot Air Balloon.Approximately 15 minutes into the flight, I descended near the [the] River upstream of the Falls at [the] State Park. A low-level inversion over the river caused the balloon to rise slightly. Shortly after a wind rotor pushed the balloon down over the edge of the falls and back into the cascading water. The mechanical turbulence of this wind was stronger than I have ever experienced. I operated the burners to arrest the descent, gain altitude and ascend out of the gorge. The balloon landed safely 2 miles from the waterfalls. There were no injuries to passengers or pilot and no damage to the aircraft.Since this incident I have spent days reflecting on what occurred, the seriousness of this event, and what I can do differently in the future so that this never happens again. I've reached out to my colleagues for peer pilot review to process this self-critique. I've reviewed the FAA Balloon Flying Handbook. My research and reflection have led me to develop a corrective procedure and make immediate changes to my flight operations. Mechanical wind turbulence- resulting from wind flowing over irregular terrain or obstructions. When the air near the surface of the Earth flows over obstructions, such as irregular terrain, (bluffs, hills, mountains) and buildings, the normal horizontal wind flow is disturbed. As a result, it is transformed into eddies or other irregular air movements. The strength and magnitude of mechanical turbulence depends on: the speed of the wind, the nature of the obstruction, the stability of the air, and the angle at which the wind moves over the obstacle. As the air flows down the leeward side of the mountain, the air follows the contour of the terrain and is increasingly turbulent. This tends to push an aircraft into the side of a mountain. The stronger the wind, the greater the downward pressure and turbulence become. Due to the effect terrain has on the wind in valleys or canyons, downdrafts may be severe. I flew the balloon too close to an irregular terrain feature, canyon, river and waterfalls where Mechanical Wind Turbulence can be present and at varying levels of severity. I will no longer conduct low level waterfall passages as part of my flight operations. Instead I will approach them at no lower than half the height of the irregular terrain similar to flying over a mountain in a balloon. For example: The Falls in [the] State Park is 100 ft. tall. My flight procedure will be to fly no lower than 50 ft. above the river and falls below. This will insure safe altitude from the effects of mechanical wind turbulence on a hot air balloon.
ASRS:1841181.s: The pilot of a hot air balloon encountered severe mechanical wind turbulence while flying low over a waterfall, causing the aircraft to descend into cascading water. The pilot used burners to recover and landed safely with no injuries, subsequently changing operations to avoid low-level waterfall passages.

ASRS:1841194.n: After landing at ZGHA, crew exited C7 and were cleared Taxiway C, C4 then cleared to cross Runway 36L at B4 then handed over from Tower to Ground frequency for onward taxi. Ground ATC cleared crew to Taxi 'B, B2 stand 123 follow follow me' which was read back verbatim. At A3, an Air Carrier Y entered the Bravo taxiway right in front of the crew. The traffic wasn't holding at A3 but was on a continuous relatively quick taxi through the holding point. Crew were given no warning or instructions by Ground Controller and due to the local language (Mandarin) crew were unaware of any taxi clearance given to any other aircraft. Crew slowed down with medium braking and taxied to the stand uneventfully.
ASRS:1841194.s: After landing at ZGHA, the crew was cleared to taxi to stand 123 when an Air Carrier Y entered Taxiway B at A3 without holding. The incident occurred because Ground ATC provided no warning or instructions, and the crew could not understand Mandarin clearances issued to the other aircraft.

ASRS:1841241.n: Upon departure and climbing through 1,500 feet MSL, a Master Caution followed by Speed Trim on the overhead panel alerted us during the acceleration phase from flaps 1 to flaps 0. Shortly thereafter, I believe the autopilot tripped off or I disengaged the autopilot leaving me to manually fly the aircraft. It was then I noticed that my control wheel trim switches were not working. I asked the FO (First Officer) if his control wheel trim switches were working, and he said NO as well.It was then I extended the manual trim handle and proceeded to manually trim the aircraft. I also asked the FO to set speed to our current speed (approximately 210 knots) so to minimized as much trimming as possible. I then asked what Master Caution light illuminated, and the FO responded it was associated with the Speed Trim Light. I then called for the Speed Trim Fail Checklist in the QRH. The FO completed the Speed Trim Fail checklist, but there was no further direction in that checklist other than to continue normal operation. Nothing led us to refer to any other checklist such as Stabilizer Trim Inoperative due to our electric trim was not working.I then asked the FO to look and see if there was an Electric Trim Failure Checklist, because we did not have a jammed stabilizer nor a runaway Stabilizer Trim and the aircraft was flying just fine with the manual trim wheel. With me flying the aircraft and the FO trying to assist with ATC, QRH, while trying to assess the true problem, it apparently created a scenario where he simply overlooked the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative Checklist Condition statement.I was busy hand flying the aircraft, and with the distractions of talking to ATC and keeping the aircraft in trim, I did accidentally allow the aircraft to descend as much as 400 ft. below our assigned altitude of 3000 ft. MSL, but recovered quickly before ATC inquired. After realizing the additional task loading we were creating on ourselves, I elected to return to ZZZ without further troubleshooting. This set in motion a different set of task priorities for the FO in order to coordinate our return with ZZZ Operations and Maintenance. We evaluated our landing weight to be below MGLWT (Maximum Gross Landing Weight) and the only other immediate concern at the time was getting a longer final so we could get the aircraft configured and trimmed without getting behind in controlling the aircraft again.Once we caught up with our duties and were turning on final, I inquired again with the FO as if we had forgotten any possible QRH checklist for our condition. He again confirmed he could not find anything else in the QRH for Electric Trim Failure. That didn't sit at ease with me, as having recently completed the MAX training of runaway stabilizer. I remembered hand flying and trimming the aircraft and there was also something specific with the flap setting chosen, I just couldn't remember at the time. Even selecting flaps 30 for landing, something was still concerning me that I briefed the FO that in the event of the go-around, I may need help trimming the stabilizer through the configuration changes. The landing went uneventfully and taxiing back I still had that feeling we forgot a checklist in the QRH. After reaching the gate we verified, along with the Mechanic, that the electric stabilizer trim was indeed inoperative. I then had time to reach for the QRH myself and search through the checklist choices. It was then I found the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative Checklist, where the Condition and Objective statements under the title clearly stated and matched what our situation was.When I showed the FO the QRH Checklist for Stabilizer Trim Inoperative, he said he completely missed that as he was looking for something about Electric Stabilizer Trim Fail as I had called for, since the Manual Stabilizer Trim was working just fine.In the heat of the moment, sometimes confusion can take place and miscommunications can be amplified. In this case it was a Speed Trim Caution Light that lead us into the QRH, but in a correctly identified non-normal would of kept us into the QRH until all the proper checklists had been completed in this scenario. I recommend [adding] to the Speed Trim Fail Checklist a step prior to '#1 Continue normal operation.' I would word it (Condition: If stabilizer does not respond to control wheel electric trim inputs: Go to the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative checklist on page XX.)
ASRS:1841241.s: During climb, a Speed Trim caution and inoperative electric trim caused the crew to miss the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative checklist, resulting in a 400-foot altitude deviation. The pilot returned to base, landed safely, and later identified the missed checklist, recommending a QRH update to link Speed Trim failures to the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative procedure.

ASRS:1841264.n: While taxiing to Runway XXL at ZZZ we notified ZZZ Operations that we hadn't received or final weights for takeoff. After about 15 minutes of delay waiting for the weights, we were advised a return to the gate was required because the baggage handlers had not correctly placed baggage around our dangerous goods. While taxiing back to the gate, our Final DG Summary was received over ACARS. At this point, we realized that we had unknowingly taxied without our Final DG Summary. Upon return to the gate the baggage was correctly located around the DG and the rest of the flight continued uneventfully.
ASRS:1841264.s: The flight crew taxied to Runway XXL at ZZZ without a Final DG Summary due to a 15-minute delay caused by baggage handlers incorrectly placing dangerous goods. The aircraft returned to the gate to correct the load, received the summary via ACARS, and continued the flight uneventfully.

ASRS:1841289.n: On date, Aircraft X, while descending on the ZZZZZ3 arrival to ZZZ with both engines power set at about 70% we noticed the engine one oil temperature increasing to about 160 degrees C. Captain was the pilot flying and first officer was the pilot monitoring. I took the radio from the PM and called for the QRH. We reduced the power to idle and we noticed the temperature slowly getting back into the green arc. Then while still at idle the temperature started to rise again, but this time at a faster rate and as it reached 205 degrees C and in accordance with the QRH we proceeded with an engine shut down procedure of engine number one.We discontinued the approach, requested priority handling, and requested vectors towards ZZZ2, where the longer runways are more suitable for a single engine, flaps 20, approach.After running our single engine procedures we got cleared for the ILS X at ZZZ2, where we landed without further problems.The emergency vehicles where precautionary positioned by the RWY, and once cleared of the RWY they conducted a visual inspection of the aircraft.No visual damages were noticed so we continued to the gate and disembarked all the passengers.
ASRS:1841289.s: The crew of Aircraft X experienced a rising Engine 1 oil temperature during descent on the ZZZZZ3 arrival, prompting a QRH-guided shutdown at 205°C. They diverted to ZZZ2 for a single-engine ILS X landing, where emergency vehicles performed a visual inspection revealing no damage before the aircraft taxied to the gate.

ASRS:1841293.n: Approximately 4 hours prior to landing EICAS MSG HYD QTY LOW 1. Fault light also illuminated. Hydraulic quantity slowly depleted over the next hour to zero, however pressure and temp was normal. Conferred multiple times with dispatch Maintenance Control and Duty Pilot about possible tow in in ZZZ if needed. After 50 more minutes with a zero quantity reading EICAS MSG had PRESS ENG 1. Engine one pressure light also illuminated. Followed QRH and continued with engine pump off. ZZZ OPS and ATC arranged for runway XX for our arrival in the event we might require a tow off. During descent when selecting flaps 5 EICAS HYD PRESS system 1 followed QRH, notified ZZZ and ZZZ OPS that a tow off would be required. ZZZ ATC at that point stated they were going to use priority handling on our behalf, we did not request one, and we provided souls on board and fuel remaining. We continued flap and alternate gear extension and proceeded with a visual approach and landing to runway XX, followed by a tow to gate. Runway was closed for approximately 11 minutes.Crew worked great together and we were well prepared for the system loss and reviewed everything ahead of time. Speculation regarding ATC wanting us in an emergency status is it's most likely a local procedure addressing a planned runway closure and airport assistance required for the tow in. ZZZ currently had runway YYR closed so our planned closure left the airport with a single runway.
ASRS:1841293.s: The flight crew managed a hydraulic system 1 failure and subsequent engine 1 pressure loss on approach to ZZZ, following QRH procedures for a visual landing on runway XX. ATC provided priority handling and arranged a tow, causing an 11-minute runway closure due to the single remaining operational runway.

ASRS:1841314.n: After takeoff in ZZZ, went to retract the gear with it in system 1, gear would not come up. We then followed the ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor) and QRH and were directed to swap to system 2. Gear retracted normally in system 2. After that, we remembered that system 2 was on MEL. We discussed this enroute and elected to continue to ZZZ1. The flight continued with a normal landing.After getting the ECAM warning, we followed the ECAM and QRH as directed like we normally would under this circumstance. We swapped to system 2 and retracted the gear normally. We then continued the flight. On departure from ZZZ landing retraction system! was system used on takeoff, gear would not retract. We followed ECAM and QRH and instinctively switched to system 2 and raised the gear and continued flight. While enroute we discussed that system 2 was in MEL although system worked normal. Continued to ZZZ1 with normal landing.Out of normal habit to follow ECAM and QRH while in busy phase of flight we switched retract position to system 2 and gear retracted.
ASRS:1841314.s: The flight crew attempted to retract the landing gear using system 1 after takeoff from ZZZ, but it failed. They followed ECAM and QRH procedures to switch to system 2, which was on the MEL, successfully retracted the gear, and completed a normal landing at ZZZ1.

ASRS:1841333.n: I was assigned this hazard report. This unidentified report brought to light a dangerous change in procedures at the LCI (Laconia, New Hampshire) airport. Pilot report: At LCI, Jeppsen airport diagram stipulates right-hand traffic for Runway 26, while permanent NOTAM for the airport states left-hand traffic for that Runway. The published pattern altitude for turbine aircraft is 2045 [feet] MSL - an unsafe altitude to clear rising terrain south of Runway 26 on a left downwind. 3,000 feet is a much better altitude - but be advised that after clearing the last of the terrain, you must fly a 5-mile final to descend the 2,500 feet to the Runway. The Runway 26 PAPI has a 3.08% inclination. The Jeppsen chart is incorrect. We contacted the FBO over the radio during arrival to ask what the REAL traffic pattern to fly for Runway 26 is, and they confirmed it is left traffic. I called the airport manager and he explained that he inquired with the FAA about changing Runway 26 to left traffic pattern. The FAA took it as a request to change and ended up changing Runway 26 to left traffic. After communicating this with the FAA, they are requesting a different form to be filled out by the manager. In the meantime, a NOTAM has been issued for left traffic for Runway 26. A NOTAM shows until permanent and at a normal traffic pattern altitude of 2,045 feet on a left pattern for Runway 26, you would fly extremely close to a ski hill at 2,382 feet. After noting this, we have put a note into our flight ops manual that will notify any crew that right traffic or a higher traffic pattern altitude for left traffic is authorized by the airport manager. I filed a report on the FAA safety hotline.I believe the traffic pattern should be switched back to right traffic.
ASRS:1841333.s: A pilot reported a hazardous conflict at Laconia (LCI) where a permanent NOTAM mandates left traffic for Runway 26, contradicting Jeppesen charts and creating unsafe terrain clearance at the published 2,045 feet pattern altitude. The pilot attributed this to an FAA procedural error and advised crews to use right traffic or a higher altitude until the chart is corrected.

ASRS:1841335.n: In cruise at FL 220 at approx. XA35, both generators failed, immediately followed by a right bleed air warming light. Secured right bleed light per checklists. Right bleed warning light extinguished and elected to leave bleed secured. Then attempted reset of both generators and managed a reset of the left generator with normal load, frequency and volts. Shortly thereafter requested a divert to nearest suitable airfield which was ZZZ. Made a normal approach and landing and taxied to maintenance hangar. No other issues to report.Warning and caution lights illuminated.
ASRS:1841335.s: During cruise at FL 220, both generators failed followed by a right bleed air warning. The crew secured the right bleed, reset the left generator, and diverted to ZZZ for a normal landing and maintenance inspection.

ASRS:1841382.n: Upon departure from XYR at ZZZ, I received a false terrain alert from the TAWS system. That caused to delay the activation of the 'nav' mode on my flight director which delayed my turn to the ZZZZZ intersection. ATC gave me an expedited turn to a heading of 350 to get me headed toward ZZZZZ. Based on what I saw on my TCAS, I don't believe there was a loss of separation.
ASRS:1841382.s: The pilot experienced a false TAWS terrain alert during departure from XYR, delaying flight director 'nav' mode activation and the turn to ZZZZZ. ATC issued an expedited heading of 350, and the pilot reported no loss of separation based on TCAS observations.

ASRS:1841383.n: Military Base started a controlled burn in a field adjacent to [the] runway in use (Runway XX). We were conducting a training flight under VFR in a Large UAS equipped with IR (infrared) cameras. Smoke from the fire was not visible on the IR cameras that we use for flight and visibility was unrestricted in IR. We decided to continue the training flight utilizing these cameras. After a couple hours, Tower queried us about our flight visibility. We responded that our visibility was unrestricted with the IR cameras. They had immediately prior to that question informed us that visibility to the North was 1 SM due to the smoke from the fires. They then said that we did not have an LAO (Local Area Orientation) with them to be able to use our IR visibility as flight visibility. We then told Tower that we would make the next landing to a full stop for flight termination. I am filing this report due to Tower reporting 1 SM of visibility which falls below Class D VFR weather minimums despite our actual visibility being unlimited.
ASRS:1841383.s: A Large UAS crew conducting VFR training near a military base continued flight using IR cameras despite smoke from an adjacent controlled burn. Tower terminated the flight after stating the crew lacked a Local Area Orientation to use IR visibility, citing reported 1 SM visibility below Class D minimums.

ASRS:1841389.n: ORF is an active Airline and GA airport. There are separate clearance, ground, and local control frequencies. With moderate to heavy traffic, a single controller was handling all three. This created multiple instances of blocked communication. The controller had to juggle all three plus ground coordination with the TRACON. This created an unsafe condition in my opinion. In decades of flying all over the country, I've never encountered this situation. During periods of slow traffic or at less busy airports it works but not under these conditions. The controller was doing the best he could but both pilots and controller were placed into a dangerous situation.Had there been an incident, poor communications would certainly have been a root cause. I would also add that too many pilots and controllers have not learned that speaking faster isn't better. Miscommunication leads to loss of separation, violations, and occasionally crashes. The pros on both sides of the mic have a well-defined cadence that chunks information which largely eliminates repeats and errors.The tower chief needs to reassess staffing requirements during peak periods.
ASRS:1841389.s: A pilot reported that a single controller handling clearance, ground, and local frequencies at ORF during heavy traffic caused blocked communications and an unsafe condition. The reporter attributed this risk to understaffing and poor communication cadence, urging a reassessment of staffing requirements during peak periods.

ASRS:1841397.n: While flying with a student on a student pilot lesson we made evasive action to avoid a conflict. I am the Flight Instructor and immediately took flight controls and made the evasive actions to avoid traffic in Class D airspace. The situation Aircraft X was on UPWIND in the traffic pattern climbing to TPA (traffic pattern altitude) and turning Crosswind. I was in Aircraft Y squaring our turn to enter a downwind at TPA. Aircraft Z was following me into the traffic pattern to come into land. Tower told us at a visual checkpoint to fly west and square our turn to enter a downwind (north) for the traffic pattern. We had a strong left quartering headwind pushing us north toward the pattern. Aircraft X was out of sight underneath the cowling. Tower asked if we had traffic (Aircraft X) in sight ahead. We did not. Student flying drifting into the pattern and slowly correcting. After Traffic came into sight it was closer than I feel was comfortable less than .5 mile. We were drifting at TPA north and toward traffic, Aircraft X was climbing and turning toward us. As Aircraft X became visual ADS-B made a 'TRAFFIC SAME ALTITUDE 12 O'CLOCK' call. I took flight controls and banked left to avoid traffic to fly south. As I was turning south Aircraft Z was getting closer to us. I stopped my turn at 160-170 and banked a slight turn right to allow Aircraft Z to pass us.The problem arose because of lack of wind correction angle, ATC call, and traffic separation. Contributing factors strong low altitude winds, high traffic congestion, lack of traffic in sight. Corrective actions were speaking about wind correction angle after landing, drawing the situation, ATC workload, the ability to say UNABLE then adjusting flight for safety of flight. Human performance considerations decision of me to allow the student to drift off course and not correct faster. ATC high workload with Aircraft zooming into land. My student and I debriefed after we landed about how we could have avoided the problem and how we will do better next time on our flight. It was a good teaching moment for high workload areas, ATC clearances, and safety of flight. For context, I am a student. I am currently transitioning from a C172 over to a Piper. While doing pattern work at ZZZ, a close call occurred during the upwind leg of the pattern. I pushed the Piper's nose down a little to clear my crosswind turn, and began to make the turn. A few seconds later I saw another one of the [FBO] aircraft, at the same altitude, not moving. I realized our aircraft were on a collision course and took immediate evasive action to avoid the oncoming aircraft. About the same time I was taking Evasive actions my CFI saw the traffic on ADS-B. Tower was not calling our crosswind and no alarms in the aircraft sounded. It is unclear if the other aircraft took evasive actions as well. The issue was resolved by rejoining the downwind and resuming normal operations.It is also unknown if Tower was aware of the other aircraft's position. I feel that if Tower had called our base, the situation would have been avoided completely. Overall this really shook me up. I regathered myself and finished the lesson, but both me and my CFI were upset with the controller and rattled by the situation. Seeing the growing silhouette of another airplane, unmoving and hanging in the air is a terrifying thing to experience, and I hope that less pilots have to go through it.
ASRS:1841397.s: A Flight Instructor and student in a Piper executing a traffic pattern at ZZZ made evasive maneuvers to avoid a collision with a stationary aircraft at the same altitude. The conflict resulted from strong winds causing drift, lack of visual contact, and insufficient ATC traffic advisories, requiring the instructor to take control and alter course.

ASRS:1841404.n: I was operating my Piper PA-28-180 at ZZZ. Gross weight was 1,875 lbs and balance was within range per the AFM with just myself and 34 gallons of fuel onboard. Wind was calm and outside air temperature was 94 F (34.4 C), altimeter 29.98. Taxiway B was planned as a takeoff abort point. Calculated takeoff distance over a 50 feet obstacle was 2,250 feet.Engine start, taxi and runup were normal, before takeoff checklist was completed. I received clearance and began a takeoff from Runway XXR. RPM and airspeed did not rise as expected. I made a decision to abort the takeoff and pulled power back to idle. After moderate braking the airplane entered the smooth gravel overrun area. After receiving clearance from Tower, I performed a 180 and taxied the aircraft back to the ramp under its own power.Based on my evaluation of a low power condition I flagged the aircraft as unairworthy and turned it over to my A&P for maintenance.
ASRS:1841404.s: The pilot of a Piper PA-28-180 aborted takeoff from Runway XXR at ZZZ due to unexpected low RPM and airspeed. The aircraft stopped safely in the gravel overrun, was taxied back to the ramp, and flagged unairworthy for maintenance.

ASRS:1841415.n: I was flying my small UAS when what was possibly a trainer aircraft flew over so low that I didn't see the aircraft until it flew over. The aircraft was so low that my drone was warning me about being too close to the aircraft as I was descending to land. I was running navigation lights as required by regulations that can be seen for 3 miles. The aircraft seemed to be around 300 to 400 feet above ground level and I was about 190 feet above ground. I am flying in class G airspace with woods all around me. My drone was kept in visual line of sight the whole time and was fully legal.
ASRS:1841415.s: A UAS operator in Class G airspace reported a near-midair conflict with a low-flying trainer aircraft while descending to land. The trainer passed at approximately 300–400 feet AGL, triggering a proximity warning on the drone operating at 190 feet AGL despite the UAS displaying required navigation lights.

ASRS:1841416.n: I was flying my drone over some woods when the controller screen went blank. The footage had been glitching all day. This is an ongoing issue with Smart Controllers and DJI Air 2S based on my research. I contacted the company and they have told me to try some things and blamed it on the software.
ASRS:1841416.s: The drone pilot experienced a blank controller screen and footage glitches while flying a DJI Air 2S over woods. The pilot attributes this ongoing issue to Smart Controller software problems, as confirmed by the manufacturer's response.

ASRS:1841459.n: IAH was landing in an east flow configuration while departing Runways 15L and 9. We were vectored for an approach in VMC conditions to runway 8R. The approach was straight forward as the winds were rather consistent meaning no gusts encountered the entire way down the approach. The aircraft was stable and configured properly and accordingly with what seemed like very little input needed from the PF to maintain the approach profile both laterally and vertically. We approached the runway and I noticed an aircraft beginning the takeoff roll on 15L and did not think anything of it. In the round-out to flare, the airplane abruptly rolled left while being pushed to the left of the centerline of the runway and then had the nose yaw to the right at about 30-50 feet RA according to the callouts I recall hearing. This also coincided with the Runway 15L threshold passing behind my right shoulder as I recall. The PF made some quick and precise control inputs to get the aircraft back over the centerline wings level and landed while still in the TDZ. As soon as the airplane was slowing and tracking the centerline the PF made a comment/question wondering what the heck happened. I stated that I had an idea, but would wait until we cleared the runway to continue the conversation. After clearing I stated to the Captain I thought we might have encountered a jet blast event due to the surface winds and the aircraft departing on 15L. I was unsure what the aircraft type was that departed 15L as from the cursory glance I gave it on final it did not look like a widebody, so again I did not even think that we might be setting ourselves up for a jet blast encounter. That being said, this was the end of our second leg in this very jet and it had performed flawlessly both flights, so I do not think that there was any malfunction that could be associated with this event.
ASRS:1841459.s: The crew landing at IAH on Runway 8R experienced an abrupt left roll and right yaw near 30-50 feet RA while a departing aircraft on Runway 15L began its takeoff roll. The pilot attributed the deviation to jet blast from the departing aircraft, noting the plane was recovered and landed safely without mechanical malfunction.

ASRS:1841489.n: While working a 4 leg day in Aircraft X eating lunch in the cockpit, I decided to open the window for some fresh air during a sit. I noticed as I tried to open the window, the window handle was jammed in the clipboard. After many attempts, I found that the only way to open the window was to move the clipboard sideways (something that DOES not occur and is not required in our 175 aircraft) and I found this to be concerning. If I was in a high stress environment during an evacuation and had to open the window to jump our with the rope, I am not confident that this would have been figured out in time. I have not seen any documentation on this. The clipboard is definitely in a different position on these aircraft in reference to the window opening handle, and that needs to be discussed, or the clipboards need to be moved.Clipboard is much closer to window opening handle on 170 aircraft than 175, and causes the window opening handle to jam unless clipboard is moved out of the way.Document this difference in the 170 aircraft, or move clipboards.
ASRS:1841489.s: A pilot on Aircraft X (170) found the cockpit window handle jammed by a clipboard during a sit, requiring the clipboard to be moved sideways to open the window. The pilot reported this configuration difference from the 175 aircraft as a potential evacuation hazard and requested documentation or repositioning of the clipboard.

ASRS:1841505.n: Our aircraft came to the gate directly from the maintenance hangar. We were given [Runway] XR for take off. I was the Pilot Monitoring (PM). Due to wind shear alerts on the approach, and WX moving toward the field, we elected to do a TOGA take off. We were on the ZZZZZ Departure, but were given a heading immediately after takeoff to avoid a cell. Approximately 5-7 min after takeoff, and cleared to climb to 16k feet, we got a 'DOOR L EMER EXIT' EICAS message. The First Officer (FO) declared it was his aircraft and we identified the need to level off at 10k. I notified Departure, and they gave us clearance to stop climb at 10k. I told him we were troubleshooting and we would need to return to ZZZ. We requested priority. The FO took over the radio, and I was tying to determine the problem and keep the passengers and flight attendants appraised of the situation. I briefed the flight attendants a couple of times on ALL, and made a PA to the passengers. The number 1 Flight Attendant told me that a cover for that over wing emergency exit had fallen off. I notified the company through ACARS that we were returning to ZZZ and they acknowledged. Meanwhile, the weather had hit the airport, and they asked us if we wanted to land with a tailwind, or if we wanted to wait for the field to be turned around. (Landing west now)We told them we would prefer to land with a headwind. They told us to expect the RNAV to [Runway] XX because the ILS was not up yet. We accomplished the descent checklist and set up for the RNAV. Approach later told the plane ahead of us that the ILS was working now, so we set up for that while being vectored. The weather was not optimal - there was a strong rain column over the field, about 1/2 way down Runway XX, but we had a good visual on the field. We discussed the need for a hard go-around if needed. After an outstanding landing from the right seat, we were met by possibly every priority vehicle at ZZZ as we taxied clear of [Runway] XX. They checked that we did not need any further assistance, and the on scene commander followed us all the way to the recovery gate. After evaluation by maintenance, we were told that the cover that had fallen off is held in place by a rather flimsy metal clip. There is a magnet on the cover, and when the cover is removed, it causes the alarm that we received. He said that the covers are routinely removed when the plane is in the hanger, and that they can sometimes get loose. They eventually adjusted the clips for both over wing exits and returned the aircraft to service. We flew it to ZZZ1 and back with no further issues.I was told that, had the handle been pulled on the emergency exit, due to the plug nature of the exit, the hatch would most likely not have moved. The slide, however, would have deployed. This would have caused major controllability issues. Additionally, after discussing it with safety, I was told that this is not a common problem, but it is one that could use greater awareness for pilots. The metal clip holding the emergency exit cover in place was either loose or had not been seated properly. Had the cover fallen off at altitude, the EICAS would have asked for an emergency descent to 10k, which would, obviously be very dramatic. Our air interrupt and any further similar events could be avoided if the pilots were trained to replace the cover before as step one in trouble shooting.
ASRS:1841505.s: The Pilot Monitoring reported that a 'DOOR L EMER EXIT' EICAS message occurred shortly after takeoff due to a loose metal clip on an over-wing exit cover. The crew returned to the departure airport for a safe landing, and maintenance adjusted the clips to prevent recurrence.

ASRS:1841553.n: Approaching ZZZ approx 30 miles to the south at 10,000 ft speed 250 knots. Received traffic call from ATC reporting aircraft at 12 oclock 9000 ft heading south. While looking for traffic received TCAS caution close 500 feet below and climbing. Caution quickly changed to warning with direction to climb. Executed TCAS procedures climbing over contact. Crew never visually acquired aircraft. Resumed previous clearance at 10,000 ft when called clear. Reported TCAS event to ATC. Be prepared for TCAS events in ZZZ.
ASRS:1841553.s: A pilot approaching ZZZ at 10,000 feet received a TCAS warning of an aircraft 500 feet below and climbed to avoid it. The crew never visually acquired the traffic but resumed their clearance after ATC declared them clear.

ASRS:1841555.n: During RNAV (RNP) M approach to ZZZ Runway XX, the crew of Aircraft X was made aware of company traffic (Aircraft Y) approaching ZZZ with a similar arrival time, as well as another company aircraft (Aircraft Z) requesting departure clearance. After descending on the approach to an altitude where the crew could remain VMC, the crew cancelled IFR to allow company traffic to obtain a clearance. Aircraft X crew broadcasted their position and FMC predicted landing time, and stated intentions to land Runway XX on CTAF. ZZZ radio advised Aircraft Z that they were released for departure. However, when Aircraft Z did not immediately depart or make a radio call stating intentions, the crew of Aircraft X queried them on the company frequency. Aircraft Z responded that they were not aware of their release, and then again contacted ZZZ radio to confirm.After receiving confirmation of their release, Aircraft Z announced that they were departing Runway YY. At this time there was a lack of clarity where Aircraft Z was on the airfield, and the crew of Aircraft X became uncomfortable with the developing situation. The crew discussed that there may be a need to discontinue the approach, but made one more attempt to communicate with Aircraft Z. Based on the presumed impending missed approach, the PF delayed calling for further configuration, and continued toward Runway XX visually, while the PM broadcasted Aircraft X's position, and attempted to determine Aircraft Y's position on the airfield. Ultimately, the crew initiated a non-standard missed approach with a climbing left turn, and announced on CTAF that they would be holding visually over the water north of ZZZ at 1,500 ft. During the missed approach turn, the crew experienced a GPWS caution for terrain that they visually determined to not be a factor. However, the PF did increase thrust and pitch to clear terrain by a wider margin. During visual holding, the PF maintained aircraft configuration at flaps 5 to allow for lower air speeds and improved maneuvering. While Aircraft X was completing a visual 360 degree turn north of ZZZ, Aircraft Z departed Runway YY with a left turn to the southeast, and Aircraft X announced their position and intention to land Runway XX on CTAF. At this time additional company traffic Aircraft Y broadcasted their position and estimated landing Runway YY within 1 minute of Aircraft X.Due to weather observed moving in southeast of ZZZ, the crew of Aircraft X determined the prudent action would be to make an additional visual holding pattern north of ZZZ to allow Aircraft Y to land, as opposed to flying a VFR downwind to Runway YY. To ensure Aircraft Y would have enough time to clear and that both aircraft would not be on approach from opposite directions at the same time, the PF of Aircraft X elected to enlarge the visual holding pattern to the north. Again, Aircraft X crew announced their position and intentions on CTAF. During the visual maneuver, the crew received another GPWS caution for terrain north of them and initiated a turn to the west. Visibility and cloud clearances were excellent in the area and the crew had all terrain well in sight. After Aircraft Y landed and while Aircraft X was maneuvering for a visual approach to Runway XX with raw ILS data tuned and monitored in the background, the crew observed that a cloud had blown in from the south across the final approach path to Runway XX, requiring the PF to fly below the glide path to maintain VMC. During this approach on short final, while on visual and ILS centerline but below glide path at approximately 800 feet, the crew received a glide slope alert which was silenced, and a persistent GPWS caution annunciation. Again, the aircraft was observed to be on centerline and well clear of all terrain, but in an attempt mitigate the GPWS alerts, the PF offset slightly left and continued a descent toward the runway. At approximately 600 feet the crew received a GPWS warning and command of pull up. The crew again observed that they were clear of all obstacles and continued to a landing without further incident.After reviewing the event, the crew determined that they should have initiated a missed approach and turn sooner and at the first indication that opposite direction traffic may become an issue. This would have prevented the crew from descending below 1,000 feet without being fully configured, and may have prevented the first GPWS caution. Although the weather supported holding in VMC, the crew could have requested an IFR clearance to climb to a higher holding altitude and follow traffic into Runway YY.
ASRS:1841555.s: During a visual approach to ZZZ Runway XX, Aircraft X crew initiated a non-standard missed approach due to conflicting traffic and terrain proximity, triggering multiple GPWS cautions and a pull-up warning. The crew landed safely but concluded they should have missed earlier to avoid descending below 1,000 feet unconfigured and to prevent terrain alerts.

ASRS:1841602.n: When we got to the airplane in ZZZ there was an MEL in the logbook that Maintenance was working on MEL 33-XX-XX-X due on [Date 1]. The Maintenance Technician signed off the MEL as fixed, and we received an amendment from Dispatch removing the MEL prior to the door closing. In ZZZ1 the release had the MEL back on it. The Captain called Dispatch about it and got transferred to Maintenance. The Maintenance team over the phone said the MEL was never closed out in their system, so according to our logbook and Dispatch we were okay, but on the Maintenance side we had an MEL open. The Captain corrected the logbook in ZZZ1 with Maintenance via phone and added MEL 33-XX-XX-X due [Date 2] into the logbook. The back end maintenance system needs to match the logbooks. Electronic logbooks can mitigate this risk by having multiple parties see the actual aircraft logs versus several phone calls going back and forth. There was a breakdown between Maintenance Control and Dispatch because our Dispatcher saw it as closed out hence he removed it and provided the amendment.
ASRS:1841602.s: The crew and maintenance teams experienced a discrepancy where Dispatch removed an MEL based on a signed logbook, but the maintenance system still showed it open. The Captain corrected the logbook in ZZZ1 after Maintenance confirmed the item was never closed in their system, highlighting a breakdown between Dispatch and Maintenance Control.

ASRS:1841605.n: We were descending via the SNDIA 4 for the ILS Runway 8. Passing ASIDE intersection I noticed that my MFD (Multi Function Display) screen when zoomed in didn't exactly match the Captain's side. As we continued down the arrival we received a clearance for the ILS 8 approach. Going through about 8,000 feet both the Captain and I were looking at a very large discrepancy now between our two screens. The autopilot was coupled to the Captain's side so it was still following what we thought was the correct track. I switched to green needles in anticipation for the turn to the localizer off the transition route and now noticed we were flying through the localizer but our FMS still had us at the previous point prior to the turn. Both the Captain and I were unfamiliar with the airport especially at night, so we were planning on flying the full approach. ATC then asked us to report any GPS issues, which I had responded with yes we believe we have lost GPS, looking for vectors.At this time I had gotten visual contact with the runway as well as the Captain who was flying. We both agreed that due to our current location it was best to discontinue the approach and try again. We went around and got vectored around. The second approach had no issues as we got vectors to final off the localizer. It was later found out that the military was jamming the GPS signal. We also received a terrain INOP yellow message displayed on our MFD's for a few minutes but no associated EICAS message. A GPS signal lost was never displayed on either FMS. We do not know how long or how far off course we were on the arrival as it appeared okay on our end, and ended up missing the turn to the localizer as our FMS was telling us we were several miles behind our current position. ATC needs to be aware of potential military GPS jamming so they can provide that information to the pilots. We did not see a NOTAM in ABQ for jamming either. Given it also being night around terrain, ATC should have provided vectors from the beginning and not the RNAV arrival since GPS signal could not be guaranteed.
ASRS:1841605.s: Two pilots flying an RNAV arrival at night experienced GPS signal loss due to military jamming, causing FMS position discrepancies and a missed turn. They executed a go-around after visual contact, noting no GPS lost warnings or terrain EICAS messages, and successfully completed a second approach with ATC vectors.

ASRS:1841622.n: Winds 140/15 gust 25, Tower broadcast landing aircraft report +-15 kts on final. Regional jet taking off ahead of us showed large downwind drift after rotation. Prior to takeoff I briefed TOGA on takeoff roll if necessary. We tracked center-line until 110 kts then the aircraft weather-vaned 30 degrees to the left (gusts exceeded rudder control). If we rejected we would have departed the runway. I applied full right rudder, right aileron and selected TOGA with the aircraft correcting and the left main gear on the left runway edge striping. Rather than risk further drift to the left I elected to rotate 15-20 kts prior to VR. After becoming airborne the right wing dipped 7-10 degrees, I neutralized aileron and rudder, called for gear up and continued the climbout. We immediately reported the windshear (horizontal) and I believe we were the last takeoff out of ZZZ. We reported the incident to Dispatch and he told us all the airports in the area were ground stopped.I believe we encountered a sudden horizontal windshear, with resulting side gusts, exceeding the aircraft capability to maintain heading at a critical phase of takeoff. I believe a runway change to [Runway] XXR would have aligned us with the wind and prevented this incident.ATC should not hesitate to change runways so that aircraft are taking off into the wind. Especially when the winds are strong and gusty crosswinds. I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) and we were cleared into position and hold for Runway XYR full length in ZZZ. The winds were gusty but nothing beyond our limits. ATIS reported 140/17G27 with LLWS in the area. In addition Tower had relayed to landing aircraft for XXL reports of +15 kts. on final near 500 ft. As we entered the runway the CA (Captain) PF (Pilot Flying) mentioned, 'We have TOGA available if we need it.' There were no reports by previous aircraft, a company 777 and an RJ, of any airspeed gain or loss on takeoff and there were no LLWS warnings issued. We were cleared for takeoff and I believe Tower reported wind gusting to 24, still well below our limits. The CA PF added power normally and we began the takeoff roll. The engines came up normally. The airspeed moved rather quickly beyond 80 to 90 kts as the engines stabilized at FLEX and I called 90. As I looked up from the engines and the airspeed the aircraft began to move off centerline slightly then began a more rapid turn to the left to the point of the right mains being to the left of the centerline. At this point I called out to the CA PF, 'Centerline, centerline, centerline.' and we continued a drift to the left. I looked down to begin stepping on the rudder with the CA PF to maintain directional control and it appeared full right rudder was applied. I then looked up and was about to call reject when the CA PF began to pitch up as we slowly regained directional control. Our airspeed was not yet at V1, probably 10 kts., perhaps a little more below. We were approximately 3000 ft down the runway I believe but I'm not certain. At this point a reject was out of the question as we were airborne and turning back towards the centerline. The CA PF held a very slight pitch up and allowed the aircraft to slowly accelerate and fly out of the windshear. As we began a slow climb, speed was still low. The CA PF did an excellent job keeping the airplane from settling back to the ground without excessive pitch and at a very slow airspeed. Somewhere in this event the CA PF went to TOGA. I have no idea when but I believe it was shortly before we became airborne and turned back toward the centerline. The aircraft continued a climb and we climbed out with a normal takeoff out of about 200 ft. There was never a call of windshear by the aircraft or a noticeable change of the airspeed. I was 100% looking outside after 90 kts. to assess where we were and what I could do to help the CA PF control the aircraft. From the time of calling centerline to the time of getting airborne could not have been more than 3 seconds. It all happened incredibly fast. It was very smooth and not a single bump climbing to 800 ft. or so. The entire scenario lasted maybe 10 seconds but it felt like 20 minutes. I'm still not 100% certain what caused the drift to the left. The turn matched with the strong crosswinds. I'm fairly certain they were the cause but it could not have been the same wind speed as what the ATIS reported and what Tower stated. It was as if we entered an area with a significant wind increase that temporarily approached our crosswind limitations. At the slower airspeed and less rudder authority the capabilities of the aircraft may have been briefly exceeded until we accelerated and got more airflow over the rudder. I've taken off near crosswind limits before and I've never had this type of event. Not even close.I'm not sure anything could have been done differently. The CA mentioned the availability of TOGA due to the winds which was crucial to the end result I believe. My call of centerline brought the CA into action to which he stated was a good thing. We were both very surprised by the rapid turn, like the startle effect almost. The only thing I could have done was call reject sooner but it was not necessary until we made the rapid turn to the left and subsequently became airborne.
ASRS:1841622.s: A regional jet crew experienced severe left drift during takeoff at ZZZ due to sudden horizontal windshear exceeding rudder authority. The Pilot Flying applied TOGA and rotated early to avoid runway departure, successfully climbing out after the aircraft corrected.

ASRS:1841627.n: Beginning descent into ZZZ, a cascading electrical failure occurred causing multiple light to illuminate and several system to fail, including iff, trim, left aft fuel pump, equipment cooling supply, pack controller left, multiple window heat over heats, etc...noted TR2 was zero amps. Ran QRH checklists...until 8,000 feet MSL when landing became primary task. Requested priority handling and landed uneventfully. Airport Support personnel assisted, no external hot-spots found. Taxied to gate. Coordinated with local Maintenance Control.A cascading electrical failure occurred on descent into ZZZ. It is unknown how to prevent electrical failures. Recommend development of QRH multiple electric failure check list...executing all individual light procedures is time consuming and diverts attention from large situation.
ASRS:1841627.s: During descent into ZZZ, the crew experienced a cascading electrical failure causing multiple system malfunctions and zero amps on TR2. They executed QRH checklists until 8,000 feet MSL, requested priority handling, and landed uneventfully with no external hot-spots found.

ASRS:1841632.n: High Speed Reject at 130-135 knots due to engine failure indication. Aircraft yawed to the right with the illumination of the Engine Fail Light. Exited runway, ran all checklists. All engines were still running within normal parameters. Contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control. They asked us if we wanted to try another takeoff. We declined. (This was a CA upgrade IOE flight.) Directed to Maintenance pad where line Maintenance downed the aircraft.[Reporter stated being] unsure [of the cause]. After reject, all engine parameters were normal.
ASRS:1841632.s: During a CA upgrade IOE takeoff, the crew executed a high-speed reject at 130-135 knots due to an engine failure indication and right yaw. Although all engines subsequently showed normal parameters, the crew declined a second attempt and the aircraft was towed to the maintenance pad.

ASRS:1841634.n: On pushback from ZZZZ ramp, mechanic on the headset advised tow bar disconnected, bypass pin removed and said he was clearing to the left. He appeared on the left, showed the pin and waived us off and walked back towards the spot. We finished after start checklist and called for taxi. Ramp cleared us and I turned the taxi light on and started to push the power up (could have been worse had we taxied on 2 engines) as I cleared to the left. Then a tug front left tire appeared from below the cockpit. I jumped on the brakes and stopped the airplane and observed the mechanic running back to the tug. It apparently had stalled and he could not get it moving at that point. Mechanic got it running and it moved clear. No contact was made and we departed for ZZZ.Cause - I was a little tired after a lengthy new hire IOE trip and do not recall looking for the tug moving away. I relied on the wave off from the mechanic. The potential for a disastrous collision was definitely there.Suggestions - I should look more intently for the tug to pull away and the mechanic should not be waving off with a tug under the aircraft.
ASRS:1841634.s: During pushback, the pilot relied on a mechanic's wave-off without verifying the tug had cleared, nearly colliding with a stalled tug that appeared under the cockpit. The pilot stopped the aircraft before contact, attributing the near-miss to fatigue and the mechanic's unsafe signaling.

ASRS:1841658.n: The Runway Awareness and Advisory System (RAAS) on the 737 MAX is a great Situational Awareness tool. However, I experienced what appears to be a design flaw in its triggers for approaching crossing runways.During takeoff on ZZZ Runway XX, Runway XXR crosses Runway XX about 700-800 feet from the threshold. Following FOM Guidance setting the thrust for takeoff, RAAS alerted us with 'Approaching Runway XXR' during a critical time in the takeoff roll. Coordination between the Pilot Flying and Pilot Monitoring for setting takeoff thrust is absolutely critical and the distraction of an unnecessary warning compromises safety. The trigger for that particular warning to be silenced is 40 knots ground speed or greater. The thrust lever angle/setting or thrust mode in TOGA should also cancel the warning.
ASRS:1841658.s: A 737 MAX crew reported a RAAS design flaw during takeoff on Runway XX, where an unnecessary "Approaching Runway XXR" alert distracted them while setting thrust. The reporter noted the warning should be silenced by 40 knots or TOGA thrust mode to prevent compromising safety during critical takeoff coordination.

ASRS:1841693.n: For this flight, I was FO PF (LCA) ZZZZ-ZZZ as Aircraft X. We had completed the before start procedure/checklist and were preparing to request a push-start clearance when the Captain noticed a STATUS message, CENTER FUEL PUMP L. The parking brakes had been released, thus initiating the Block-Out phase of flight. Therefore, we were initially planning to address the issue once airborne (write it up in the aircraft logbook).In less than a minute after receiving the STATUS message, we received an amber Advisory message, CENTER FUEL PUMP L, which was quickly followed by an amber EICAS CENTER FUEL PUMP L message with an associated checklist. Per our procedures, the captain asked me to reference the checklist and perform the tasks as required. Note, we were still at the gate with the engines shutdown. Following the checklist as instructed caused the message to blank. At that point, the Captain referenced the laminated flow chart, which stated we could continue and write up the problem upon landing. I recommended to the Captain against following the flow chart, rather to write up the message and to contact dispatch/maintenance, which he and the crew agreed was appropriate.Prior to calling Dispatch, we decided to take a look at the Company Document, as well as the ETOPS Critical systems section of the FOM, to see what guidance they provided, although the flow chart didn't state this was necessary due to the message going blank after completion of the non-normal checklist. What we found was quite alarming.First, this is an ETOPS Critical system, which requires the PDSC to be completed again prior to block-out. Following the flow chart would have missed this important step. Second, per the Document, a reduction of 80,000 pounds of payload was required to comply with the Document ZFW limit reduction. Again, following the flow chart would have caused this to be missed.Last, the Document specifies there needs to be enough fuel in the wing tanks to ensure your ability to reach the suitable airports if the remaining center tank pump fails. There is no way the crew would be aware of this requirement if they simply followed the flow chart, continued as directed (the message blanked after completing the non-normal checklist) and wrote the issue up upon landing, as directed by the flow chart.The flow chart, while a useful tool, needs to be modified.The flow chart states to reference the appropriate Document if a message doesn't blank. I would suggest modifying the flow chart to always reference the Document and reference ETOPS Critical Systems chart when appropriate prior to making a determination to proceed and write up an issue upon landing. Further, it's my opinion to write up any discrepancy occurring before takeoff and have maintenance address/defer it before departing is the safest course of action unless the item is crew deferrable.
ASRS:1841693.s: The First Officer and Captain on Aircraft X encountered a CENTER FUEL PUMP L message at the gate during the Block-Out phase. They determined the flow chart was insufficient for this ETOPS Critical system, as it omitted required payload reductions and fuel checks, prompting them to contact maintenance before departure.

ASRS:1841715.n: We were on a visual approach to Runway 36L in MEM on a clear and light wind day. I was the Pilot Flying and was hand flying. We were lined up with Runway 36L and right on the LOC. Around 100 feet I heard ATC say, '36 left traffic go-around'. There was no call sign but as we were the only traffic besides the Company behind us and as there was no time to discuss it I said 'Go-Around' and we went around. A true startle event. Switching to Departure, they asked the reason for the go-around and we said, We don't know and we were told to go-around!" We went around the pattern and then landed without further event.
