We wrote up the malfunction in the logbook and asked maintenance to come out so we could explain what had happened.Date 3I arrive at work to fly another turn to ZZZ3 from ZZZ and immediately checked the logbook.I found that the rudder pedal position was on MEL for positions 0 to 3.Since I set my rudder pedals within that position, I asked the Captain to refuse the aircraft citing safety concerns.I have pictures of the write ups and logbook entries.Date 4ZZZ4-ZZZSame aircraft as Date 2 and similar situation. Just prior to starting the Departure roll the rudders slipped in position and I quickly corrected them for takeoff. The remainder of that takeoff was normal. However, I was certain that I had properly set my rudder pedals back at the gate and checked them.I went back to my records and realized this was the same aircraft I had a problem with approximately six months prior. I briefed Captain on my previous experience. In cruise the pedals remain locked in place as normal. I was the pilot flying and on touchdown on Runway XY in ZZZ as I applied brake pressure the rudder pedals again went all the way to 12.Once again, we entered all the information in the logbook and requested maintenance come to the gate so we could explain the situation. The Captain requested follow up through a report but to my knowledge he had never received any.This morning almost 11 months from the original time this happened and in a different aircraft. I did not expect it to be the same problem. Initial I thought I had made a mistake and not locked the pedals. Unfortunately, it appears it is the same problem as on the other aircraft and I am quite concerned. This is potentially serious malfunction that has happened on two different aircraft. I am happy to provide any further information that could assist in making sure this safety concern does not happen again.Some additional notes- I understand from my systems knowledge there is no difference in the positioning of the rudder pedals whether in the air or on the ground. However, all three times the pedals seem to stay locked in place in the air.- At the gate when I reset my rudder position, I always push on them to confirm they are locked in place. A suggestion my Captain had was to possibly add a rudder check for the first officer during taxi. This added check may be another barrier for the crew.[Suggest] Inspections of malfunctioning item that has caused this in two of our aircraft that I am aware of.
ASRS:1842442.s: First Officers on multiple Airbus A319 flights reported rudder pedals failing to lock during taxi and landing, though they remained secure in cruise. The pilots attributed this to a potential systemic malfunction rather than user error, prompting logbook entries and a recommendation to add a preflight rudder check.

ASRS:1842461.n: When airborne, we were notified by our Dispatcher that one of our positions had dry ice that was not accounted for in the DG [Dangerous Goods] paperwork.Uncertain as to the cause given the event occurred at some point during the loading or ULD [Unit Load Devise] build process.Uncertain, as the process breakdown occurred external to the flight crew. At XA:31 [name 1] informed me that Aircraft X, position Y, had 6kgs of dry ice that was not accounted for in the DG [Dangerous Goods] manifest. The flight was on the active runway ready for take off. At XA:31 I informed Duty Officer [name 2], of the event. I also told him I would inform the crew via ACARS. We agreed the flight is still legal, it is safe and within limits. Aircraft X may proceed to ZZZ1. At XA:32 I informed [name 1] of my discussion with the Duty Officer. I requested from [name 1] the Ramp Agent's employee number #X, [name 3]. At XA:44 I sent an ACARS message: 'Hello Aircraft X. At XA:31 I was made aware that position Y has 6 kg of dry ice that was not accounted for in Dangerous Goods [manifest]. Duty Officer has been notified. Please file a report, I will be doing the same.We have determined that the flight is safe, legal, and within limits. I called [name 3];to inquire about the event. [Name 3], said it was a can from ZZZ2 that came in from another area, when the Hazmat agent updated the DG summary the aircraft had already blocked. [Name 3], received an alert and called [name 1]. [Name 3] the can was originally assigned to a can aircraft cargo container type that is not in this aircraft's configuration for this flight. It took the Hazmat agent time to correct it, he entered the information after the aircraft blocked.I suggested Hazmat agent make a phone call to Operations or ramp agent as soon as he encountered the error rather than trying to figure out how to correct the error and entering the information in the DG Summary after the aircraft blocked.
ASRS:1842461.s: A dispatcher notified the flight crew of 6kg of unaccounted dry ice on Aircraft X while on the active runway, caused by a Hazmat agent updating the manifest after the aircraft blocked. The Duty Officer confirmed the flight was safe and legal, allowing it to proceed to ZZZ1.

ASRS:1842479.n: I was the First Officer and Pilot Flying on Aircraft X from ATL to ZZZ. After reaching our flap retraction altitude of 1,000 feet we began accelerating to 200 knots and the flaps were retracted to zero. At approximately 1,500 feet AGL we encountered the wake from an Airbus 321 which rolled us in both directions. I turned off the autopilot and countered both rolling moments with approximately 3/4 aileron deflection. We received the stick shaker momentarily at approximately 190 knots. The Captain requested an offset track from the Airbus. We were given a right turn towards a different fix a few minutes later. The flight continued with no further incidents. Calm winds and close proximity to the Airbus 321 during takeoff. [Suspected cause.]
ASRS:1842479.s: The First Officer on Aircraft X encountered wake turbulence from an Airbus 321 at 1,500 feet AGL during climb, causing roll and a momentary stick shaker. The crew manually countered the roll and received a right turn offset, with the incident attributed to calm winds and close proximity to the Airbus.

ASRS:1842541.n: On take off I noticed a smell of dirty feet. It went away after a couple minutes. I didn't say anything because I honestly thought someone in the back took their shoes off. It wasn't until we were in the van on the way to the hotel that the Captain asked if we smelled dirty socks on landing. I told him I didn't smell it on landing, but I did smell it on takeoff. He said that he wrote it up, but no one ever said anything or called to ask if we smelled anything.
ASRS:1842541.s: The pilot smelled dirty feet during takeoff, which dissipated after a few minutes. The Captain later reported the odor on landing, but no maintenance action was taken because the crew initially assumed it was a passenger issue.

ASRS:1842568.n: I was on my second double and was filling a part for a RON [Remain Over Night] in ZZZ1. We were very busy during this time and it was only myself and the crew chief. I pulled the part and rushed the process to make sure that it would get on a flight to ZZZ1. Maintenance ordered 3 more of the same parts for ZZZ2 and our crew chief had to call them because our count was off and we could not fill that for them. I got distracted with so many stuff going on that I just overlooked the hazardous part of the process. I take full responsibility and will make sure that this will never happen again in the future.This occurred because I had a lot of stuff going on and I just overlooked this hazardous part.I will slow down what I'm doing when it comes to sending out parts from our station and double check everything.
ASRS:1842568.s: A maintenance technician and crew chief at a busy station overlooked a hazardous step while rushing to ship a part for a RON flight to ZZZ1. This distraction caused a parts count error that prevented fulfilling an order for ZZZ2, prompting the technician to commit to slowing down and double-checking future shipments.

ASRS:1842581.n: We departed on a training flight. It was a VFR day with no issues noted on the aircraft prior to departure. After doing maneuvers we landed on runway 17 at the ZZZ airport. During takeoff on runway 17 with a simulated engine failure during takeoff before VMC, the left side of the aircraft dropped on the runway. From our perspective it appeared as a collapsed gear. The aircraft was immediately shut down and exited. Upon looking at the left-wing area it was noticed the left main gear strut had snapped in half with the wing resting on the wheel. The weather was VFR. Upon pre-flight inspection, no issue with the landing gear or airplane was discovered. During start, taxi, runup, takeoff roll, and initial gear retraction on climbout, the landing gear functioned normally. Upon reaching ZZZ a landing was performed by student. Throughout the maneuver, the landing gear functioned normally. After the landing, we taxied back to the approach end of runway 17 and the landing gear continued to function normally. During initial takeoff roll a simulated engine failure was demonstrated, I retarded the throttles to idle and applied brake pressure. Immediately following, the left main strut snapped, and the airplane rolled onto its left side causing the left prop to contact the pavement. The left main gear failure occurred at approximately 1,750.
ASRS:1842581.s: During a training flight takeoff on runway 17, the left main gear strut snapped at approximately 1,750 feet after the pilot simulated an engine failure and applied brakes. The aircraft rolled onto its left side, causing the left propeller to contact the pavement, though no pre-flight defects were noted.

ASRS:1842590.n: During flight training, the student pilot flared aggressively resulting in the airplane being 4 or 5 ft. above the Runway at low speed with flaps fully extended. I told the student to go around. He delayed but added full power after a second or two. He then raised the nose abruptly resulting in an immediate stall warning. I attempted to lower the nose but the student remained on the controls and continued to pull back. As a result, I was unable to reduce the angle of attack. The airplane stalled and began to roll and yaw to the left. The airplane was only a few ft. above the Runway. The student released the controls but the aircraft was stalled and had no control effectiveness. I reduce the thrust to idle to arrest the incipient spin and the airplane landed on the left main landing gear. It was not a hard landing but the airplane continued to roll to the left. The left wingtip contacted the Runway surface. We were then at about a 45 degree angle to the Runway Centerline and exited the Runway into the grass. I regained directional control and brought the airplane to a stop.There were no injuries. As of this writing, the only damage I am aware of is a cracked and broken plastic wing tip and some slightly bent aluminum at the left wing tip. Mechanics are inspecting the airplane now.
ASRS:1842590.s: During flight training, a student pilot's aggressive flare and delayed go-around caused a stall and left wingtip runway contact. The instructor arrested the incipient spin, resulting in a gear-only landing with minor wing damage but no injuries.

ASRS:1842637.n: Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZ1. 10 minutes prior to scheduled departure time, briefings and checklists complete, awaiting numbers from Preliminary Weight & Balance. The Ops Agent came down with a NOTAC form requiring Captain signature for two boxes of radioactive material, not in the remarks on the release. I looked up FOM [reference section] Radioactive Pharmaceutical Shipments XXXXXX as Cargo to determine if it was acceptable HAZMAT. I determined from the NOTAC that the Transport Index was in the acceptable range, and that it was stowed correctly. We received an ACARS amendment to the 'Remarks' on the Release 'HAZMAT ON BOARD REFER TO NOTAC (time) XX'. I called the Dispatcher to confirm that, according to what I was reading in the FOM, we were safe and legal to carry the HAZMAT on this flight. He was in concurrence. We got our numbers and departed normally. Approximately an hour into the flight, I was reviewing the NOTAC and realized that although it had the correct 'origin' and flight number, it had ZZZ2 as the destination. The flight was not a through flight. Upon arrival in ZZZ1, I called the Dispatcher to confirm that ZZZ1 was the destination. He looked up the waybill and confirmed that ZZZ1 was the destination. I went down to the A bin and confirmed that ZZZ1 was the destination. I then called the Chief Pilot on Call to relay the information to him and see if he had any questions or additional input.I think there is a certain amount of continuation bias in the way we handle HAZMAT. The Ops Agent assumed that the Dispatcher okayed everything, the Dispatcher assumed that the Ops Agent okayed everything. I am not sure if anyone (other than me) actually looked up the policies regulating our carriage of medical HAZMAT. Introducing this scenario, 10 minutes before departure, greatly decreases the time available to trap errors. I believe that ZZZ2 was a typo. I should have caught it before departure. I caught it after departure, at cruise, where I had more time to examine it without distractions.
ASRS:1842637.s: The Captain of Aircraft X discovered a destination typo on a radioactive material NOTAC during cruise, after the Ops Agent and Dispatcher had mutually assumed the other verified the HAZMAT details. The error was attributed to continuation bias and insufficient time for verification prior to departure.

ASRS:1842646.n: I was the relief FO on the flight. Preflight was normal with the exception of a 'SLATS DRIVE' EICAS message which none of us had ever seen before. We called maintenance and they troubleshot the problem for about 30 minutes. Ultimately they were able to extinguish the EICAS message and a new flight release was issued. Taxi, takeoff, and initial climb out were uneventful and I went on first break. As I was climbing into the bunk, I was called back to the flight deck. When I arrived, we were in holding, the SLATS DRIVE message had returned, and the crew was setting up to dump fuel and return to TLV. The Captain had me run landing distance for RWY 12 for max landing weight. In general, I observed the crew manage the situation, and making sure someone was always flying the airplane, and that checklists were complete. As I joined the problem late, I verified they had issued an alert to ATC (they did, both with Nicosia control and Tel Aviv arrival). Because TLV typically jams the GPS, SATCOM was garbled but the Captain was able to communicate with Dispatch via ACARS. Arrival and landing were uneventful other than the expected Brake Temperature EICAS message which we handled per the proper checklist. (We did request vehicles who inspected us upon exiting the runway and followed us to gate.) Arrived at gate saw unusual EICAS Slat drive message. Entered as MRM code and called TLV Operations to have maintenance come to aircraft. Maintenance worked the issue and cleared the item. Uneventful taxi and takeoff. About 90-120 miles from TLV communication with Nicosia control we got Slat Drive EICAS. We communicated to Nicosia we had a flight control issue, declared emergency and told of our intentions were to return to TLV. We requested hold and informed Nicosia we would have to jettison fuel as well. Nicosia authorized the fuel Jettison. We entered hold about 118 miles North of TLV and worked the Slat drive EICAS and the un-annunciated fuel jettison checklist. Both checklists completed successfully. It had been the FOs leg but after checklists had been completed I opted to fly the airplane back to TLV.We were within 180 miles of TLV which required us to talk to BGN control to request re-entry into their airspace and to also declare the emergency. They asked if we were a priority aircraft and we affirmed. During the hold we tried to Satcom dispatch after we had already notified them of the nature of the issues via ACARS and included our intentions. Satcom was weak so we sent ACARS to dispatch to work out our landing distance needed with our slat drive malfunction. We came up with approximately 7,000 feet runway needed and dispatch came up with 7,200. After checklists completed and fuel jettisoned down to MLW we requested clearance to TLV. TLV offered us straight in RW 12 which we accepted. Land although fast 182kts at flaps 20 was uneventful (auto brakes 4 used) we rolled to almost end of runway for a slow uneventful turn off.We expected hot brakes and advised Tower to tell CFR trucks to inspect wheels brakes. They noted nothing and we taxied uneventfully to gate. CFR had expressed they were given only 12 minutes notice to roll trucks and wanted to know when we had actually requested priority. We explained well before contact with approach control. Final write up made at blocks was hot brakes. My crew acted like a well oiled machine great CRM, and all was included in the debrief. Dispatch was also a great help throughout the problem.
ASRS:1842646.s: The relief First Officer reported a recurring 'SLATS DRIVE' EICAS message during climb, causing the crew to declare an emergency, jettison fuel, and return to Tel Aviv. The aircraft landed safely on Runway 12 at maximum landing weight with hot brakes, which were inspected and found normal after maintenance cleared the fault.

ASRS:1842720.n: When accepting the aircraft in the morning I noticed that the First Officer's (FO) MCDU (Multi-function Control and Display Unit) was deferred for LSK 6R not working. It was deferred under MEL XX-YY-2, which allows for MCDU 1 specifically to be inoperative. When I read the MEL I was confused about whether the FO's MCDU could be deferred under this MEL since it specifically mentions MCDU 1 being able to be deferred but not MCDU 2. Operational factors and pressure to depart on time got me distracted and I did not think about it again until later in the evening after having completed the day and was on the overnight. I believe the MEL was improperly applied in this situation and because of that the aircraft may not have been airworthy. Since I wasn't involved in the actual deferral I don't know what operational factors could have contributed to this. Proper execution of the MEL by maintenance control could have solved it as the MEL has provisions for the FO's MCDU not working involving swapping the units. Additionally, a call for clarification to maintenance control by myself in the morning when I realized it may be a problem would have helped to clarify any confusion about the MEL and could have gotten Maintenance involved with correcting the deferral. When accepting the aircraft in the morning I noticed that the First Officer's (FO) MCDU was deferred for LSK R6 not working. It was deferred under MEL XX-YY-2 which allows for MCDU 1 specifically to be inoperative. When I read the MEL I was confused about weather the FO's MCDU could be deferred under this MEL since it specifically mentions MCDU 1 being able to be deferred but not MCDU 2. Operational factors and pressure to depart on time caused a distraction and we did not think about it again until later in the evening after having completed the day and was on the overnight.I believe the MEL was improperly applied in this situation and because of that that aircraft may not have been airworthy. Since I wasn't involved in the actual deferral I don't know what operational factors could have contributed to this.Proper execution of the MEL by maintenance control could have solved it as the MEL has provisions for the FO's MCDU not working involving swapping the units. Additionally a call for clarification to maintenance control by the Captain in the morning when realized. It may be a problem that would have been helped by clarifying the confusion about the MEL and could have gotten maintenance involved with correcting the deferral.
ASRS:1842720.s: The Captain reported that the First Officer's MCDU was deferred under MEL XX-YY-2, which only permits MCDU 1 to be inoperative. Due to operational pressure, the Captain did not seek clarification, resulting in a potential improper MEL application that may have rendered the aircraft unairworthy.

ASRS:1842770.n: After departing ZZZ1 for ZZZ2, my alternator failed, so I turned off non-essential electrical items and tried to fly as directly as possible to ZZZ2 to conserve battery power so I could contact ATC at ZZZ2. In attempting to fly a direct course, I may have penetrated the southwest corner of ZZZ Class D without establishing contact with the Control Tower. This Class D has a keyhole shape, and I may have penetrated the very corner. If I was in Delta, it would have only been about one minute as I turned left to ensure I did not remain in Delta. Dealing with the electrical problems kept me from giving a wider berth to Class Delta.
ASRS:1842770.s: The pilot reported an alternator failure after departing ZZZ1 for ZZZ2, requiring conservation of battery power. This distraction may have caused a brief, unintentional penetration of the southwest corner of ZZZ Class D airspace without establishing contact with the Control Tower.

ASRS:1842804.n: Before take-off, I performed my normal pre-takeoff checks, and everything was perfect, including a brake check, flight controls free and correct, auto pilot off, and trim set for takeoff. I also had a passenger who is an experienced RV pilot that I frequently fly with him, either in his airplane or mine. I was cleared for takeoff on Runway XX by the Control Tower. My normal takeoff procedure is to do a soft field takeoff, where I have the control stick full aft as I start to feed in power. As the airplane starts to roll and increases speed, the nose wheel comes off the ground, and I relax aft pressure on the stick and hold the nose wheel off the ground until the airplane flies itself off the ground. On the day this occurred, I was in takeoff attitude, with the nose wheel off the ground, and was accelerating down the runway. I started to feel forward pressure on the stick, which became heavier and heavier. I glanced down at the trim indicator and it showed a full nose down trim indication. I immediately pulled power to idle to abort the takeoff and was now focused on keeping the airplane under directional control and getting it stopped. As I applied braking to stop the airplane, I realized that I was getting close to the south end of Runway XX. I applied heavy braking being careful not to skid the tires and risk a blow-out. When I reached near the end of Runway XX, I felt that I was still moving too fast to safely make the 90 degree left turn onto Taxiway Alpha. I elected to taxi straight ahead and get the airplane stopped or go off the runway pavement and into the grass. I was not able to get the airplane stopped, so I went off the runway pavement and approximately 20 ft. into the grass. I made an immediate 180 degree turn back onto the runway pavement, made a right turn toward Taxiway Alpha and exited the runway onto Taxiway Alpha. After clearing the runway, I called the Control Tower and advised them that I had aborted my takeoff and that I had a malfunction with my trim and that I was going to troubleshoot the malfunction while I was in the run-up area for Runway XY, and I would call them back with my intentions. My airplane is equipped with electric pitch and roll trim, which is activated by a hat switch located on each control stick grip. After troubleshooting the system, we determined that I had experienced a runaway trim condition. I called the Control Tower and informed them that I wanted to taxi back to my hangar. They gave me the taxi clearance and I taxied to my hangar. The airplane is grounded until I can get a satisfactory understanding and repair to the electric trim system. There was no personal injury to me or my passenger and there was no damage to airport property. The main gear fairings were scraped on the bottom presumably when the aircraft transitioned from concrete to the grass.
ASRS:1842804.s: The pilot aborted a takeoff on Runway XX due to a runaway nose-down electric trim condition that caused increasing forward stick pressure. The aircraft overran the runway end into grass, sustaining minor fairing damage, but no injuries occurred before the pilot taxied to the hangar for repairs.

ASRS:1842805.n: While taking of from a 900 foot gravel bar a wind shear/ down draft was encountered. The event forced the aircraft back down and damaged the aircraft.
ASRS:1842805.s: The pilot encountered wind shear and a down draft while taking off from a 900-foot gravel bar. This event forced the aircraft back down and caused damage to the airframe.

ASRS:1842809.n: The aircraft was slowing from 250 kts. to 220 kts. approaching the ZZZZZ fix (Initial Approach Fix) for the RNAV XX approach. As the Flying Pilot, I asked the FO (First Officer) for Flaps 10 at which point he moved the flap handle from zero to ten and advised me the flaps were not moving. I asked him to bring the flap handle back to zero and try again. The FO attempted the second attempt but the flaps did not move. I advised the FO to let ATC know that we would need to break off the approach due to a flight control problem. We were given headings and I took over the radios and flew while the FO ran the Partial flaps/Jammed flaps checklist. I advised ATC that I needed the longest runway available at ZZZ1 and needed some headings and or an orbit to delay the approach until we ran the checklists and loaded the approach into the FMS and set up our navigation system. The Controller was very helpful and provided excellent air traffic control services while we accomplished the things we needed to do to set up and brief the no flap approach into Runway XYR using the ILS. The approach and landing went without incident and the aircraft was safely landed and taxied off the runway. After landing checklists were accomplished and the aircraft was taxied to FBO where we parked and deplaned our one passenger. Aircraft was shut down and the flaps were written up and Maintenance and Company were advised.
ASRS:1842809.s: The pilot and First Officer experienced a flap jam while slowing for the RNAV XX approach at ZZZZZ fix. They aborted the approach, ran checklists, and safely landed on Runway XYR using an ILS no-flap procedure after ATC provided delay headings.

ASRS:1842820.n: I was departing OQN at approximately XA:00. Climbing to 2,800 ft. Became distracted with Auto Pilot setting course heading. Looked up at altimeter and found myself at 3,300 ft. in Class B segment 30/70 north of ILG. Immediately descended out of airspace to 2500 ft.
ASRS:1842820.s: A pilot departing OQN climbed to 3,300 ft in Class B airspace north of ILG while distracted by autopilot settings. The pilot immediately descended to 2,500 ft to exit the restricted airspace.

ASRS:1842821.n: During after landing taxi, I took a wrong turn on an unauthorized taxiway due to fatigue & confusion with my position on the ground. To prevent recurrence, after clearing the active runway, I will stop the aircraft to ensure I look at the taxi diagram closely to clarify our taxi instructions before proceeding towards the ramp.
ASRS:1842821.s: The pilot deviated onto an unauthorized taxiway during after-landing taxi due to fatigue and positional confusion. To prevent recurrence, the pilot plans to stop after clearing the active runway to review the taxi diagram and clarify instructions before proceeding to the ramp.

ASRS:1842852.n: I am submitting this report because This is the second time I've experienced this situation. After sending an email to [the] Manager the first time and not getting a response, I am submitting this report. It has been a relatively new procedure to leave hydraulic switches off during preflight inspection. It used to be that hydraulics switches were always left on. Because the hydraulic pumps were off during our preflight inspection, we did not observe the hydraulic leak that was present. During the 'Pushback' checklist when the hydraulic switches were finally turned on, we received an 'RF' message on the EICAS within about 4-5 seconds. I then contacted Maintenance Control. Upon Maintenance Technician arriving, he advised we had a serious hydraulic leak spraying fluid all over the wheel well. Long story short, we ended up being almost 2 hours delayed getting the leak repaired. If we had NOT received the 'RF' message, we would've most likely had taken off with this leak and would've gotten a B hydraulic low quantity or even worse loss of hydraulic B pressure inflight!I've asked many people in several chief pilot offices, and sent emails to training and no one has offered a reason, other than standardize with other fleet type. I believe this is a safety issue. Leaving the hydraulic pumps off during preflight makes observing possible leaks impossible.
ASRS:1842852.s: The pilot reported that leaving hydraulic switches off during preflight inspection prevented detection of a serious leak in the wheel well. The leak was only discovered after turning pumps on for pushback, triggering an EICAS 'RF' message and causing a two-hour delay for repairs.

ASRS:1842885.n: Approximately 15 minutes prior to descent into ZZZ we were informed that a passenger heard a pop and smelled something electrical in the vicinity of row 22. Initially the flight attendants could not verify an odor. As we began our descent, a few more passengers smelled an odor and it was confirmed by one of the flight attendants. We ran the smoke, fire, and fumes checklist to step X at which point the fumes had dissipated. At no point was any smoke ever noticed and the fumes were only confirmed by a few passengers. By the time we completed the checklist and the odor was gone we were in the terminal area at ZZZ. We elected to land at ZZZ and taxi to the gate as the odor was gone and no evidence of smoke or fire existed.
ASRS:1842885.s: During descent into ZZZ, passengers and a flight attendant reported an electrical odor near row 22. The crew completed the smoke, fire, and fumes checklist; the odor dissipated with no smoke observed, so they landed and taxied to the gate.

ASRS:1842906.n: Collapsible Scooter / Wheelchair - Lithium Battery Not Removed per FAA requirement.
ASRS:1842906.s: A collapsible scooter or wheelchair with a lithium battery was loaded without the battery being removed, violating FAA requirements. The report identifies this procedural failure as the safety issue but does not describe a specific aircraft, flight phase, or resulting incident.

ASRS:1842939.n: Leveling at FL240 during descent into ZZZ, ATC asked us to report our altitude because she was not receiving anything from us. When we looked down, the Captain noticed that IFF 2 had a fault and switched it to his side. At about that time we both noticed a power surge which made my clock blank momentarily and the Captain noticed lights on his panel flash. Next we had a series of lights come on spaced apart by a few minutes at first and then began to come on more quickly as time passed. First we had a cooling fan supply light. Then when cleared to descend via the arrival, I pushed recall and noticed the left pack light remained illuminated. Suspecting something wrong with the power distribution system, I cycled through electrical panel wafer switch positions and found no amps coming from TR 2 or 3 and negative 3 amps on the battery. I hacked my clock. About 5 minutes had already passed. I took the radios while the Captain ran the checklist for the pack light next and shortly after, we lost the left aft fuel boost pump. I told the Captain I thought we had a power distribution problem and we were draining our battery. I thought we might be slowly shedding components due to their power sources being associated with the battery. As we passed 10,000 ft. I told the Captain and he put away the book and ran the landing checklist. While on the descent, I recommended [requesting priority handling] so we could land ASAP. I configured early in prep for a slam dunk and the Captain and I agreed to starting the APU just in case. By this time we were on base and more lights had come on. We lost the B Electrical Hydraulic Pump, had a right side window over heat light, battery discharge light, TR fail light, and a few pitot lights had come on. Then while turning to final, I noticed the short vectors would overshoot me so I clicked off autopilot and turned. That's when I noticed I had no electric trim. The Captain manually ran the trim for me as we slowed and configured and we had an uneventful landing. After the fire trucks greeted us and found no hot spots around the E & E bay, we discussed whether we had enough power on the battery and I noted the time had been 17 minutes from when I noticed the negative amps on the battery and started the clock. We continued to taxi to the gate and after the fire crew came up I went with them down to the E & E bays to do my own inspection. I didn't see or smell anything. Aircraft X is an old airplane. The older planes get the more they will have gremlins like this. Maintenance discovered a faulty number 2 generator or regulator with some certainty that an Aircraft phase was not getting to the busses. How many more lights would have come on eventually? Just thank goodness we were so close to landing when it failed.
ASRS:1842939.s: During descent into ZZZ, the crew experienced a progressive electrical failure caused by a faulty number 2 generator or regulator, resulting in multiple system losses including electric trim. The pilots managed the situation by manually trimming and landing safely, with maintenance later confirming the generator fault prevented power from reaching the busses.

ASRS:1842975.n: As aircraft accelerated, prior to 50 kts., a red CAS msg (acft configuration) required Pilot Flying to reject the takeoff. After Rejected Takeoff, Pilot Monitoring (SIC/RT SEAT) advised Tower, and taxied clear of Runway. Requested taxi to XXL holding point to consult with Maintenance. The problem corrected itself while discussing with Maintenance. Scheduled flight continued with no further incidents. Always consult with Maintenance with any mechanical issues. Trust and verify.
ASRS:1842975.s: The Pilot Flying rejected the takeoff before 50 kts due to a red CAS message indicating an aircraft configuration issue. The fault cleared while consulting Maintenance, allowing the flight to continue without further incidents.

ASRS:1842997.n: Seat belt signs were inoperative in J class. Flight Attendant's Rest area air supply warning light was illuminated. FA panel also inop, concerns that evacuation command buttons also inop.Operation should have a safety first approach rather than an on time performance approach.
ASRS:1842997.s: Cabin crew reported inoperative seat belt signs in J class, an illuminated rest area air supply warning light, and a failed FA panel with concerns regarding evacuation command buttons. The reporter attributed these issues to an operational focus on on-time performance over safety.

ASRS:1843009.n: On Date Aircraft X [Company] Rev 00 deferral per MEL 25-XX-XX was put in place for the two forward life-rafts removed (due overhaul) while parked at ZZZ, the 3rd life raft remained installed. Due to the remote location of the aircraft vs home base, the flight crews physically performed the life raft removal and transport to the service facility absent of direct maintenance personnel, acting as the Maintenance Director designee as requested, instead of talking the crew through performing the deferral per our operations manual I performed the electronic paperwork side of the process without verifying that an INOP placard was applied to the empty cabinets by the crew. The lack of proper [Company] MEL placarding wasn't discovered until after an event revealed the lack of placarding several weeks later after Aircraft X flew more than 50 miles from shore.Recommend adding routine discrepancy/MEL training for all [Company] personnel to build comfort with deferral writing and operating manual procedures in place, in this case, specifically as it applies to responsibilities for corrective/deferred actions. We could also emphasize how important it is for flight crews to monitor the deferral list prior to every departure and be free to ask questions about discrepancy questions to our Maintenance Director. I will also ask for a picture of the in place placard for the next deferral opportunity.
ASRS:1843009.s: Flight crews removed two life rafts from Aircraft X at ZZZ and deferred them per MEL without applying required INOP placards, as the Maintenance Director failed to verify the crew's work. The missing placards were discovered weeks later after the aircraft flew over 50 miles from shore.

ASRS:1843017.n: At approximately XA30 the Captain started both engines and gave signals to ground crew to disconnect ground power and clear the aircraft. The Captain called for the after start checklist. The First Officer read each item on the checklist and heard the correct response from the Captain for each item. On the checklist item 'Ground Equipment' the First Officer looked out the window and did not see the Ground Power Unit and tug or the ground crew members near the aircraft and announced 'clear right'. The Captain verified the call by challenging 'Ground Power clear?'. The First Officer responded 'yes, Ground Power is clear'. The First Officer then received the taxi clearance, read it to the Captain and the Captain acknowledged the clearance, completing the after start checklist. The Captain flashed the taxi lights to the ground crew signaling the aircraft was ready to taxi, the ground crew did not immediately respond. The Captain flashed the taxi lights a second time. The ground crew held light wands in a position that indicated the aircraft could taxi forward and the Captain advanced the propeller levers to begin taxiing forward. Within a few seconds, a collision between the ground power unit and the aircraft occurred. The ground crew gave signals with light wands to the pilots to stop taxiing. The Captain stopped the aircraft and shut down both engines.
ASRS:1843017.s: The flight crew cleared the aircraft for taxi after visually confirming ground equipment was absent, but the First Officer failed to see the Ground Power Unit. The Captain advanced the propellers based on ground crew signals, resulting in a collision with the unit before the aircraft was stopped.

ASRS:1843019.n: I haven't flown in years and just got back in an aircraft with a Flight Instructor. I didn't add sufficient power when realizing I was low on the glide-slope and this led to touching down short of the displaced runway threshold. This can be avoided in the future by aiming for the numbers, pitching for approach speed and using power to control the rate of descent.
ASRS:1843019.s: A pilot returning to flight with an instructor touched down short of the displaced threshold due to insufficient power while low on the glide-slope. The reporter attributes the incident to poor power management and recommends aiming for the numbers and using power to control descent rate.

ASRS:1843022.n: On climb I began to experience significant engine roughness which would not cease despite multiple efforts. I alerted ATC of the problem and requested a return to my departure airport ZZZ. I received vectors and altitude assignments for the return. With the airport in sight ATC assigned me vectors away from the airport. I thus [requested priority handling] as I wasn't sure the engine would remain running for the vectored route and an assured landing at the airport. I received clearance direct to the airport and landed without incident. I then [advised ATC]. I felt given the circumstances I took the safest approach for my safety and the safety of others.
ASRS:1843022.s: During climb, the pilot experienced significant engine roughness and requested a return to departure airport ZZZ. After ATC initially vectored away, the pilot requested priority handling and received a direct clearance, landing safely without incident.

ASRS:1843025.n: When arriving at SQL after the Tower had just closed I attempted to turn on the Runway Illumination Lights. At first the lights turned on and the approach was normal. On short final the lights turned off and could not be turned back on by my aircraft. I initiated a go around to re-evaluate the situation and try again. Our aircraft was not able to turn the lights on after multiple attempts.Another C172 entered the pattern shortly after initiating the go-around. That aircraft was able to get the lights to come on. I am uncertain why they were able to turn them on and we could not. Our radio had no issues communicating with ATC on the flight over to SQL. We landed immediately after the second aircraft and never determined whether or not our aircraft could cycle the Runway Illumination Lights. Considering this issue has been documented at SQL before and has since been considered resolved, perhaps the intermittent lighting issue still exists.
ASRS:1843025.s: A pilot arriving at SQL reported that runway illumination lights failed on short final and could not be reactivated by their aircraft, necessitating a go-around. Another C172 subsequently entered the pattern and successfully activated the lights, suggesting an intermittent lighting issue at the airport.

ASRS:1843027.n: While giving instruction, we were performing pattern work at ZZZ. After successfully executing several take off and landings, we were holding short of XXL. The previous three patterns were right traffic patterns. To the best of my knowledge, all other local traffic was also right traffic patterns. We were given clearance to take off, and this time asked to fly left traffic. I initiated a normal takeoff and began to climb out. As we were climbing out, we experienced electrical problems, and the alternator dropped off line. I completed a right turn on crosswind and another right turn onto downwind and leveled at pattern altitude. After we were stabilized on downwind, we performed an alternator reset, and the alternator came back on line. At this time the Tower Controller informed me that I was supposed to make left traffic. I immediately recalled my takeoff instructions at that point, and knew I had made inadvertent right turns during the confusion of the electrical issue. I apologized on the Tower frequency and no further mention was made. We landed uneventfully and as we taxied back to the holding point at XXL, I apologized again. We then executed two more turns in the pattern making right traffic. On the second, and final pattern, we experienced the electrical issue again. And the alternator dropped off line. At this time I informed ZZZ Tower that we were experiencing electrical problems and we needed to land. We declined to [request priority handling], but the Tower Controllers were outstanding, giving us priority to land. We landed uneventfully. ZZZ Ground asked if we needed any assistance, and I said I believed we did not and taxied to the Hangar. The airplane is currently down for maintenance, to trouble shoot the electrical problem. I believe the confusion of the electrical issue lead to fixation on my part and I defaulted to what we had done the previous three times. We should have ended the flight after the initial electrical occurrence, but we believed it was a one off occurrence. Since we were planning to stay local, I was not writing down the takeoff instructions. In the future, I plan to write down takeoff instructions for all flights.
ASRS:1843027.s: The pilot experienced alternator failures during pattern work at ZZZ, causing fixation that led to inadvertent right turns despite a left traffic clearance. After resolving the issue and landing, a second failure prompted a priority landing, leaving the aircraft grounded for maintenance.

ASRS:1843054.n: This report was composed by an Instructor at FBO (at ZZZ). I am not the Students primary Instructor. A Student had to initiate a go-around after getting close to 'traffic to follow' while on short final to Runway XX. The private pilot Student completed FAR 91.103 requirements before proceeding with his local pattern flight. Weather was not a factor during today's mishap. ATIS information (XA56Z) reported winds calm, 10 miles visibility, sky condition clear, temperature 29, dew point 2 degrees Celsius, altimeter 29.97, visual approach to Runway XX. Fuel onboard was 20 gallons. Student was also familiar with Runway lengths as well as takeoff and landing distances. Student had on his person government issued photo ID, medical, proper logbook endorsements, and Student pilot certificate. Onboard aircraft (required documentation complied with).Student's last flight was 9 days ago. An aircraft had dropped FOD on the active XX Runway while the Student was on a solo flight in the pattern. Runway XX was closed temporarily while airport vehicles were dispatched to find the FOD. Meanwhile the Student was told to hold South of Runway XX. After the Student asked for clarification the controller told him to make 360s south of the airport. Student made 3 360s south of the Runway, meanwhile the FOD was found and Runway XX operations were resumed. Student then re-established himself on the left downwind for XX when he was then told to extend his downwind. Student was told number 3 to land Runway XX. Student waited till number 2 traffic was 45 degrees off his left shoulder before turning base. Student quickly overtook traffic on final and initiated a go-around while the traffic to follow was still on short final. Prior to this go-around Student had been told to initiate a go-around by Tower. A compilation of unfamiliar radio calls in the traffic pattern, 360s, downwind extension, a temporary runway closure, and two go-arounds narrowed the margin of safety and nearly exceeded the Student pilot's piloting capabilities, leading to a close spacing on final which lead to a go-around. The Student pilot feels remorse for what happened and the event has been debriefed in detail. The Student pilot has learned from his mistakes. The primary cause was pilot error, a high workload led to decreased situational awareness in the pattern.
ASRS:1843054.s: A student pilot executing a solo local pattern flight at ZZZ initiated a go-around on short final to Runway XX after overtaking traffic. The reporter attributes the close spacing to pilot error, where high workload from multiple radio calls and runway delays reduced situational awareness.

ASRS:1843066.n: I have been flying a weekly mission for a company. They have contracted with Construction company and have hired me to fly for mapping purposes. The mission was [in an area] which is controlled airspace near ZZZ. The company applied for a COA which I've been using and will last until the end of the year. Last Date I unlocked the app like usual and flew the mission. It's at 300 feet, and usually takes an hour. At the end of the mission I was approached by a Sheriff's officer. I was advised that a TFR was in place. I failed to look for any TFR's and should have known better since there was an active air show in progress. I have now learned to use tfr.faa.gov and will do so from now on.
ASRS:1843066.s: A pilot conducting a mapping mission in controlled airspace near ZZZ at 300 feet was approached by a Sheriff's officer after violating an active TFR for an air show. The pilot admitted to failing to check for TFRs despite holding a COA and committed to using tfr.faa.gov in the future.

ASRS:1843083.n: I was working the shift when there was a reentry Dragon rocket. The packet with the information only had the landing zone and the monitoring aircraft. The problem was there was no information on the reentry flight path so it caught me by surprise when it was coming in over the top of my traffic. All of the airplanes started asking what it was and I didn't know which direction to call traffic for any of them or give them an option of the area to miss if they were uncomfortable with the situation.My recommendation is more information passed along. I had multiple airplanes close to the flight path and I had no way of helping them if they needed vectors because they were uncomfortable.
ASRS:1843083.s: An air traffic controller reported being surprised by a Dragon rocket reentry over their traffic due to missing flight path data in the information packet. Consequently, the controller could not provide traffic advisories or vectors to multiple aircraft near the path when pilots inquired about the object.

ASRS:1843108.n: At 200 ft. AGL on climbout we entered wake turbulence from the 757 in front of us. The aircraft rolled to the right and we continued to climb just right of course. 0.18 was shown on the MFD. Winds were 150 at 07 and we were LNAV to RONII. Before we could get back on the track, ATC assigned us to heading 070 and stated we were south of our track. In our next radio call we stated what happened and the Controller cleared us to continue the departure. I feel increased separation from 757's would mitigate these occurrences from happening.
ASRS:1843108.s: During climbout at 200 ft AGL, the crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding 757, causing a right roll and track deviation. ATC assigned a heading correction after the crew reported the incident, and the departure was cleared to continue.

ASRS:1843128.n: Aircraft X experienced an upset aircraft state as a result of severe turbulence encountered on approach to ZZZ Runway XXR. The aircraft pitched to approximately 20 degrees nose up and 10 to 15 degrees left bank, disengaging the autopilot and causing the autothrust to increase power toward max. The airspeed decayed from 250 KIAS to 220 KIAS as the aircraft climbed from 10,000 ft. to 10,900 ft. before upset recovery procedures returned it to stable flight at 10,000 ft. and 250 KIAS. There were no injuries as passengers and flight attendants were seated early in anticipation of turbulence. There was no aircraft damage. Aircraft X made an uneventful landing on Runway XXR. The severe turbulence encounter was reported to Air Traffic Control and the Company. A full debrief was conducted with Flight Operations.Prior to descending into ZZZ, the First Officer (FO) and I discussed concerns about thunderstorms and convective activity in the terminal area. We had plenty of gas and I noted that ZZZ1 weather was excellent. I briefed the flight attendants to be seated approximately 20 minutes before touchdown. I then confirmed that they were seated. I made a PA to the passengers that I expected very bumpy conditions and I emphasized the need for them to obey the Fasten Seat Belt sign. The FO and I briefed windshear precautions, indications, and procedures while inbound to ZZZ2 for the ZZZZZ [arrival]. We did not re-brief the Upset Recovery procedures as they had been briefed prior to departure. (In retrospect, I think this could be good to review when windshear concerns are expressed as the windshear could result in an upset.) We were initially cleared on the ZZZZZ arrival. We loaded the Runway XXL ILS approach. Shortly into the descent, we had an AUTOFLT RUD TRIM 1 FAULT ECAM. I wrote it up as we were descending. Shortly after that, ATC vectored us off the arrival. ATC did not tell us what we should expect, but I heard several aircraft ahead of us receiving clearances to ZZZZZ1 for what I assumed would be the remainder of the ZZZZZ arrival. Radio communication congestion was significant. I sensed ATC was struggling to manage the number of arrivals from the north. I did not hear anyone receiving holding clearances. Holding might have alleviated the density of traffic and eased the friction for ATC. Eventually, we were told to do a 360 degree turn. Out of the turn, we were cleared to descend to 10,000 ft and given a heading of 190deg. I had heard another aircraft given a vector toward the ZZZZZ2 intersection, so I put it on the fix page for situational awareness. At that time, I was watching the radar which showed a cell next to the ZZZZZ2 intersection and another cell to the southwest. The two aircraft ahead of us were vectored through that gap. A 777 was behind us. At that time, we still did not know what arrival or approach clearance to expect. As we passed through the gap between the two cells, ATC said to advise when we could take a turn direct to ZZZZZ3. We did not have ZZZZZ3 loaded into the FMC. The FO did not know what ZZZZZ3 was. I asked him to load it and I spelled it out. (We still had Runway XXL loaded.) As we tried to get ZZZZZ3 loaded, along with the remainder of the ILS XXR approach, while still in the gap between the two cells, we experienced the severe turbulence and upset. After recovering the aircraft, I gave direction to the FO to load DIRECT ZZZZZ3 and I spelled it again. He did so, and we turned direct to the fix. He then connected the rest of the approach and it was flown uneventfully.As far as the execution of the Upset Recovery procedure, I did not comply with all the procedures. I also did not verbalize the steps and I did not silence the autopilot aural which resulted from the disconnect for quite some time. I had trouble focusing on the instruments and the 'Startle Effect' was significant. Descending into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ arrival, we were taken off the arrival. I am assuming it was because of the convective weather in the area. We had flown in from the north and were being vectored west away from ZZZ. It seemed ATC was overwhelmed with all of the aircraft and bad weather in the area. Because we knew there was adverse weather around the airport the Captain sat the passengers and flight attendants well in advance. At one point while being vectored west we were told to fly multiple different headings which eventually made us complete a giant 360 degree turn. At the end of the turn I noticed that ATC was vectoring aircraft towards ZZZZZ2 intersection which seemed like ATC had found a gap they were funneling aircraft through. I pulled up ZZZZZ2 intersection on the fix page so we could see we where it was in relation to our position on the nav display. ATC gave us a heading of 190 that was towards ZZZZZ2 intersection. At this point ATC did not tell us which runway or routing to expect. While flying on a heading of 190 and 250 kts. at 10,000 ft. we flew into a cloud and at that point we experienced an upset event of severe turbulence. The aircraft gained about 900 ft., dropped 30 kts., banked 10-15 degrees and disengaged the autopilot. The Captain was flying and immediately returned us to straight and level flight. The Captain reported the incident to ATC and I checked in with the Flight Attendants and no injuries occurred in the cabin. After the event ATC told us to go to ZZZZZ3 intersection and to expect Runway XXR. We landed the airplane and contacted the company about the event.
ASRS:1843128.s: The flight crew encountered severe turbulence while being vectored to ZZZZZ3 at 10,000 ft, causing an upset with autopilot disengagement, a 900 ft climb, and 30 kt airspeed decay. The Captain recovered the aircraft to stable flight with no injuries or damage, attributing the event to the turbulence and noting a significant startle effect.

ASRS:1843189.n: Operating Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZ1 we pushed back from Gate X in ZZZ and were pulled to the top of the alleyway near spot 1. After starting engine 1 and disconnecting the push back tug, I smelled a slight fume smell. Wasn't immediately sure if it was a concern or not so I notified the Flight Attendants and asked if they could smell anything unusual in the cabin. They did not. Then after starting engine 2 as we taxied up to spot 1, the fume smell got stronger in the flight deck. The First Officer now stated that he could smell strong odors. I checked with the Flight Attendants again, and they now said they could start to smell something. We notified ground control from spot 1 that we had to return to the gate and we shut down engine 2. Ground control had us taxi from spot 1, Taxiway 1, Taxiway 2, and hold short of Taxiway 3 awaiting a gate assignment. We notified Ramp Control that we needed to quickly return to the gate because of fume smells. We had donned O2 masks and tried a few times to get a gate assignment but Ramp Control kept asking multiple times what the issue was after we had already told them. I then [requested priority handling] with Ground Control, and they replied for us to contact Ramp Control. I also [requested priority handling] with Ramp Control and started taxiing from Taxiway 4 to Taxiway 5 spot 2 in anticipation getting into Gate 2. Ground Control then asked if we needed [priority] equipment. We acknowledged yes send the personnel to check the outside of the aircraft. We parked at Gate 2, shutdown, and deplaned the passengers as soon as possible. The Flight attendants had left the aircraft with the passengers by the time I had given my report to Dispatch, Maintenance, and the [airport authorities].The First Officer and I both had dull headaches, burning sore throats. I notified safety and they said to call the Duty Pilot on call and they would facilitate our being examined by a medical professional. After talking to the Duty Pilot/Chief Pilot, I was told to call a Paramedic if I was concerned about my health. Both of us stopped by the Airport station and asked if they could have the Paramedics take our vitals. After this was done, I drove the First Officer to ER where they examined us both. [The cause was] Maintenance issues with older aircraft. After pushing back from the gate, we started both engines. There was a faint smell of exhaust/fumes that went away and returned back even stronger. The Flight Attendant said that they could smell it in the cabin, however, it was not that strong. As we were holding on the taxiway awaiting to get back into the ramp, the smell would dissipate and return again. The smell was very strong. I started coughing and having a dry throat sensation. We donned our O2 masks and [advised ATC]. The smell occurred after starting an engine.
ASRS:1843189.s: The flight crew of Aircraft X experienced strong fume odors and physical symptoms after starting engines during pushback and taxi, causing a return to the gate and passenger deplaning. The reporter attributed the incident to maintenance issues with the older aircraft.

ASRS:1843245.n: At 400 feet on the RNAV 25L glide path we passed under a drone that was 50-100 feet directly above us hovering.
ASRS:1843245.s: The pilot reported passing under a hovering drone 50–100 feet above the aircraft while at 400 feet on the RNAV 25L glide path.

ASRS:1843317.n: During climb passing approximately FL280 the flight attendant called and informed me that a passenger believed we were trailing fuel out of our #2 engine. All engine indications appeared normal including engine fuel flow. Checking our fuel we determined we were showing an imbalance of approximately 1500 pounds with the right wing being low. We continued to monitor to determine if the fuel imbalance remained stable or if the imbalance was increasing. We received a second call from the flight attendant informing us we had a company A320 instructor pass riding. He and I spoke and he told me it appeared to be fuel trailing the #2 engine. I sent the First Officer back to the cabin for a visual inspection and told him to look forward and aft of the wing and specifically any damage he might see on the forward edge of the wing. While he performed a visual inspection, the flight attendant in the cockpit showed me cell phone video of the leak. I leveled off at FL380 and verified the fuel imbalance was increasing to about 1700lbs with the right wing on the low side. I referenced the QRH for fuel leak and sent dispatch a message that we had a fuel leak, needed to divert and would be shutting down the #2 engine. The First Officer returned and informed me of the same information and we began running the fuel leak QRH. Dispatch recommended ZZZZ and looking at our distance and time required for descent I determined it to be a proper divert location. I [requested priority] with ZZZZ Center and requested an immediate turn to ZZZZ and descent to FL 200. The First Officer and I ran the fuel leak QRH which directed an engine shutdown for a fuel leak out of the engine or pylon followed by the engine shutdown checklist. We shut the engine down in an idle power descent and I started the APU. I then transferred flying duties to the First Officer. ZZZZ Center handed us off to ZZZZ Approach. ZZZZ is an non radar airfield. They told us to report 30 miles from the airfield and asked if we could maintain VMC. Weather was scattered to broken with some vertical development but was sufficient to maintain VMC and the field was reporting 6,000 scattered. Approach gave us a descent to 7,000 and offered the [non-precision] Approach to Runway XX. I asked for the ILS for XX. Approach asked if we could fly a visual to Runway 26 and conditions were sufficient for that and we were cleared for the visual approach. We never received guidance information on our ILS though it was programmed correctly. After an uneventful landing by the First Officer we taxied to a hard stand. Foreign Country aviation authorities inspected our certificates/medical/airworthiness certificate/insurance certificate which the company instructor was very helpful working that while I worked with operations. Operations moved the passengers indoors to a gate seating area. I worked with the Chief Pilot and Maintenance Control. They informed me that the passengers would be taken on a flight from ZZZZ-ZZZZ1-ZZZ. I made several announcements and trips to the gate holding area and informed all passengers of our plan. Most of the passengers had left carry-on bags on the aircraft, but Foreign Country security wouldn't let them return to retrieve it. I coordinated with Station Operations to have aft air stairs brought up so we could get the passenger to come back and file front to back through the airplane to retrieve their items before their inbound flight arrived and coordinated with Foreign Country security. Foreign Country security eventually agreed but only allowing 4 passengers at a time. On climbout from ZZZZ1 we were passing FL280 when the Flight Attendant (FA) called us. He said a passenger (who is a pilot) said that it looked like fuel was coming out of our #2 engine. We monitored the fuel page. The engine fuel used totals were identical, as were the wingtip tanks. The inboard wing tanks showed an imbalance of 1000 pounds. Over the remaining 5 minutes of our climbout we watched the imbalance increase to 1400 pounds. During this time we got another call from the FA. He put us on with an Airbus Instructor that was non-revving in the back. He told us it appeared that fuel was coming from the engine exhaust.The Captain took over the aircraft and I went back to look for myself. There was nothing visible on the front of the wing or the front of the engine. I went back to row XX and could clearly see a fluid coming out of the exhaust of #2. I returned to the flight deck and told the Captain. We ran the Fuel Leak checklist and it directed us to shut down the engine. After starting a descent to FL200, we did so. We secured the engine and talked to dispatch. He directed us to either ZZZZ1 or ZZZZ. ZZZZ1 was further and the weather was reported as suboptimal. We chose ZZZZ.The Captain and I turned the aircraft back to ZZZZ and finished the descent to FL200. We briefed up the approach and I took control of the aircraft. Approach control informed us there was no radar service. We used the local MSA to ensure terrain clearance until we were clear of the clouds and could see the airfield. I maneuvered the aircraft to a 6-7 mile final and we configured the aircraft for landing. There was no glideslope which we knew, but the localizer wasn't working either. We confirmed with Tower that they could see us and that we were lined up on the correct airport. During the confusion we forgot the Before Landing Checklist, but the Spoilers Not Armed message reminded us. We accomplished the checklist and were fully stable and complete by 500 ft. AGL.Landing was normal, the Captain took the aircraft around 80 knots on the rollout. We taxied clear to a hard stand near the terminal. Most of the passengers deplaned into the terminal. We coordinated with the Foreign Country equivalent of the FAA, as well as dispatch and maintenance. After the passengers got on the rescue airplane, we closed up the plane and went to the hotel.
ASRS:1843317.s: During climb, pilots observed a fuel leak from the #2 engine exhaust and an increasing fuel imbalance, prompting a diversion to ZZZZ. The crew executed the fuel leak QRH, shut down the #2 engine, and landed safely after a visual approach due to non-functioning ILS components.

ASRS:1843337.n: We were cleared to 2000 ft. on the lateral path of Runway XX. I was at 210 kts. and in level change descending to 2000 ft. We called the runway and were cleared visual approach for Runway XX around ZZZZZ. I thought VNAV was engaged and asked for touch down elevation. I did not verify that VNAV was engaged. I asked for flaps 1 and flaps 5 to slow down. I was inadvertently in level change and the aircraft pitched nose down to maintain the 210 kts. I disconnected the autopilot and leveled the aircraft. During the repair, ATC called low altitude alert. We acknowledged that we were correcting and continued the landing normally. Aircraft automation was selected with LNAV and level change while descending to 2000 ft. Subsequently cleared visual approach and PF (Pilot Flying) started configuring to slow and asked to set touchdown elevation in the altitude window. PF and PM (Pilot Monitoring) didn't verify appropriate vertical mode for phase of flight and aircraft pitched for speed on pitch descent below glidepath. PF disconnected automation and corrected while PM communicated altitude correction to Tower.
ASRS:1843337.s: The flight crew descended to 2000 ft in Level Change mode while configuring for a visual approach, causing an inadvertent nose-down pitch to maintain 210 kts. The Pilot Flying disconnected the autopilot to level the aircraft after an ATC low altitude alert, and the landing continued normally.

ASRS:1843366.n: While coming into ZZZ after holding for weather, an aircraft before us was able to get into the field at minimums. We were cleared to cross the initial app had fix at or above 3,000 ft. After crossing, I, the First Officer, had set the new altitude for 2,100 ft. which was the lowest altitude on that segment of the approach. After leveling off I had set the MDA of 800 ft. Prior to the FAF the Captain had suggested to switch to a flaps 45 landing instead of 22 to get a lower deck angle. I agreed so the Captain was heads down for a few moments while getting the new speeds. We were told to contact tower and after check-in they said to check our altitude. I had noticed we were lower than the segments assigned altitude and promptly corrected back up to the correct altitude. This was correct before the FAF so we continued the approach. This was followed by a missed approach.Lack of crosschecking and part of the crew was heads down during a critical phase of flight. [Suggest] Heads up cross check on final approach segment. Also not changing the configuration of the airplane at such late notice on arrival/ approach.
ASRS:1843366.s: The First Officer and Captain descended below the assigned 2,100 ft altitude during the approach to ZZZ while the Captain was heads down configuring flaps 45. The crew corrected the altitude before the FAF but executed a missed approach due to a lack of crosschecking and late configuration changes.

ASRS:1843370.n: While coming into ZZZ we checked the weather and the ceilings were not quite what we needed for the RNAV XX. We had plenty of gas and decided to ask for a hold. After holding we were informed of an aircraft that had broken out right at minimums. We decided to start the approach. We were cleared to cross the Initial Approach Fix at or above 3,000 ft. After crossing the fix the FO (First Officer) pilot flying, set the new altitude for 2,100 ft. which was the lowest altitude on the segment for the final app fix. After leveling off the First Officer then set 800 ft. for the MDA. Prior to the FAF I suggested flaps 45 instead of flaps 22 so we could get a lower deck angle and see the field better. He agreed so I was heads down while getting the new numbers. I was also told to contact Tower and after checking on he mentioned to check our altitude because he saw us low. At that point the FO was already correcting and we returned to the previous altitude promptly. This was corrected before the FAF so we didn't see a reason to terminate the approach. Not properly monitoring and heads down in a critical phase of flight. I shouldn't have suggested the late flap change. If I hadn't I could have noticed the FO descending early before ATC did. Next time I will keep what we have and after a missed approach I could change and try again.
ASRS:1843370.s: The Captain and First Officer descended below the cleared 3,000 ft altitude during an RNAV approach to ZZZ after the Captain distracted himself suggesting a late flap change. The First Officer corrected the altitude after Tower intervention, and the Captain attributed the error to poor monitoring and unnecessary configuration changes.

ASRS:1843380.n: I was the Pilot Monitoring while on an Initial Operating Instruction flight training with a new First Officer (FO). During climb out of ZZZ on the ZZZZZ7 Departure Procedure, a smoldering singe smell resembling an electrical or wire insulation became apparent to me at approximately 8,000 feet. As we climbed through 10,000 feet, the smell became very strong, and my FO and I mentioned the smell simultaneously. I called my flight attendant and inquired if she also smelled the fumes, to which she said, 'yes it is pretty strong.' I asked her to check areas of potential fire including the forward closet, galley, lavatory and cargo areas. I requested to stop my climb at 12,000 feet, notified ATC about the fumes resembling a potential fire. We also requested to return to the airport in ZZZ, and [requested priority handling] and descended to 8,000 feet under ATC clearance. We notified the flight attendant we would be returning to the field in about 10 minutes and to expect a briefing shortly. I elected for the FO to continue flying the aircraft. Given his experience level I continued communication with ATC, ran checks, and coordinated with the flight attendant. The FO and I donned our O2 Masks and ran the smoke evacuation QRC/QRH checklist. After that initial check was complete I coordinated a report with the flight attendant, ACARS dispatched about the return to field, and made a brief passenger announcement. By this time, we had an ATIS, approach and landing data for an approach to ZZZ, and were on a about 12 mile base to turn for ILS XXR into ZZZ. I briefly looked at the smoke fumes checklist as well. Given the time to landing, it became apparent there would be no time to diagnose the source of the fumes and we already 'vented' the cabin. All circuit breakers were in and systems performed normally. I elected to stop that check, take the controls from the FO, and make an overweight landing in ZZZ. Priority personnel had been notified and were waiting to inspect the aircraft. Upon [arrival] no reasonable indications of external fire or smoke, I taxied the aircraft to the gate with Crash Fire Rescue following. After shutdown, passengers were deplaned normally with no known injury to passengers or aircraft damage. We departed runway XXR on the ZZZZZ7 departure after making the initial turn direct to ZZZZZ and climbing I began to smell what was a burning wire or a rubber insulation smell. I took note as PF and continued to climb through 8,000 feet. When we approach closer to 12,000 feet the smell was extremely strong and that is when I questioned the Captain if he too was smelling the burning smell. After confirming this, the Captain called the flight attendant who also confirmed this smell coming from the forward part of the aircraft. After confirming our suspicions, the flight attendant began searching in the forward part of the aircraft and the rear to observe the baggage compartment. The Captain told me to keep flight controls and he began to observe systems pages and the circuit breakers. We saw nothing, which we began running checklists in the QRH. I programmed the approach back into ZZZ, the Captain requested priority handling and from there we donned our oxygen masks. After confirming crew communications, I got the ATIS and built the approach, and the Captain handled communications and checklists. ATC brought us around very quickly to the final approach course and with suspicion of fire the Captain and myself did not want to waste any time. We continued on the approach and with a heavier than normal aircraft, once everything was set up the Captain landed the plane. We had the support vehicles waiting and followed us into the gate. We had them look for visible flames and tried to get thermal scan on the aircraft. We had advised Dispatch of what happened and maintenance as well. [The] Captain performed extremely well through the process and as a cockpit I believe we did very well as a crew considering the circumstances.
ASRS:1843380.s: During an initial operating instruction flight, the Pilot Monitoring and First Officer detected a strong burning wire smell at 8,000 feet while climbing on the ZZZZZ7 departure. The crew returned to ZZZ for an overweight landing after running smoke checklists, with no fire source found and no injuries reported.

ASRS:1843408.n: While taxiing from the southeast ramp, westbound on taxiway 1, Ground Control issued us the following clearance, 'Aircraft X, taxi to Runway XXL via [Taxiway] 2, cleared to cross Runway XY, give way to Aircraft Y on [Taxiway] 3.' As we turned southbound onto Taxiway 2, as I was looking right to clear for crossing the runway, the Captain brought the aircraft to an abrupt stop and I noted a 767 taxiing westbound on Runway XY. Luckily the Captain saw them before we hit them. We queried Ground Control about the conflict and we noted that the 767 crew remarked, 'That was a close call'. There was never any mention of giving way to a 767 taxiing westbound on Runway XY in our taxi instructions. Human Factors breakdown. While taxiing to Spot X on Taxiway 1, Ground issued the following clearance just prior to reaching Spot X: 'Aircraft X Taxi to Runway XXL via [Taxiway] 2, cleared to cross Runway XY, give way to Aircraft Y on [Taxiway] 3.' As I turned the airplane onto Taxiway 2 (north side of Runway XY) to cross Runway XY, I had to yield/stop uninstructed to give way to a 767 aircraft taxiing on Runway XY westbound from my left to avoid a taxi incursion with that aircraft.
ASRS:1843408.s: The flight crew received a clearance to cross Runway XY but had to stop abruptly to avoid a 767 taxiing westbound on that runway, which was not mentioned in the instructions. This unannounced conflict caused a near-miss taxi incursion attributed to a human factors breakdown in the clearance issuance.

ASRS:1843411.n: Approaching ZZZ airport for Runway XX for a visual approach with the PAPI light out of service, there is a hill and the runway has a uprising slope. At 1,300 ft. AGL the system detected that we were at 1,000 ft. due to the terrain just before the airport when in reality we were 1,300 ft. I adjusted the rate of descent just over 1,000 ft to be stabilized for the approach. The aircraft EGPWS announced terrain terrain pull up, so I adjusted by vertical descent to 800 FPM then proceeded to land on a stabilize approach. Adjusting vertical rate of descent close to the airport with the uprising hill near the approach end of Runway XX at ZZZ. Being stabilized at 2,000 ft. for this approach will help avoiding the terrain occurrence.
ASRS:1843411.s: During a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ with the PAPI inoperative, the crew encountered an EGPWS "terrain pull up" warning at 1,300 ft AGL caused by a nearby hill. The pilot adjusted the descent rate to 800 FPM to stabilize the approach and landed safely.

ASRS:1843434.n: As of Date the company has again instituted their [attendance] procedures. This results in Flight Attendants having to jump through major hoops going to a special clinic if they call out sick. If they don't comply, they face termination. This further results in flight attendants who would rather go to work sick with the possibility that they are COVID positive than go through the process defined by the company. I myself along with many other passengers and crew have been exposed to COVID by these flight attendants in the past. I do not feel safe going to work knowing that there is a greater possibility of flight attendants who are going to work sick putting myself at greater risk of being exposed to COVID-19.
ASRS:1843434.s: A flight attendant reported that strict company attendance procedures force sick crew to work rather than face termination. The reporter states this policy increases the risk of COVID-19 exposure for themselves, other crew, and passengers.

ASRS:1843496.n: Myself, a Commercial pilot, CFI-I and a Private Pilot who owned the aircraft were flying back into ZZZ and had requested the overhead break approach. The approach controller cleared us for the approach and informed us to report a 2 mile initial for the approach. At the same time a C172 was on the ILS XX at ZZZ above us. When we reported the 2 mile initial for the overhead break we had just passed underneath the C172 and subsequently lost visual contact on the aircraft as they were above and behind us. The tower cleared us for a right break over the departure end of Runway XX and to wait for the tower to call the base turn. I am not sure why but both myself and the other pilot on board misinterpreted the exact location to start the approach. We both believed that we should start the turn over the approach end of Runway XX, even after correctly repeating back the instructions for starting the turn on the departure end. Again, I am not entirely sure why two experienced pilots both misinterpreted a relatively simple instruction, but a misunderstanding between pilot and controller was evident. The pilot who was on the radio asked the control tower for clarification on when to start the break and we were met with no answer. I began the right turn over the approach end of the runway. The control tower immediately requested to know what our intentions were. Again, we asked for clarification on when to start the turn on the break and the tower instructed us to continue the downwind and wait for clearance to turn base. This was where the major mistake was made, as I continued the right turn into the final approach corridor. I am not sure why I made this mistake, most likely due to stress and loss of situational awareness, however I believe continuing the right turn was probably the worst reaction to those stressors as I knew there was an aircraft somewhere near my altitude and on a converging path. The appropriate reaction would have been to turn away from the final approach corridor. We came close to colliding with the C172, although I never had visual contact on the aircraft so I am not sure how close. A few key points that I believe helped in creating the misunderstanding were the clearance for the overhead break.
