The intentions of the tower and the intentions of the pilots were very different in this case. The tower needed us to extend our upwind and then extend our downwind. We were anticipating an overhead break approach where we kept a tight break into a descending approach onto final. I believe both myself and the tower could have made our mutual intentions clearer to each other to help avoid this near miss from happening. I believe there was also an error with the sequencing of the aircraft. We were brought in underneath an aircraft on the ILS and that led to loss of SA, knowing that we were going to be turning back into the direction of that plane. Doing an overhead break approach to Runway XX at ZZZ I was given instruction to break over the departure end of the runway and land #2 behind traffic on final. I have done the overhead break approach over 100 times and have always gotten break over the numbers or midfield. I know now that the controller wanted me to break over the far end of the runway (over number XY), not over the number XX. I didn't understand the sequencing and asked for clarification 3 times. The controller repeated the instructions twice (which I still didn't understand) and the 3rd time didn't answer me. I broke over the numbers XX and announced my break to the controller and asked if we were cleared to land. I was still at 1500 ft. AGL and turning right base, and the controller told me to establish on the down wind. At this point I was not clear which way to go and was eventually told to maintain heading and climb (in a series of radio calls). We came around and repeated the maneuver and was cleared to break over the numbers without any issues.My mistakes were not understanding that I was expected to break at the far end of the runway (which was the first time I had ever gotten this direction), not understanding what the controller wanted me to do when he realized we broke early, not asking for a go around early in the process because of the lack of understanding on my part.
ASRS:1843496.s: Two pilots flying a commercial aircraft into ZZZ misinterpreted an overhead break clearance, turning early over the approach end instead of the departure end. This error, caused by confusion over runway sequencing and stress, led to a near collision with a C172 on the ILS before the tower issued corrective instructions.

ASRS:1843521.n: While conducting a student training flight under Part 91, I had asked my student to track the 270 radial to the ZZZ VOR/DME. The entire flight was conducted under positive control and we were receiving traffic advisories from ZZZ Approach. I was scanning outside looking for traffic, and upon reaching the ZZZ VOR/DME, a BE36 approached from our 2 o'clock position, crossing south to north, coming within what I can approximate as 50 ft. or so. My initial reaction was to climb and bank, similar to a chandelle maneuver in order to avoid a collision. After resuming level flight now on a 270 heading, I asked approach if they had issued a traffic advisory, assuming I may have missed it. Approach had told me they had indeed not, and was not seeing any traffic in my area. I continued to keep the traffic in visual contact as they proceeded north, evidently unaware they had almost been in a mid-air collision. I then resumed my instructional responsibilities as normal and proceeded back to ZZZ1 for touch-and-goes.It is possible I became distracted as a result of trying to relay information to my student, but also that the incident aircraft was not equipped with a properly reporting transponder. Whatever the reasoning, I do believe this could be resolved in the future by equipping the facility with the ability to read ADS-B sources, as the other aircraft in the near collision was reporting ADS-B data according to my cellular device, allowing me to view their registration number. It also could be prevented by equipping the aircraft I was using with an ADS-B in receiver, to view said data.
ASRS:1843521.s: During a Part 91 student training flight near ZZZ VOR/DME, a BE36 crossed within 50 feet while Approach provided no traffic advisory. The pilot attributed the near collision to potential distraction or the other aircraft's non-reporting transponder, suggesting ADS-B implementation to prevent recurrence.

ASRS:1843526.n: On a flight in Aircraft X, I was the PIC (Pilot in Command) with my son. I have provided my son two ground sessions of about 1 hour each before allowing him to sit in the front seat of the aircraft. I always fly from the backseat and felt comfortable flying there. During a planned touch and go, I aborted the touch and go and ended up off the runway 60 ft. into the EMAS (Engineered Material Arresting System). There were no injuries and very little damage to the aircraft from entering the EMASBackground: We took off and flew for 30 minutes and on return to ZZZ, the DEEC (Digital Electronic Engine Control) light illuminated indicating the DEEC reverted to a manual mode. This had happened on a previous flight earlier in the day and I reset the DEEC as I had done on the previous flight and the DEEC returned to normal operation. I had it in my mind to do one touch and go when we returned to the pattern at ZZZ and failed to change my plan as the smart thing would have been to full stop and investigate the problem since it was the second occurrence of the day. I flew a normal overhead pattern, completed the before landing checks and was cleared for a touch and go on Runway XX. I flew a stable final approach and landed the aircraft on speed, with full flaps, in the touchdown zone of Runway XX. I landed in the touchdown zone of Runway XX on speed with full flaps. I selected flaps 25 and smoothly brought the throttle up to take off power. The aircraft accelerated but at a slower rate than normal. I looked inside and saw 64% N1 and decided to abort the touch and go. I estimate I was just past mid field at this time. I brought the throttle to idle and applied the brakes with the brake lever on the stick. The airplane didn't decelerate. I tried a second time and got the same response so I grabbed the emergency brake lever and began a slow gradual application so as not to skid the tires. I should have made sure the nose was fully lowered and the nose wheel weight on wheels switch was fully depressed but in the moment I could see the end of the runway coming up and didn't make the correct decision. I had been able to use the normal brakes correctly I would have stopped the aircraft before entering the EMAS at the end of the runway. If the nose wheel weight on wheels switch is not fully depressed, the normal braking system is deactivated. During the stopping process, I thought about shutting down the engine to help eliminate residual thrust, but had my hand on the emergency brake lever. I also thought about going to 0 flaps, a technique emphasized on my checkride, but again had my left hand on the emergency brakes.I should have never flown the aircraft after it had an uncommanded switch to manual DEEC mode until Maintenance had inspected the aircraft. Secondly, I should not have attempted a touch and go after an uncommanded reversion to manual DEEC mode. During the abort, I should have pushed forward on the stick and selected 0 flaps before reaching for the emergency brake lever as it would have afforded me anti-skid braking and would have prevented me going off the runway. If there was a malfunction with the nose wheel weight on wheels switch we will never know as that was part of the very minor damage done to the aircraft when it went into the EMAS. I have debriefed thoroughly with two other Aircraft X qualified pilots who helped identify the errors and instructional fixes. I have reread the manual and reviewed a similar accident investigation finding on an Aircraft X who also aborted a takeoff and had similar mistakes as the mistakes I made.After the main wheels touched the runway, I smoothly brought the throttle to take-off power position, and selected flaps to the take off position for the touch and go. I felt the aircraft accelerating but less than normal acceleration. I decided to execute an aborted take off procedure. I brought the throttle to idle, moved the stick forward to lower the nose to the runway and applied brakes.
ASRS:1843526.s: The PIC aborted a touch-and-go in Aircraft X at ZZZ after observing reduced acceleration following a DEEC reversion to manual mode. The aircraft overran the runway into the EMAS because the pilot failed to lower the nose wheel to activate normal brakes before applying emergency brakes.

ASRS:1843556.n: Climbing out of ZZZ I was on an IFR flight plan in VMC conditions in a climb just about to transition altimeter setting to 29.92 transitioning into the flight levels. Engines were set at climb power (37.5' Mp 2400 RPM full rich) and the autopilot was engaged on Nav mode Direct ZZZ1 in Vertical Speed mode at about 800 FPM climbing at approximately 155-160 KIAS.The nose yawed hard right and I heard a tone change in the right engine. At this time I disconnected the autopilot to hand fly the aircraft. The mixtures were already full rich so I advanced the props forward to 2500 RPM. I normally would have pushed both throttles full forward but knowing I had more than sufficient obstacle clearance below me and not wanting to put additional stresses on the left (good) engine I left the Mp on that engine at 37.5' and pitched for airspeed of 155. Normally you would pitch for VySE however to maintain cooling and a higher margin of directional control I intentionally kept speed at 155KIAS and accepted any change in vertical speed which may have resulted. I [notified ATC] and on multiple occasions told the controller to stand by and I did some trouble shooting and made a decision on what to do. Leaving the left engine at about 37.5' and now at 2500 RPM I noted the right engine was producing only about 15' of manifold pressure, flowing 38 GPH of fuel with good pressures and oil temps with CHT's decreasing quickly. As I moved the right throttle forward thrust rapidly decreased on the right engine causing more yaw. When I decreased throttle to verify the thrust came back somewhat. I made the decision to shut down, feather and secure the right engine which I did.I trimmed the aircraft and considered what was going on thinking this was likely an issue with the right turbo based on my engine inputs. Although the engine was secured and I knew I could make an emergency landing single engine I decided to attempt one restart on the right engine under the thought process that one good turbocharged engine and one engine essentially operating as normally aspirated was better than one turbocharged engine and a feathered engine. My aircraft has a digital engine monitor so if the right engine ran out of oil pressure or produced pressures or temperatures out of range I would get a visual alarm on the annunciator light in front of me.I told the controller that I wanted to divert to ZZZ2 and I turned towards the airport. The controller cleared me to ZZZ2 and told me to let him know when I had the ATIS information. Hand flying the aircraft with a very frightened wife beside me I tuned in ATIS on my Comm 2 wishing the controller had given me the altimeter, wind, runway in use field elevation and a vector and a frequency for tower. I descended to pattern altitude and made an entry onto a right downwind and switched to tower. Tower told me they briefly saw me trailing smoke. I asked whether the smoke was black or white and they said it was white. They stated white so I now knew I was losing oil somewhere. I made a partial flap landing (20 degree) at 110 KIAS and made a slightly long landing. After clearing the runway I shut down the right engine and performed an after landing checklist. With the assistance of Ground I taxi the aircraft to the FBO and began making arrangements to get my wife home on a commercial flight and I called ZZZ Center, my Mechanic and an experienced CFI to get the link on how to file a report. Contributing factors were my relatively low time in type and time flying high performance turbocharged aircraft. I believe that my actions were for the most part good however I am still on the fence as to whether restarting an engine after shutdown was a good idea or whether I should have kept it feathered and headed straight for ZZZ2 with it feathered. Factors affecting human performance were primarily fear and adrenaline. I was very shaky during this event. I believe that my biggest mistake was not being more firm withATC. I should have requested in no uncertain terms that ZZZ Center give me the local altimeter setting runway in use winds and tower frequency when I wanted them. I should not have taken my attention away from flying the aircraft single engine to turn in ATIS on my Com 2 and try to get basic information while listening to him direct other aircraft. In the future I will remember that ATC is there to assist me and I will be more direct with requests during an [urgent situation].All in all I think everything turned out fine. The failure appears to be catastrophic failure of the outboard turbo on the right engine. A post mortem on the turbo and further inspection and oil analysis of the oil, screens and engine components and an analysis of the data from the engine monitor will tell shed further light on what happened.
ASRS:1843556.s: The pilot of a turbocharged aircraft experienced a catastrophic right outboard turbo failure during climb-out from ZZZ, causing severe yaw and smoke. After securing the engine, the pilot diverted to ZZZ2 and landed safely, attributing the incident to the turbo failure and noting that fear and low type experience affected performance.

ASRS:1843594.n: 900 miles out of ZZZ, just past ZZZZZ. We received ATA Fail> AUNX MAU (Master Avionics Unit) 3A Fail. ADS 3 Fail. Spoiler Fault. FDR AFT Fail. Auto Config Trim FailAll nav indications on the FO (First Officer) side is gone. Flight director is gone. Auto throttle disengaged and auto pilot disengaged. We performed QRH for the AUNX (Annunciator Message). We found that we have lost systems and flight controls, i.e. multi-functional spoilers and speed brakes. In addition we were not for sure if we had lost OB brakes...no indication on the status page. This concerned us given, #2 OB locked up on validation flight. We made a crew decision to turn back for ZZZ. Once it was decided we were turning back, we proceeded off tracks, made a climb to proper altitude, and then intercepted track back to ZZZ. Notified ATC and Airline that we were returning as a [priority handling] aircraft.
ASRS:1843594.s: The crew experienced multiple avionics and flight control failures, including lost navigation and spoiler faults, 900 miles from ZZZ. Concerned about potential brake issues, they followed the QRH, turned back, and returned to ZZZ as a priority handling aircraft.

ASRS:1843605.n: Upon landing at ZZZ for fuel, a normal wheel landing was conducted on Runway XX, which was in use per ATC. Landing was smooth and as airspeed bleed below 40 kts., tail settled to ground smoothly after slightly floating. Once tail was on the ground, it felt like something bit into my right main and aircraft canted hard right. Full left rudder and left brake were applied but I was unable to maintain directional control of the aircraft as it skidded towards the runway edge at approximately 35 degrees. As the aircraft slowed and braking became more effective, the aircraft canted back towards the left and stuck the wingtip on the ground and came to a stop on the runway. I noticed that I had trouble moving the aircraft on the ground due to an issue with my right main gear but was still able to taxi off the runway. While I am not exactly sure what caused this incident, the week prior I spend working with a school that specializes in Pitts training. Being current on the aircraft after spending some time away from flying the Pitts was extremely helpful and this situation would have undoubtedly ended different if I had not attended that course.
ASRS:1843605.s: The pilot landed a Pitts on Runway XX, but the right main gear struck an object, causing a skid and wingtip contact. Although the cause was unknown, the pilot attributed maintaining control and taxiing off to recent training.

ASRS:1843624.n: Aircraft X checked in 14,000 [ft.] descending via the Throne arrival. I issued converging traffic 12 NM NW descending Aircraft Y leaving 13,000 for 12,000 restricted above Aircraft X on the arrival. Approximately 4 NM converging when Aircraft X was level 11,000 on arrival I saw Aircraft Y start a descent out of 12,000. I issued a traffic alert and told Aircraft X to turn right immediately to heading 280. I reissued the traffic and told Aircraft X to descend to 8,000. I Told the Hemet controller to stop the descent of Aircraft Y but separation was already lost. Aircraft X reported Aircraft Y in sight was then instructed to maintain visual separation and proceed direct CRCUS to rejoin the Throne arrival when able. The Throne arrival crossing altitude at 11,000 when aircraft are descending to 12,000 on the Disney STAR leaves very little room for error on a descent and is a collision hazard for aircraft not adhering to the arrival restrictions. Aircraft X, was descending via the Disney Arrival for SNA. I had traffic from the east also descending via the Disney arrival that was going to be a tie. I vectored Aircraft X off the arrival on heading 170 and descended them to 8,000 feet to get them underneath unidentified traffic that was tracking the Disney arrival at 12,500 [ft.] and descending. Aircraft Y was descending via the THRNE arrival at 11,000. I handed Aircraft Y off to NORR and switched them to NORR. The aircraft were converging and Aircraft X was descending out of 12,000 when the NORR controller alerted me to the conflict and they called traffic to Aircraft X. I instructed Aircraft X to stop their descent and issued traffic. The aircraft crossed paths at EROCK with approximately 500 feet vertical. Neither aircraft responded to a TCAS RA. I should have stopped Aircraft X at 12,000 [feet[ when I gave them the vector to ensure they stayed above Aircraft Y on the THRNE at 11,000 [feet].
ASRS:1843624.s: An Air Traffic Controller reported a loss of separation between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y during descent on the Throne and Disney arrivals. The conflict, resulting in a 500-foot vertical crossing, occurred because the controller failed to hold Aircraft X at 12,000 feet while Aircraft Y descended at 11,000 feet.

ASRS:1843669.n: During takeoff/climbout (200') we entered wake turbulence from a 757 in front of us. The aircraft rolled to the right and we continued to climb just to the right of course. (0.18 was shown on the MFD). Winds were 150/07 and we were LNAV to RONII. Before getting back on LNAV track, ATC assigned us to a left turn to 070 and stated we were south of our track. In the next transmission, we stated what had happened (wake turbulence) and the Controller cleared us to continue the departure.
ASRS:1843669.s: During takeoff/climbout at 200 feet, the crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding 757, causing a right roll and deviation from the LNAV track to RONII. After ATC assigned a left turn to 070, the crew reported the incident and received clearance to continue the departure.

ASRS:1843697.n: At V1 a loud boom was heard [and] aircraft veered to the left. Normal rotation. Two more loud booms were observed audibly aircraft again veered left. We ran the appropriate checklist [and advised ATC]. Decision was made to proceed to ZZZ landing visually. All check list and procedures were followed no major errors occurred. Normal pushback, taxi and takeoff roll. At V1 speed experienced a loud bang and aircraft yawed to left. Applied max power and continued takeoff. The left engine stalled 3 more times during climb out, cleared stall by retarding thrust lever to idle and ran the engine limit or surge or stall checklist. Was able to increase power per checklist, engine responded ok. [Requested priority handling] and landed at ZZZ.
ASRS:1843697.s: The crew experienced a loud boom and left yaw at V1, followed by three left engine stalls during climb. They executed the engine surge checklist, recovered the engine, and landed visually at ZZZ with no major errors.

ASRS:1843711.n: The Jeppesen approach plate for Denver RNP to Runway 26 seems to have an inappropriate speed restriction for the initiation of the RF legs from both sides of the airfield. Both speed restrictions require an 'AT 210 knots;' all other RNP approaches similar in design have 'Below 210 knots.' The use of a hard 'AT 210 knots' for our aircraft means you must be in a manual speed control mode which is not desired for the approach being flown. Clean maneuvering speed (212-215 knots) of the aircraft is typically above the speed requiring the use of flaps and a manual speed window be open, which is a non-standard configuration for this type of approach. Recommend the approach plate be updated to show 'Below 210' knots max speed at the initial fix.
ASRS:1843711.s: A pilot reported that the Denver RNP Runway 26 approach plate incorrectly lists a hard "AT 210 knots" speed restriction instead of "Below 210 knots." This error forces manual speed control and a non-standard clean configuration, prompting a recommendation to update the plate.

ASRS:1843730.n: As I stopped short of exiting the Southport on the Bravo line, waiting for ATC clearance, our nose wheel rolled into a hole. I had the right engine running. I could not exit the hole on one engine. I started the second engine and could not exit the hole with normal breakaway thrust. We coordinated with ramp and increased the thrust to 70% and still could not break out. I was just about to shutdown and request a tug, but tried once more, moving the nose wheel and a little more thrust as we were able to break out. This hole needs to be filled.
ASRS:1843730.s: The pilot reported that while waiting for ATC clearance on the Southport Bravo line, the nose wheel entered a hole. The aircraft required both engines at 70% thrust to break free, prompting a recommendation to fill the hole.

ASRS:1843879.n: I was flying in Aircraft X. I left ZZZ1, where the plane is hangared at, headed to ZZZ. I have friends that talk about landing on the sandbars on the river. I decided to check it out while I was that close. I flew for a while and found one that I thought was suitable to land on. I made several reconnaissance passes to find a landing zone. I found what I thought was suitable landing zone and started my approach. At about touchdown I noticed a sand dune (which turned out to be a shelf of sand) that was about 2 feet high. I decided to abort the landing right at touchdown. As I advanced the throttle the mains dug into the sand which slowed the plane down. I was able to become airborne again but didn't get high enough to clear the dune/shelf. The gear hit the new softer sand and slowed the plane down which brought the nose down into the sand. The plane tipped forward and left. The left-wing tip hit the ground and I had a prop strike. The left-wing tip is bent and the prop is rolled. There doesn't appear to be any further damage to the plane.
ASRS:1843879.s: The pilot of Aircraft X attempted an unauthorized landing on a river sandbar. The aircraft struck a sand shelf during an aborted touchdown, resulting in a prop strike and bent left-wing tip after the plane tipped forward.

ASRS:1843897.n: After a personal training flight to practice landings at a nearby airstrip where a straight headwind was from 180 degrees, I returned to finish my flight at ZZZ. I was about 1 hour into the flight. Winds at 8 kts. gusting to 17 were being reported at ZZZ, so I made a plan to use Runway XX, a turf strip with favorable winds. As I neared ZZZ at about 10 miles out I noticed traffic was using Runway XY at ZZZ. I listened again to weather and the winds had calmed and no gusts were being reported. I decided to change my plan and set up to land on Runway XX.My approach was normal and everything was smooth until the last instant, just after touchdown, my plane lurched to my left. I pushed in throttle to get airborne. I had 40 degrees of flaps in at this time. The plane lifted free of the ground and stayed there, climbing only a slow rate and now at a 30 degree angle corresponding to direction the plane was facing as it left the runway.I now found myself heading toward the airport hangers and climbing slowly with little airspeed. I knew I was now straight into the wind and at this slow an airspeed a turn seemed not a good choice. I cleared the hangars and slowly let out some flap angle to gain some speed. I climbed slowly, reducing flaps a bit and keeping the nose and climb angle slight.After the plane was cleaned and climbing I flew straight at 2,000 ft. to calm down. This had all happened very fast and I took a few minutes to go through a cruise checklist. I now resolved to indeed land on Runway XX and set up a pattern for that strip. This landing went very smoothly and I taxied in and tied down the plane.As I thought about this it is my thought that I may very well have hit the left brake upon touchdown.
ASRS:1843897.s: The pilot, flying a personal training flight to ZZZ, experienced a left lurch immediately after touchdown on Runway XX. The pilot aborted the landing, climbed slowly past hangars, and later attributed the incident to likely accidental application of the left brake.

ASRS:1843899.n: I was cleared by ATC to turn base and follow traffic in on final. I had a white Skyhawk in sight on final, so I reported traffic in sight. ATC cleared me to turn. After turning base I saw another Skyhawk extremely close to me. ATC told me to hold present altitude and they told the Skyhawk to hold present altitude. I received vectors away from the GA corridor. After that I was again cleared to turn base. It was a miscommunication between both pilots and ATC I believe. I knew there was another Skyhawk somewhere in the pattern, and I thought it was further away (I heard its radio calls & it was about 10 miles out).
ASRS:1843899.s: The pilot reported a near-miss with a Cessna Skyhawk while turning base after being cleared to follow traffic. The reporter attributed the incident to a miscommunication between both pilots and ATC regarding the second aircraft's position.

ASRS:1843913.n: Following a day flight, while flying as an observer pilot in a multi-engine prop aircraft. After dropping their passenger off at ZZZ1 on the return leg Captain and First Officer were forced to make a weather diversion to ZZZ2. They filled the aircraft with fuel and following hours of waiting were cleared to fly at night back to ZZZ. Shortly after takeoff, Captain was adjusting his GPS across the cockpit in front of First Officer, during this short period he became disoriented in the clouds at night. When both pilots peered back over at the steam gauges they were all spiraling, indicating a major problem. As they broke out of the clouds they saw multiple lights in a line, ZZZ2 Approach began yelling at the aircraft asking if everything was OK, and the steam gauges continued spiraling. After multiple quick scans and remembering his training, First Officer determined the lights were on the ground and they were in an inverted spiral. First Officer took control of the aircraft and communications, rolled the aircraft upright and executed a four G pull to prevent both pilots' demise only about 200 ft. above the ground. Conditions were night, IFR, low-light with a ceiling of 1200 ft. overcast.Captain was the pilot and aircraft owner based out of ZZZ.
ASRS:1843913.s: The Captain and First Officer in a multi-engine prop aircraft entered an inverted spiral at night after the Captain became disoriented while adjusting the GPS. The First Officer recovered the aircraft from a 200-foot altitude by rolling upright and executing a four-G pull.

ASRS:1843917.n: During a training flight with a student we experienced an electrical failure/fault with our ammeter indicating a discharge. My student and I flew to another airport 50 NM away from our home airport for a night flight to satisfy PPL (Private Pilot) training requirements. We preflighted the aircraft and all systems were operational. Our runup was uneventful with normal indications and the ammeter showed an appropriate charge indication. We completed two full stop taxi-back landings at the other airport and departed back towards our home airport. About 25 minutes from our destination we heard an odd feedback in the headset and noticed the ammeter was ticking and indicating a discharge. We attempted to cycle the master switch/alternator switch but that did not remedy the situation. We heard the radio start to sound garbled as well. I elected to discontinue the training flight and head back to our home airport where the airplane could be serviced. However, due to the discharging battery, I turned off all electrical equipment in the aircraft including navigation lights and ADS-B out to conserve power so that we could put the landing light and navigation lights on during our approach and landing. This resulted in us not having ADS-B out or navigation lights on in airspace in which they are normally required. I felt it necessary to deviate from the regulations in order to safely get the aircraft back into our home airport where repairs could be made. I also avoided known busy airspace so as to deconflict from any other traffic in the area. We landed uneventfully and the plane was squawked so that it can be inspected.
ASRS:1843917.s: A pilot and student experienced an alternator failure during a night training flight, causing the ammeter to indicate discharge and radio interference. The pilot conserved battery power by turning off required ADS-B Out and navigation lights to safely return home, landing uneventfully for inspection.

ASRS:1843945.n: This is a general concern of safety regarding the (Company) vaccine mandate. After the mandate was announced on (date), I noticed many employees were distracted by the impending decision between their livelihood and a permanent medical decision. On the push back during one flight, a ramp crew member stated their concern. Other crew members stated their concern about this mandate and this could lead to distractions at work, which could in turn lead to unsafe conditions. If employees were given a choice or an option for this mandate, I believe the distractions would be eliminated.
ASRS:1843945.s: A pilot reported that company vaccine mandates caused employee distraction and safety concerns during pushback, as ramp and cabin crew expressed anxiety over the choice between their livelihood and medical decisions. The reporter believes offering an option would eliminate these distractions and prevent unsafe conditions.

ASRS:1843976.n: During preflight in ZZZZ a SEC2 Fault occurred. After calling Maintenance Control and attempting to reset, the fault remained. Local maintenance was called. Only one Technician was available. English is a second language and all procedures were written in English. The language barrier combined with lack of experience on Airbus caused some lack of confidence on the Technician's part. I was required to assist in understanding what the procedure said and had to point out the systems required to be deferred. I consulted Maintenance Control again to ensure all items were accomplished per the deferral. Upon completion of the deferral and receiving a new Maintenance Release, we were ready to depart. However, the Local authorities would not release us stating, the Technician did not document the event correctly. I called the Chief Pilot and they coordinated with the station and after a 90 minute delay, we were released. The remainder of the flight was uneventful.
ASRS:1843976.s: During preflight in ZZZZ, a SEC2 fault required deferral assistance due to a technician's language barrier and lack of Airbus experience. Local authorities initially withheld release for incorrect documentation, causing a 90-minute delay before the flight departed uneventfully.

ASRS:1844007.n: I took off from ZZZ on a reposition flight to ZZZ1. At 900 ft. I turned the autopilot on with the master switch. At no point during the event did I ever engage the autopilot by selecting a mode. The 'ready' annunciation turned on and then it turned off. At the time I was flying runway heading. Approach then gave me a right hand turn at which time I noticed the turn coordinator had frozen and was not turning with me. It had previously worked fine on the ground. I decided to return to ZZZ. Approach gave me another right hand turn and that is when the aircraft controls became very stiff. It was difficult to turn the aircraft and even more difficult to hold altitude. After I leveled out in that turn, approach attempted to make a radio call that was very broken up and I asked her standby. She then informed me I was almost completely unreadable but when I asked her standby a second time she heard me a little better. I recycled the autopilot master switch and it once again showed ready and then the ready disappeared. I turned the autopilot master switch back off and pressed the red autopilot disconnected button but nothing changed. I then leaned over to try to pull the circuit breaker. After a few moments of not being able to pull the circuit breaker, I still couldn't get it. At this time I requested priority handling. I said if [I] could get out of IFR I would like to [have] the Approach Controller turned me again to more of a downwind leg for Runway XX. Another aircraft called and said they had the field in sight at 2000 ft. and 5 miles from the runway. I told Approach to send me there. She gave me a small turn and descended me to 2,000 ft. When I made it to 2,000 ft., I checked the trim to see if moving forward and back would alleviate the problem. I moved it backwards (towards nose up) and everything with the trim seemed to be working properly but have no affect on the controls stiffness. I pushed the trim wheel forward and then back to level flight. At this time, the aircraft had started a small descent which the VSI also showed but the attitude indicator showed a 10 degree nose pitch up. After returning the aircraft to level, I noted the attitude indicator was becoming sluggish and not matching the movements of the aircraft as quickly as it normally does. The stiffness of the controls wanted the aircraft to pitch nose down and made it difficult to turn, however when I got to just outside the final approach fix flying in the opposite direction, I was still unable to see the runway so I had to shoot the ILS Runway XX into ZZZ. The only reduction in stiffness came when I pulled the power for in range and it lessened the pull I was having to put on the yoke to maintain altitude and heading. All engine gauges including the suction gauge were normal throughout the event. I was met at the hangar after landing by the Airport Support Personnel and [other] airport personnel. I wrote up the aircraft afterwards and discussed everything that happened per [each] instrument with the Mechanic so he could have a better picture of the situation.
ASRS:1844007.s: The pilot experienced stiff flight controls, a frozen turn coordinator, and a sluggish attitude indicator shortly after takeoff while flying an IFR reposition flight. The pilot returned to the departure airport, requested priority handling, and landed via ILS after troubleshooting the autopilot and trim systems without resolving the control stiffness.

ASRS:1844019.n: Roughly XA:20 into the flight, southwest of ZZZZ, the HYD QT LOW R alert displayed on the MFDU (Multi function Display Unit). Accomplished the checklist. Selected the HYD page from the Systems menu and noted the right hydraulic quantity indicated .34. Called dispatch and requested Maintenance Control be conferred in. Requested Maintenance Control's input on securing the right engine primary hydraulic pump. Maintenance Control concurred it would be beneficial to secure the right engine primary pump, and it was secured. The right electric demand pump activated. The right hydraulic quantity continued to decrease. Secured the right electric demand pump. The right hydraulic quantity indicated .16 when the right electric demand pump was secured. After conferring with dispatch and Maintenance Control, it was determined that the preferred course of action was to continue to ZZZ. The right hydraulic quantity stabilized at .12.
ASRS:1844019.s: During cruise southwest of ZZZZ, the crew received a HYD QT LOW R alert and secured the right engine primary and electric demand pumps per Maintenance Control advice. The right hydraulic quantity stabilized at .12, allowing the flight to continue to ZZZ.

ASRS:1844022.n: During cruise at FL360 the First Officer and I felt a pressurization change in our ears. We checked the overhead pressurization panel and saw that the cabin climb indicator was indicating a rapidly climbing cabin. The cabin altitude indicator was also increasing. We donned our oxygen masks and I elected to follow the Rapid Depressurization Checklist in the QRH. We [requested priority handling] and were cleared to descend. We descended to 10,000 ft. then completed the remaining normal procedures checklist before diverting to ZZZ. One major factor in the event was crew communication in the cockpit. With the speakers on and the breathing noises carrying over the interphone we had to repeat ourselves numerous times increased the workload of the event. Reading the checklist and verifying the actions combined with ATC instructions, the Flight Attendant briefing and announcements to the passengers proved to be challenging. Another factor was the decision to go with the checklist that I felt was the safest for the passengers and crew. I felt that taking any extra time to look at the other checklists that may apply would be time consuming and compromise our margin of safety. [I suggest] reviewing and using oxygen masks in the simulator more.
ASRS:1844022.s: During cruise at FL360, the flight crew experienced rapid depressurization and descended to 10,000 ft before diverting. The pilot attributed increased workload to interphone breathing noises and prioritized the Rapid Depressurization Checklist to maintain safety margins.

ASRS:1844039.n: After landing, left main gear showed abnormal brake temperatures. The outboard brakes were at 400 degrees and increasing while the inboard brakes were at 21 degrees. The right main landing gears showed normal temperatures expected after a normal landing. BRK OVERHEAT and LG NO DISPATCH caution messages populated on EICAS. FO (First Officer) and I discussed it and thought it was most likely was a faulty indication. I asked FO to perform a post flight walk around and report back what he finds. FO came back and said the inboard wheel was missing on the landing gear. After landing parking at the gate, both pilots noticed that the left main gear outboard brake temp was unusually high to over 450C while inboard brake remained at around 22C. The brake overtemp EICAS msg popped out couple seconds after following with LG no Dispatch message after the flight crew shut down the engine. First Officer noticed right away the left side inboard landing gear the wheel was missing during post flight walk around
ASRS:1844039.s: Pilots reported abnormal left main gear brake temperatures and EICAS cautions after landing, which they initially suspected were faulty indications. A post-flight walk-around by the First Officer revealed the left inboard wheel was missing, causing the brake overheat and no dispatch messages.

ASRS:1844053.n: Climbing through 13,000 ft. we got an 'Elevator Split' caution message. I continued to fly the airplane and took the radios while the Captain ran the QRH. The QRH directed us to land at the nearest suitable airport. We decide to return to ZZZ and [requested priority handling] since we had a flight control issue. After completing the QRH the Captain notified the cabin crew and passengers. We also notified ZZZ Operations of our return. Once we were ready to land the Captain took control of the aircraft. Our approach, landing, and taxi to the gate was uneventful.
ASRS:1844053.s: During climb through 13,000 ft, the crew received an 'Elevator Split' caution and executed the QRH to return to ZZZ with priority handling. The aircraft landed and taxied to the gate uneventfully after the Captain resumed control.

ASRS:1844081.n: After landing on Runway XXR at ZZZ I taxied onto taxiway 1. Ground instructed to taxi to parking via [taxiway] 2 [and] 3. I read the instructions back and proceeded to 3 via 2. This flight was part of my IOE with a more senior company pilot who, out of habit, directed me to turn onto 1, which was closed by NOTAM. I assumed I must have been in error and turned. ZZZ's ground controller immediately intervened and corrected our improper turn. I made a right 270 to continue down 2 to 3. The main incident occurred as I made the slight right turn to the SE Ramp from taxiway 3. The plane's turn radius to the right was too large and I noticed my left wingtip approaching a parked 53-foot trailer. I was already applying full right rudder with no brakes, and then I applied right brake pressure but the turn did not increase. Seemingly suddenly, the airplane pulled to the left and pointed the nose directly at the trailer.I then applied full brakes on both sides, but there was little or no braking. I applied full reverse thrust and it brought the plane to a full stop in a few feet. The plane stopped at approximately a 60-degree angle to the left of the intended direction on the taxiway center line. Me and the other pilot decided to shut down and exit the aircraft. The nose wheel was at the maximum left turn position after we were out of the plane.The plane is being inspected for any mechanical issues related to the gear and brakes.
ASRS:1844081.s: An IOE pilot and senior pilot taxied a landing aircraft at ZZZ, deviating onto a closed taxiway before nearly striking a trailer due to a large turn radius and ineffective brakes. The aircraft was stopped using reverse thrust and is now undergoing inspection for gear and brake issues.

ASRS:1844109.n: After preflight at the airplane's home base of ZZZ, I departed alone for ZZZ1. All systems are normal at this time. In ZZZ1, I take four (4) friends for short, individual flights totaling 0.9 hours. I get 5 gallons of 100LL from the ZZZ1 self service fuel pump, a pump I am familiar with, before beginning my return flight to ZZZ. I am accompanied by Name, as a non-pilot passenger to help with the ground handling and hangaring of the airplane at ZZZ. I preflight the airplane, inspecting control surfaces, landing gear, engine compartment, oil level, and fuel sump. I have 10 gallons of fuel at takeoff, equivalent to at least 1.5 hours of flying with reserves. Engine start up is normal, as is run up. No indicators of any malfunction were present. My passenger and I take off from Runway XX around XA:30pm and head south-south-east to fly over [named] Lake while climbing to 6,500 feet at a consistent vertical rate of 200-300 ft/min. At approximately XB:10 I begin my descent from 6,500 ft. At 5,500 ft. I notice RPMs are hovering around 1,400. I open the throttle to return power and the tachometer does not change. Our rate of descent is -500 ft/min and airspeed at 90 mph. I pitch to best glide speed of 60 mph and begin to try to restore power through carb heat application and cycling the magnetos. No change in tachometer as we cross 4,000 feet. I declare to my passenger our engine is out and we will be making an off field landing. Searching for southward facing open fields, I locate my landing spot and begin to circle over the field. At 500 ft. I cross Farm Road X and prepare for final landing in the field I have selected. I fly over the hay field, clear the fence, and touch down in the cow pasture. As the wheels touch down, the prop stops wind milling and I apply brakes to prevent a collision with the next fence. Once the plane is stopped I instruct my passenger to get out of the plane and meet me at our rendezvous point behind the tail, power off radios, magnetos, and shut off the fuel. It is XB:18. Taking a few moments to collect myself, I attempt to restart the airplane. The engine starts and runs for 1 minute, but shortly dies thereafter. With the sun starting to move lower in the sky, my passenger and I begin walking to find the property owner. The owners arrive, the [local authorities are sent] to assess the situation, and the FAA is contacted. No damage to any persons, property, or the airplane are sustained.
ASRS:1844109.s: A pilot and passenger experienced a total engine failure during descent from 6,500 feet, likely due to fuel starvation, forcing an off-field landing in a pasture. The aircraft sustained no damage, and the engine briefly restarted before failing again, with no injuries reported.

ASRS:1844110.n: Reaching the boundary with US airspace Between Country 1 and US I was monitoring the frequency with Country 1. I then heard Country 2 Accent, I found that odd due to the fact that we were with Country 1. I asked my First Officer if he had swapped back to Country 2 Control for some reason. I switched back to Country 1's frequency and tried to check in again to make sure they were not calling us. My com 1 screen was not working and com two did not allow us to out any frequency. I could put the frequency on standby, moved it to active but then it would go back to a frequency XXX.XX. I was able to communicate with them which was ZZZ Airport. I mentioned what was going on, my location and if he could relay a message with ZZZ1 Center. I recall he gave a couple frequencies for me to contact but was not able. I asked for a landline number to be able to call from the sat phone on board. By this time the radio kept swapping frequencies automatically and I lost contact with ZZZ Airport. I squawked 7600 [and] brief my copilot and passengers and began our descent to follow our loss on comms procedure. On the descent I was able to get a hold of ZZZ1 Center and was instructed on heading and altitudes. Reaching ZZZ2, ZZZ1 Gave me another number to call which was Approach and that they would be the one to guide me and give me landing clearance. In the meantime I was being vector i believe 11,000 feet and 190 on the heading. Once I got a hold of Approach on the phone we were instructed and landed without an issue. I contacted our repair station and both radios were bad. Both radios have been replaced.
ASRS:1844110.s: The flight crew experienced a dual radio failure while transitioning between Country 1 and US airspace, causing automatic frequency swapping and loss of contact. After squawking 7600 and following lost communications procedures, they used the satellite phone to coordinate with ATC and landed safely; both radios were subsequently replaced.

ASRS:1844113.n: I was one of three aircraft conducting pattern work for training at the uncontrolled airport. I was not keeping close track of where the other planes were (Problem 1), only that they were in the pattern ahead of me. After one of my touch-and-go's I climbed to 700 ft (Traffic pattern altitude - 300 ft) and started my crosswind turn. During that climb, I did not have the C152 in sight and was not paying attention to its specific position in the pattern (Problem 1). Because of my speed and climb advantage over the C152 I turned left crosswind for Runway XX inside of the C152. The C152 saw me cutting in front of them at nearly the same altitude as we were both about to turn left downwind, and took evasive action to create vertical separation by descending to 600 ft. At this time the instructor contacted me on the radio and asked if I could see him visually. I asked where he was. He responded that he was in a left downwind for XX. At this point, I saw the C152 below and in front of me. I slowed down, but continued to fly downwind (Problem 2). I intended to extend my downwind until after the C152 turned left base for XX. I did not see it turn base, and instead of contacting it to see what their intentions were, I turned base and started a descent thinking that they were leaving the pattern (Problem 3). At this time, the instructor in the C152 once again asked if I still held him visually, at this point the C152 came into view below and right of me flying in the same direction (left base for XX). I then maintained my altitude at 800 ft, turned and over flew the runway at that altitude. The C152 made a full stop landing. I completed another pattern and made a full stop landing to discuss the incident with the instructor in the C152. He help provide the details for this incident. The third plane in the traffic pattern was not a factor during this incident. What should have happenedProblem 1. I should have maintained a near exact position of the other aircraft in the pattern, especially the one right in front of me. On takeoff, I was dwelling on my last landing instead of putting my full attention on flying and collision avoidance. I should have waited to turn left crosswind until after I had seen the C152 turn left crosswind and ensured proper separation.Problem 2. At this point, I should have made a right turn out of the pattern and climbed to create both vertical and horizontal separation and to give the lower critical aircraft room to maneuver at a safe altitude.Problem 3. I should have communicated with the C152 instead of making assumptions. I should NOT have turned base and should NOT have descended without knowing exactly where the C152 was and ensuring there was not collision factor.
ASRS:1844113.s: The pilot of a training aircraft cut in front of a C152 during a crosswind turn at an uncontrolled airport, causing the C152 to descend for separation. The incident resulted from the pilot's failure to maintain visual contact, make assumptions about the other aircraft's position, and communicate intentions.

ASRS:1844135.n: After departure from ZZZ Airport we experience a possible elevator control problem that made it very difficult to comply with turns, altitude and speed. We were finally able to bring the aircraft into controlled flight but not after it had incurred altitude deviation. Our maintenance is looking into the reasons for elevator trim freezing causing the aircraft to go into uncommanded attitude and making it very difficult to control. This issue has been intermittent in the past and seems to be getting worse and more often an issue. My primary objective when this took place was just to fly the aircraft. The elevator trim sometimes hang up and make the aircraft go nose low and once freed up it goes nose high and it makes it challenge to say the least for both pilots to maintain & keep control. This issue must be fixed as it effect altitude hold and command bars on MFD.
ASRS:1844135.s: Pilots reported an intermittent elevator trim freezing issue shortly after departure from ZZZ Airport, causing uncommanded nose-low and nose-high attitudes that resulted in altitude deviation. The malfunction made controlling turns, speed, and altitude extremely difficult, affecting MFD command bars and requiring maintenance investigation.

ASRS:1844181.n: On approach into ZZZ, near the ZZZZZ waypoint at an altitude 6,000 feet on the FMS ZZZZZ1 Visual Runway XXR approach course, the First Officer (FO), who was PF, asked for Flaps 1. I moved the Flap handle from UP to position 1. A TE FLAP DISAGREE EICAS message appeared. I informed ATC we would not be able to continue the approach. ATC provided radar vectors off the approach course to the west of ZZZ. The FO continued in the role as PF as we ran the TE FLAP DISAGREE non-normal checklist.I [requested priority] with ATC.With clear, day VMC, a headwind on final, a 3,450 foot runway requirement, and two 10,000+ foot runways available, ZZZ was the obvious best choice for landing. I typed an ACARS message to Dispatch stating PRIOR TRAILING EDGE FLAPS DISAGREE FLAP 20 LANDNG ZZZ (sic). Dispatch replied with an ACARS message that the tower had been advised.After the event I spoke with the dispatcher and we discussed my ACARS message. He correctly interpreted the 'Prior' in my message as 'Priority.' In the future, I would not abbreviate that word so that no interpretation would be involved.I appreciated that he could see we were at a low altitude in the terminal area with a landing at ZZZ being the obvious best course of action with nearly perfect weather and ample runway, and that he kept his communication during this event brief and to the point.I called the purser and [briefed them], with no Evac preparation necessary or special instructions. I then made an announcement to the passengers explaining our delay and that we would be landing in ZZZ shortly.The FO and I then changed roles and I acted as PF for the Flaps 20 landing, flying the ILS XXL with the full runway length available in visual conditions. During taxi-in we decided to leave the flaps at 20 and informed ramp and operations. We are able to proceed and park at gate X.We entered a Maintenance defect. I discussed the defect with Maintenance who arrived on the flight deck. This person described a component, apparently visible in the wheel, that indicated a protection feature had activated. The FO and I debriefed the event using the debrief card as our guide. We felt the event had gone well.In particular, the aircraft had a history of flap and slat Maintenance defects, and the FO had brought this to my attention during preflight planning. Prior to our event, we had already looked at the QRH for one of the previously reported Maintenance defects and read through the checklist, identifying switches and selectors, and saw that a Flaps 20 landing would be the likely outcome. We both felt this exercise proved to be useful. Arriving on ZZZZZ5 into ZZZ, we had just passed ZZZZZ2 and were cleared to 6K. At 230 kts, we selected Flaps 1 and got TE Flap Disagree EICAS. This was a repeat maintenance write up. I was flying, so Captain requested to break off approach and get vectors while we ran the QRH checklist. He also coordinated with ATC, informed dispatch and the FA's. He [advised ATC], and we requested ILS XXL once we were ready to land. Flaps were configured to 20 using the alternate extension. CA took over Pilot Flying duties once the checklist was complete. We made an uneventful F20 [Flaps 20] landing on XXL and taxied to the gate.
ASRS:1844181.s: During approach to ZZZ at 6,000 feet, a TE FLAP DISAGREE EICAS message appeared after selecting Flaps 1, causing the crew to break off the approach. The Captain took over as Pilot Flying to execute a Flaps 20 landing on ILS XXL using alternate extension, attributing the issue to a protection feature activation and prior maintenance history.

ASRS:1844192.n: After reviewing the Aircraft log for Aircraft X, I concluded that I was unable to operate the aircraft due to MEL and the maintenance notes associated. The aircraft had been operating with this MEL and was to continue operating for another 2 days before getting fixed. The aircraft arrived from a 24 plus hour maintenance delay down in ZZZZ due to a hydraulic issue. I felt the prudent thing for Aircraft X was to have some time at a maintenance hanger to address MEL before operating another revenue flight. We were swapped into Aircraft Y and I was unable to select Aircraft X for this report. Just want to make sure there is no confusion.
ASRS:1844192.s: The pilot refused to operate Aircraft X due to existing MEL items and maintenance notes following a 24-hour hydraulic delay in ZZZZ. The crew was swapped to Aircraft Y to allow Aircraft X time in the hangar for repairs before further revenue flights.

ASRS:1844197.n: At cruise and approaching Denver at FL360 in smooth air with the A autopilot in command mode and LNAV/VNAV engaged, DEN Center instructed us to descend and maintain FL320. Shortly after initiating a VNAV descent to comply with the clearance we experienced an upset event due to wake turbulence. While completing the upset recovery procedure the most bank I saw was 35 degrees and while we did deviate slightly from our clearance laterally we promptly returned to our route and were easily able to comply with our vertical clearance, leveling at FL320. While I ensured there were no injuries in the cabin the F/O reported our wake turbulence encounter to ATC. DEN Center took our report but then delayed our clearance to descend via the CLASH 3 RNAV arrival until we were well above our vertical path. We accepted the clearance and began a descent but after a further ATC speed restriction to 260 knots we realized about 5 miles prior to EVRLY we would be unable to comply with the altitude restriction of FL200. Due to ATC frequency congestion we were unable to inform ATC of how high we were and crossed EVRLY approximately 400 feet above the restriction of FL200. We then returned to our vertical path and landed at DEN without further incident.
ASRS:1844197.s: The crew encountered wake turbulence during a VNAV descent to FL320, causing a 35-degree bank and minor lateral deviation. Later, ATC frequency congestion prevented reporting an inability to meet a speed restriction, resulting in crossing EVRLY 400 feet above the FL200 limit before landing safely.

ASRS:1844205.n: During cruise at FL400 the oil filter bypass light for engine #2 EICAS message began blinking and then remained on steady. I told the First Officer to continue flying and to advise ATC of the problem. I said I would reference the QRH 'ENGINE OIL FILTER BYPASS'. Reading the checklist we realized the procedure might have us shut down the engine. We asked for a descent from FL400. There was traffic below us at FL390 so ATC said it would be a minute before we could descend. We started to look for a suitable diversion airport at that time. I sent a message to Dispatch to 'call me'. We waited to retard/reduce the power to idle (as stated by the checklist) until the descent was initiated due to drift down airspeed restrictions at FL400 and traffic right below us. The oil filter bypass QRH required us to shut down the engine because the light did not extinguish when the throttle was brought to idle. We continued the checklist and shutdown #2 engine with the (MAX) 'ENGINE FAILURE OR SHUTDOWN' checklist. We [requested priority handling] with ATC. Dispatch responded within a few minutes but the frequency was garbled and somewhat busy. Communicating with Dispatch we received weather and NOTAMs for ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 and we collectively decided to divert to ZZZ3. Dispatch said they would send landing data for Runway XXR at ZZZ3. I also looked up the non-normal landing distance performance table. So many performance non-normals it was hard to find the One Engine inoperative section. Later I realized the aircraft/config performance non-normals table was alphabetized! It was an idle descent all the way down as the airport was only 80 miles away from where we shutdown the engine so we did not have to consider the drift down QRH. Dispatch stayed on the frequency if we needed any more assistance. I advised the purser [and] communicated with the passengers to advise them of the problem and our need to land in ZZZ3. We asked for extended vectoring with ATC to complete checklists and approach briefings. The First Officer continued to fly as we had discussed this during the descent and he was comfortable landing. Based on the situation and conditions I felt he was more than competent to execute a safe landing. Checklists were completed and an uneventful single engine approach and landing were completed. Airport Fire Department met the aircraft after landing and we taxied to a hard stand where passengers were able to deplane via air stairs. The First Officer and I had a meaningful debrief. I then contacted Dispatch and the Chief Pilot to debrief. A logbook entry was made and I had a discussion with Maintenance regarding the engine shutdown. We were operating Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on a B737 MAX-9. We had completed a delayed flight from ZZZ4 and had to do a quick turn in ZZZ. I started preparing the flight deck while the Captain did the walk-around and dealt with jumpseaters and a new-hire pilot doing an 'observation ride' with us in the flight deck jumpseat. With the preflight done, we pushed on time and started both engines on push-back due to the long start times on the LEAP engines. Both engines, specifically #2, appeared to start normally. Taxi out, takeoff, and initial cruise was normal. Approximately, 50NM East of ZZZ2, we had a #2 Engine 'Oil Filter Bypass' flashing amber annunciation. I took the radios from the Captain and continued to fly while he looked up the MAX QRH for an oil filter bypass. The first step in the checklist is to disengage the auto-throttles. So we did that. The next step is to retard the affected thrust lever until the bypass light extinguishes or the throttle is closed. The Captain said we needed to descend to close the throttle since we cannot maintain FL400 on a single engine. I looked up the engine out info page on the FMC to see what our target altitude should be. It said FL244. The Captain quickly sent a 'Call Me' ACARS message to Dispatch. While he did that I requested a descent to FL300 with ATC, because we felt there was a chance the bypass light would extinguish as we retarded the throttle on our way down to FL300. This piqued the interest of ATC which appropriately asked if we needed any assistance. At that time, I told them to standby due to us running a checklist. On our descent, we closed the throttle completely and the bypass light did not extinguish. Per the checklist, step 3 says if the light does not extinguish we are to proceed to the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist. We were a little surprised there were not any more steps involved with the checklist, such as checking other engine indications for corroboration. So before proceeding to engine shutdown we re-examined the fault, we made sure we were in the correct checklist, and that we had not erred or missed anything that would prevent an engine shutdown. Our conclusion was that we had not and an engine shutdown was necessary. After securing the engine, [I requested assistance] with ATC and requested FL240, I also began slowing the aircraft down to a more drift-down speed so we would not get too far away from ZZZ2, which appeared to be VMC, as well as prevent us from having large amounts of asymmetrical thrust at level-flight at a low altitude. While this was occurring, the Captain was briefing the Flight Attendants. He was also coordinating with Dispatch. Dispatch informed us that the weather in ZZZ2 was not VMC and he recommend ZZZ3 instead due to weather. Hearing Dispatch on frequency was a challenge due to the lag in relays, static on the frequency, and other parties transmitting on the same frequency. That is one area specifically that I feel could use improvement. Communicating to Dispatch should be as easy as communicating to ATC in a high stress, time limited situation. After agreeing of diverting to ZZZ3, I notified ATC of our new destination and we received vectors direct to the airport. The Captain made a PA to the passengers to explain the situation and plan. Next, the Captain began running the single engine landing checklist to prepare for landing in ZZZ3. I simultaneously began loading the ILS XXR approach in the FMC and prepared the aircraft for an approach into ZZZ3. We requested a delay vector for an extend final so we had ample time to complete all the checklists. Once we were set up, we completed the deferred items and began configuring the aircraft for landing. We had emergency equipment standing by upon our arrival as a precaution. The XXR runway was plenty long for our brakes 3, flaps 15, increased Ref speed approach, and we made an uneventful single engine landing. We were able to taxi under our own power to the ramp for passenger deplaning via air-stairs and busing to the terminal. We ensured everyone safely exited the aircraft and submitted a maintenance write-up for an engine oil filter bypass annunciation with a corresponding inflight engine shutdown. I feel everyone worked well together with excellent CRM including the Company new-hire observation First Officer, Name. I also feel safety was not in jeopardy at any time.
ASRS:1844205.s: The crew of a B737 MAX-9 experienced an Engine #2 oil filter bypass light during cruise at FL400, requiring an engine shutdown per the QRH. They diverted to ZZZ3 due to weather, completed checklists, and executed an uneventful single-engine landing with emergency services standing by.

ASRS:1844298.n: Pushback operator alerted us to a fuel leak at the center of the fuselage. Maintenance was called. Maintenance asked for an immediate APU shutdown. No power on aircraft. Fuel odor and fumes filled the cabin. I asked the A Flight Attendant to initiate an Emergency Deplanement. She did. Passengers returned to terminal. Maintenance fixed the leak signed the book and we re-boarded and departed. The Mechanic seemed pretty serious about shutting down the APU and left with no other input. Given the information I was presented with I would react the same again.
ASRS:1844298.s: The pilot reported a fuel leak at the fuselage center during pushback, prompting maintenance to order an immediate APU shutdown. This caused cabin fumes, leading to an emergency deplanement before the leak was repaired and the flight departed.

ASRS:1844305.n: After starting engines and completing the before takeoff checklist on the ZZZZ Ramp, ZZZZ Tower Control cleared us to back taxi & lineup/wait runway XX, and the I correctly read those instructions back to the controller. Before taxiing onto the runway from taxiway C--which is approximately 3,500 ft. from the approach end of Runway XX--we verified that both the runway and final approach areas were clear, especially since it was still dark out, wet runway, and the weather was reported scattered at 2,000 ft AGL.With about 2,000 ft. of taxi distance remaining, both the Captain & I observed an approaching aircraft's landing lights breaking out of the weather. (Call sign of that aircraft is unknown.) Captain observed on TCAS that the approaching aircraft was only about 500 ft above our position at field elevation. At no time did we hear communication between the approaching aircraft and tower prior to observing the landing lights. This also highlights that the actual weather on approach to Runway XX was significantly lower than the reported 2,000 ft. scattered.I immediately communicated via tower freq 'The approaching aircraft needs to go around, we are still on the runway' at which point we observed a climb from the approaching aircraft while the tower controller and approaching aircraft pilot were communicating in non-English. With the approaching aircraft go-around underway, we completed our back-taxi, and were cleared for an uneventful takeoff & departure shortly thereafter.We operated strictly IAW flight manual and ICAO procedures, to include maintaining SA of the aerodrome environment which allowed us to see the traffic and direct the go-around, preventing a more dramatic outcome. The cause is very simply sub-standard Country ATC operations that allowed this situation to arise. (Regrettably--and even though this was the first experience for me in the dozen or so times I have operated in Country--events like this are purportedly not uncommon in Country based on fellow pilots' accounts. Country operators do not adhere to the highest standards of ICAO procedures.) In this case, it is safe to assume that there was a likely ATC coordination breakdown between approach and tower controllers since we were cleared onto an active runway while an approaching aircraft was on final approach. And for whatever reason, the approaching aircraft was not on tower freq until well inside the final approach fix, otherwise we would have heard the check in. Also, had it been VMC, we would have likely seen the aircraft on approach and declined to take the runway.NEVER get complacent operating in Country. We were given clearance to back taxi and to line up and wait on Runway XX in ZZZZ. After receiving the clearance, I confirmed with my First Officer, turned on all aircraft lighting, checked for traffic, and proceeded. While taxiing on the runway, we observed landing lights breaking out of what appeared to be an overcast layer from an approaching aircraft. My first officer immediately transmitted on the tower frequency that 'the approaching aircraft needs to go around, we are on the runway'. I recall that simultaneously the aircraft started a climb and there was communication in non-English on the tower frequency. We were subsequently given clearance for takeoff.Human error on ATC. Add a parallel taxiway at ZZZZ airport.
ASRS:1844305.s: The flight crew received a clearance to line up and wait on Runway XX at ZZZZ but observed an approaching aircraft on final in low visibility. The crew initiated a go-around for the other aircraft, attributing the conflict to ATC coordination failure and human error that allowed simultaneous runway occupancy.

ASRS:1844338.n: Wake turbulence encounter following a Boeing 747 on final approach. On radar downwind in VFR conditions we were cleared a visual approach following a 747 that was already established on final. On the dog leg to final I was descending to arrive at the FAF at what would be a normal intercept for glideslope to runway 07R. Autopilot and autothrottles were connected at this time. I noted on TCAS that we were 6 miles behind the heavy as we were about be aligned on final. Suddenly we encountered the wake turbulence from the preceding aircraft and the aircraft rolled quickly to the left. I took over controls manually and disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles while simultaneously recovering the airplane from the sharp bank to the left. The event happen very quickly, so I am unsure as to what bank angle we reached but estimating more than 30 and less than 45deg. We received a roll authority alert as the auto pilot had been unable to maintain level flight with the quick onset from the wake turbulence. The aircraft recovered and we re-established ourselves on final. I mentioned to the First Officer that I was going to climb and maintain above the preceding aircraft flight path and also stay above glide slope for the remainder of the approach, planning to touchdown at 2,000 feet. The rest of the flight was uneventful and we landed normally in Anchorage.Looking back on this event I could have easily avoided encountering the wake turbulence. When cleared for the visual approach behind the 747 I should've maintained my altitude instead of starting a gradual descent. I had plenty of time to descend later and descending at that time only increased the chances of encountering the wake. At the time, I was considering the fact that our distance was adequate and that we wouldn't have any issues following the 747 using normal visual cues /angle approaching the runway. I was wrong. Even 6 miles behind the heavy the turbulence was strong and the rolling tendency abrupt. Not worth the risk, not to mention the discomfort to the passengers and crew. In the future I will certainly keep this in mind for a visual behind a preceding heavy aircraft to avoid this type of encounter.
ASRS:1844338.s: The pilot encountered wake turbulence from a preceding Boeing 747 while descending on a visual approach to runway 07R, causing an abrupt left roll exceeding 30 degrees. The pilot manually recovered the aircraft and completed a normal landing, attributing the event to an unnecessary early descent that increased wake exposure risk.

ASRS:1844348.n: After arriving at the aircraft, we completed our normal pre-flight duties. The only irregularity was a temp controller MEL which we reviewed.During climb talking to the 2nd or 3rd center controller, he asked if we were on a heading. I referenced the FMC and told him we were direct DEFUN. He didn't respond for a few seconds, then cleared us direct MVC flight plan route. We thought this question was unusual and spooled back to the beginning.Reviewing our clearance/CPDLC during cruise, we realized our mistake. During pre-flight we were discussing the new EPCOT1 departure and the need to load a runway for departure to load properly. After the recent FL airspace update the departure runway is now included in the clearance, and I brought that up to my partner. The CPDLC came back and we verified clearance and jumped to page2/3 to check for runway. Runway 36R was listed and we proceeded to to load the runway and verified the legs/restrictions on the EPCOT1. Fixating on the runway and departure with the usual just before closing door activities caused us to miss the page 3/3 load prompt for a route change after MUGLS to DEFUN. The controller sorted it out without any issues, but in the future I will make sure the entire clearance/route gets reviewed again after loading the runway and departure.Being able to print entire clearance without scrolling 3 pages might have helped us catch this error promptly.
ASRS:1844348.s: The flight crew missed a route change from MUGLS to DEFUN during climb due to fixating on loading the runway for the EPCOT1 departure. An air traffic controller identified the discrepancy and issued a corrected clearance to the flight plan route without incident.

ASRS:1844355.n: Right aux bladder had been replaced the previous week. Noticed a fuel imbalance during preflight and maintenance said they only had 35 gals in the right aux since they replaced the bladder. We added fuel and left. First landing was uneventful but due to weather, we had just used the fuel in the aux tanks and were just a little bit into the mains tanks. The airplane was fueled and sat for about 1.5 hours while the crew coordinated the next inspection. When crew went to leave, another aircraft was parking on the ramp in front of our airplane while we had the main cabin door open. Crew noticed fuel/exhaust smell in aircraft but attributed it to the exhaust of the other aircraft. Crew started engines and taxied out for takeoff. Several comments were made by the crew members on how bad the smell was inside the aircraft. After takeoff, fuel fumes became more present in the cockpit and cabin. Burning eyes, irritation in throat was experienced by all crew members. Crew elected to go on supplemental Oxygen and return to departure airport for precautionary landing. Crew was getting vectors and believed the smell was getting worse. In order to not have any delays, PIC [requested priority handling] for immediate landing. No further assistance required. Landed without incident. PIC called off [support] trucks when switching to tower.Crew believes there was improper installation of the right fuel bladder causing a fuel leak in the belly of the aircraft.
ASRS:1844355.s: The crew experienced fuel fumes and respiratory irritation during takeoff and climb after a recent right auxiliary bladder replacement. They returned for a precautionary landing, attributing the leak to improper bladder installation in the aircraft belly.

ASRS:1844391.n: This report is for the dangerous situation of inadvertently approaching an airport in mountainous terrain. at night at too low of a height above the airport.This issue happened because I did not crosscheck information provided by the Garmin GTN 625 Navigator for VNAV profile with airport information. The button sequencing on the GTN 'zeroed out' the 1;000ft AGL offset I programed into the VNAV feature. This appears to occur with all GTN 6xx/7xx navigators.I was flying a personal flight to SAF. I knew that I would be arriving at night, and planned to approach from the Albuquerque area to avoid terrain. In order to have a safe approach to the airport, I setup VNAV in my GPS Navigator, a Garmin GTN 625. I used the VNAV feature to give a 3 degree glide path to a point 1 mile from the airport at 1;000ft AGL.In setting up the VNAV, for altitude I entered a value of 1;000ft, then hit the MSL/AGL soft key to enable AGL.When I reviewed the added point VNAV waypoint in the flight plan on the GTN, it autofilled a crossing altitude of 6;349ft MSL. I had understood this to be the MSL altitude of 1,000 AGL. When approaching the airport, I descended through 7;000ft and noted that the terrain illuminated by city lights appeared closer than the approximately 1;600ft I was expecting. I arrested my descent, and climbed visually to an appropriate height visually with the airport in sight. I finished my traffic pattern and landed. I noted that the elevation of the field was 6,349 MSL.Later I tested my keystrokes in the GTN625. I tried to enter a VNAV waypoint with the following keystrokes:Enter 1;000ftHit the MSL/AGL buttonUpon doing this, I noted that when you hit the MSL/AGL button, the altitude/height reverts to 0. I learned that you must enter the AGL value AFTER hitting the MSL/AGL value. I also learned to always check your VNAV crossing altitudes with the chart.
ASRS:1844391.s: A pilot flying a personal flight to SAF at night inadvertently approached mountainous terrain too low due to a Garmin GTN 625 VNAV setup error. The device reset the programmed 1,000ft AGL offset to zero, causing the pilot to arrest the descent and climb visually before landing safely.

ASRS:1844394.n: There were 5 planes in the traffic pattern and 1 on the departing runway. I approached Runway XX (the favoring runway) from the east, at 4 miles out I announced my location and that I would break off the long final approach and join the traffic pattern on the upwind leg. Once in the traffic pattern I announced I was on the upwind leg for XX, full stop. As I turned crosswind a plane on the runway announced its departure. Not being sure about maintaining separation with the departing aircraft, I announced I would do a right-hand loop giving the departing aircraft time and distance from my aircraft. At the same time a C-172 announced a 45 to down wind and gave me some room.Completing the loop, I turned crosswind, announced, and then turned downwind and announced. On the downwind leg I came up quickly on a C-172. It is unclear where the plane came from, but it was the C-172 on the 45 downwind earlier. Fortunately, he was lower than me (which was odd because I was at pattern altitude), and he appeared to take action to stay clear of me coming up behind by descending even further and veering to the right. I passed the C-172 above and to the left, but it seems we both got a little closer than we should have. The C-172 asked if I saw him, and I acknowledged I did, under the belief he was taking evasive action to keep us separated. I continued on to turn base and then final for a full stop on XX.Though separation existed, it was closer than needed be. I thought by performing a loop, I provided adequate time and distance for all in the pattern, but in hindsight, given the pattern was busy I should have left the pattern entirely and rejoined when spacing was favorable. I also should not have assumed the C-172 had remained clear of my flight path.
ASRS:1844394.s: The pilot reported a close call with a C-172 on the downwind leg while operating in a busy traffic pattern at Runway XX. The pilot attributed the proximity to assuming the C-172 remained clear after a right-hand loop, noting the other aircraft descended and veered right to maintain separation.
